The following information pertains to the use of Convallaria majalis (commonly known as Lily of the Valley, Jacob's Ladder, May Bells, or May Lily) in medical contexts, including its dosing, interactions, contraindications, and safety considerations: Dosing Information: Oral Administration (PO): Average dose: 600 mg/day. Tincture: Up to 6 g/day, divided into three doses (TID). Liquid extract: 600 mg/day, divided into three doses (TID). Dried extract: 150 mg/day. Indications: This plant is traditionally used for conditions such as circulatory disorders, heart palpitations, arrhythmias, congestive heart failure (CHF), cardiac edema, cardiac asthma, kidney and bladder stones, and urinary tract infections (UTIs). It contains cardiac glycosides similar to those found in digitalis. Drug Interactions: 1. Severe Interactions: Digoxin: Co-administration is contraindicated due to pharmacodynamic synergism, which can increase toxicity. 2. Moderate Interactions (Monitor Closely): Diuretics (e.g., bendroflumethiazide, bumetanide, chlorothiazide, chlorthalidone, cyclopenthiazide, ethacrynic acid, furosemide, hydrochlorothiazide, indapamide, methyclothiazide, metolazone, torsemide, and senna): These increase the risk of cardiac toxicity due to potassium depletion (K+ depletion). Caution and close monitoring are advised. 3. Minor Interactions (Significance Unknown): Beta-blockers (e.g., acebutolol, propranolol, esmolol): May increase toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergism. Antiarrhythmics (e.g., amiodarone, disopyramide, encainide, flecainide, ibutilide, lidocaine, mexiletine, procainamide, propafenone, quinidine, sotalol): Potential for increased toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergism. Calcium salts (e.g., calcium acetate, calcium carbonate, calcium chloride, calcium citrate, calcium gluconate): May enhance the effects of Lily of the Valley through an unspecified mechanism. Other agents (e.g., adenosine, diltiazem, verapamil): May increase toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergism. Contraindications: Pregnancy and Lactation: Pregnancy: Use only under qualified supervision, as overdosing can be fatal. Overdose symptoms include nausea, vomiting, headache, stupor, visual disturbances (e.g., color perception disorders), and irregular heartbeat. It is generally advised to avoid use during pregnancy. Lactation: No data available. Safety Considerations: Taking more than the recommended dose can lead to serious side effects, including nausea, vomiting, headache, stupor, visual disturbances, and irregular heart rhythms. The plant is potentially fatal if overdosed. Cost and Availability: Information on cost and availability is not provided. This information highlights the importance of cautious use of Convallaria majalis due to its potential for significant toxicity and interactions with other medications. It should only be used under the guidance of a qualified healthcare provider.
[Human papillomavirus (HPV) self‐sampling to encourage the uptake of cervical screening] [Objectives]This is a protocol for a Cochrane Review (intervention). The objectives are as follows:To assess the effect of inviting women to take a self‐sampling test compared to the effect of inviting or reminding women to undergo conventional cervical screening.[Description of the condition]Cervical cancer is the fourth most common cancer and the fourth leading cause of cancer death amongst women worldwide, with an estimated 570,000 new cases and 311,000 deaths in 2018 (GLOBOCAN 2018). Cervical cancer is more common in young women, particularly in those aged 25 to 45 years (GLOBOCAN 2018). A woman's risk of developing cervical cancer by age 65 years ranges from 0.8% in high‐income countries to 1.5% in low‐income countries, and more than 85% of all cervical cancer deaths occur in low‐ and middle‐income countries (GLOBOCAN 2018). The large geographical variation in cervical cancer rates and survival correlates with the availability of primary and secondary prevention strategies, as well as the prevalence of high‐risk human papillomavirus (hrHPV) infection.Nearly all cases of cervical cancer are due to a persistent infection with hrHPV. To date, more than 100 types of HPV have been identified, of which 14 are classified as hrHPV. Nearly 75% of all cervical cancers or precancers are associated with human papillomavirus (HPV)16 and HPV18 in all world regions except Asia (IARC 2014;Li 2011). In Western/Central Asia, 82% of invasive cervical cancer is HPV16/18‐associated, compared to only 68% in Eastern Asia (Li 2011).Early cervical cancer is often asymptomatic. In cases with a symptomatic presentation, abnormal vaginal bleeding, particularly post‐coital bleeding, is the most common symptom. Advanced disease can also be associated with dyspareunia, pelvic pain, vaginal discharge, and non‐specific symptoms such as changes in urinary or bowel habit and weight loss (Principles and Practice of Oncology 2019). The finding of cervical abnormalities during screening or in the presence of symptoms may lead to a colposcopy examination and collection of tissue biopsies for histological diagnosis.Cervical cancer management strategies vary around the world and depend on the grade and stage of disease, together with the prevailing national resources and health care policies. Survival decreases with increasing age (ONS 2015). In Europe and the USA, the five‐year survival rate is between 63% and 72% (CONCORD 3;Jemal 2008), while in Taiwan, Korea and Japan, the five‐year survival rate is between 70% and 77.3% (CONCORD 3).Prevention of cervical cancer is based on strategies for reducing known risk factors (primary prevention) and the early identification and treatment of pre‐invasive disease (secondary prevention).Available evidence suggests that persistent infection with hrHPV is the most important primary cause of cancer of the cervix, with studies estimating the world‐wide HPV prevalence in cervical cancers to be 99.7% (Walboomers 1999;Wentzensen 2017). Other known risk factors for cervical cancer include smoking (Brinton 1986;Bosch 2011), early age at first sexual intercourse, multiple sexual partners, the presence of other sexually transmitted diseases (STDs;La Vecchia 1986;Mitra 2016), and a compromised immune status (Schneider 1983;Stanley 2015). Individuals who receive immunosuppressive therapy for organ transplants and those infected with HIV are therefore at a higher risk of developing pre‐invasive disease. Primary strategies to prevent the development of cervical cancer focus on reducing these known risk factors through vaccination and encouraging smoking cessation and adoption of 'safer' sexual behaviours (Shepherd 2011).The best intervention for the primary prevention of cervical cancer is prophylactic HPV immunisation before exposure to HPV. HPV vaccines are made from the viral capsid (coat) proteins that self‐assemble to make virus‐like particles (VLPs); these proteins are non‐infectious, as they are effectively empty shells that do not contain any viral DNA. Four HPV vaccines have been developed that contain VLPs for one or more hrHPVs: the monovalent (HPV16), bivalent (HPV16 and 18), quadrivalent (HPV16 and 18 plus HPV6 and 11 (non‐hrHPVs that cause genital warts)), and nonavalent vaccine (HPV6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, and 58). All except the monovalent vaccine are licenced for use. The vaccines promote the development of an immune system response, mediated by the production of antibodies against hrHPV. The mechanism of the cancer‐preventive effect of HPV vaccines lies in the prevention of the persistent hrHPV infections that lead to high‐grade cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) and adenocarcinoma‐in‐situ (AIS), precancerous conditions that can progress to cervical cancer (Schiffman 2011).The three‐dose schedules of the monovalent, bivalent, and quadrivalent vaccine have shown effectiveness against precancerous conditions and persistent hrHPV infections in girls and women aged 15 to 26 years, with no increase in serious adverse events (Arbyn 2018a). After five to eight years of vaccination, the prevalence of HPV 16 and 18 decreased by 83% in girls aged 13 to 19 years, and by 66% in women aged 20 to 24 years; this constitutes compelling evidence in support of the vaccines' effectiveness (Drolet 2019). One study published in 2020 demonstrated a significant reduction in the incidence of cervical cancer in a population with high HPV vaccine uptake, especially in those vaccinated as younger adolescents (Lei 2020).The systematic review by Bergman and colleagues highlighted that two‐dose regimens of the bivalent, quadrivalent, and nonavalent vaccines each provided equivalent immunity compared to the three‐dose regimens, with stronger antibody response when the interval between the two vaccine doses was between six and 12 months (Bergman 2019).The quadrivalent vaccine offers similar protection compared to the nonavalent vaccine in reducing the incidence of the combined outcome of high‐grade CIN, AIS, and cervical cancer in females and males aged nine to 26 years (Bergman 2019). Furthermore, the quadrivalent vaccine showed a decreased incidence of external genital lesions amongst boys aged 10 to 26 years (Bergman 2019).Many countries have rolled out HPV immunisation programmes. In the UK, HPV vaccination has become part of the routine schedule of vaccination in boys and girls between the ages of nine and 13 years.Vaccines provide protection against hrHPV infection in individuals who are naive to the viruses, but are ineffective in individuals with pre‐existing HPV infection, who will remain at risk of developing cervical cancer. For these reasons, secondary prevention methods, such as screening for hrHPV nucleic acids and for abnormal or precancerous cell changes, remain the mainstay of efforts to reduce cervical cancer risks.The objective of cervical screening is to detect and treat precancerous changes early. More than 90% of cellular abnormalities occur in a small area of the cervix called the transformation zone. Because the disease progresses slowly, there is time to detect and treat precancerous lesions before they become an invasive cancer. Conventional cervical screening involves the Papanicolaou (or Pap smear or smear) test (IARC 2014;Sankaranarayanan 2001); it is aimed at women in the 25‐ to 65‐year age bracket and has been available for many years. During conventional cervical screening, a healthcare professional uses a speculum to visualise the cervix and collect cells from the transformation zone, which they then spread onto a slide. The cells are examined in the laboratory for cytological changes. Guidelines and recommendations vary from country to country, but in most cases, screening is recommended every one to five years.The quality of the Pap smear test depends on accurate specimen sampling and preparation. The test result is considered inadequate if the cervical sample contains an insufficient number of cells, is not representative of the transformation zone, or is obscured by inflammatory cells, blood, or mucus (NICE 2003). Up to 10% of Pap smear test results are classified as inadequate and cannot be interpreted, leading to repeated smears and a consequent increase in burden on the healthcare system and on women (Sherlaw‐Johnson 2004).An alternative method, called liquid‐based cytology (LBC), was developed in an attempt to improve the diagnostic reliability of the Pap smear test. Unlike the conventional smear, where cells are spread directly onto a slide, LBC involves transferring the cervical sample into a small vial containing a fixative solution, where blood and any other obscuring material can be separated. Following centrifugation, a thin layer of cells is spread onto a slide for cytological examination. Studies have found LBC to be a reliable and cost‐effective technique (when performed by trained individuals with appropriate quality control in place), with superior sensitivity and lower rates of inadequate samples compared to Pap smear (Karnon 2003;Moss 2003). LBC became the standard technique for cervical screening in the UK in 2008 (NHS 2010).In high‐income settings, the introduction of national cervical screening programmes has successfully reduced cervical cancer incidence and mortality (Elfstrom 2015;Vaccarella 2013). Unfortunately, there is a marked disparity between high‐income countries and low‐ and middle‐income countries regarding the availability of standard screening tests and adequate funding for national screening programme implementation (Randall 2016). While more than 80% of high‐income countries have cervical cancer policies and strategies in place, cervical cytology is generally available in approximately 35% of countries in the African Region (WHO 2020). In view of this, it is not surprising that 85% of cervical cancer cases and deaths occur in low‐ and middle‐income countries (Randall 2016;La Vigne 2017).Furthermore, socioeconomic status, ethnic origin, age, and education are all factors that affect the uptake of screening. Studies have found lower uptake rates in women who are older, less well‐educated, from lower socioeconomic groups, and resident in rural locations (Denny 2006;Lim 2017;NHS England 2019). In addition, there are lower reported rates of cervical screening uptake in certain ethnic groups, including African‐American, Hispanic, and Native American women in the USA, and Asian women in the UK (Luke 1996). For this reason, it is important to develop interventions to encourage the uptake of screening, taking into account these wider sociodemographic factors, as well as available resources.Conventional screening is now undergoing a conceptual change with the introduction of primary hrHPV testing as a method of secondary cervical cancer prevention. This involves testing the screening sample for the presence or absence of hrHPV. If hrHPV is not detected, the woman will be offered routine screening again in three to five years, depending on her age. If hrHPV is detected, cytological analysis is performed on the sample to assess whether precancerous changes have developed and, if required, a colposcopy examination is offered (NHS CSP 2020). This stems from the fact that infection with HPV is found in over 99% of cervical carcinomas worldwide, with the hrHPV types 16 and 18 being the most prevalent, and HPV‐negative cervical cancers are extremely rare (Walboomers 1999;Li 2011). Therefore, if a woman does not have HPV infection, her risk of cervical cancer is negligible.Research has shown that hrHPV testing has a higher sensitivity for high‐grade lesions compared to cytology (Koliopoulos 2017), but a lower specificity, which may lead to a rise in colposcopy referrals and an additional burden in terms of the cost and resources needed to provide this service, particularly in middle‐ and low‐income countries (Meijer 2012). Nevertheless, a negative hrHPV test is more reassuring than a negative cytological test, as it is less likely to be a false negative (Koliopoulos 2017).When a clinician performs hrHPV testing, they use the LBC sample collected when the woman attends for cervical screening. However, women can also perform this test on themselves. Self‐collection does not require a pelvic exam; the woman uses a swab or soft brush to collect a vaginal sample. Analysis of the sample involves the use of polymerase chain reaction (PCR)‐based or signal amplification (SA)‐based assays. Results of test accuracy studies of vaginal self‐samples versus clinician samples vary according to the type of assay used. PCR‐based assays appear to be superior to SA‐based assays: the sensitivity of hrHPV tests for detection of CIN2+ or CIN3+ is similar for self‐collected samples and clinician‐collected samples, whilst the sensitivity is inferior for self‐samples when analysed with SA‐based assays (Arbyn 2018b). Moreover, it is possible to use a dry swab for HPV self‐sampling, with no difference in the detection of hrHPV. This is an added advantage, as it implies a lower risk of spillage of the transport medium or accidental consumption of the transport medium (containing harmful chemicals such as sodium azide) by a child at home (Jun 2016;Wolfrum 2012). For all these reasons, hrHPV self‐sampling is highly acceptable to women and could help to improve screening uptake (Madzima 2017;Nelson 2017).While the benefits of self‐sampling are seemingly clear in terms of increasing uptake without any apparent reduction in disease detection, one downside to this approach is that women in whom HPV is detected have to attend a follow‐up visit for LBC (the current accepted triage test). However, as we understand more about the molecular biology of HPV, together with the advances made in hypermethylation detection/hrHPV genotyping and its correlation with disease state, there is scope for applying such methodologies as the triage test on the same self‐sample (De Strooper 2016;Del Mistro 2017). The introduction of a combined self‐sampled screening and triage test would likely increase test rates in low‐ and middle‐income countries, where the lack of adequately trained cytopathologists and suitable infrastructure hinders the implementation of expertise‐heavy techniques. By using self‐sampling combined with a molecular‐based triage test, healthcare decision‐makers could centralise the process of detecting high‐risk women as part of a system similar to that of primary HPV screening in the UK.One major obstacle to the success of cervical screening worldwide is the uptake of the programme by women, which remains stubbornly low. Uptake rates are 72% in the UK and 81% in the USA (Hall 2018;NHS England 2019). In Asia, the numbers are even lower, with uptake rates of 67% in South Korea and 42% in Japan (Cancer Stat Japan 2019;Suh 2016). The Cochrane Review by Everett and colleagues found evidence to support the use of invitation letters to increase the uptake of cervical screening and limited evidence to support educational interventions, although it was unclear which intervention format was most effective (Everett 2011). Most published studies are from high‐income countries, so the relevance of their findings to low‐income countries is unclear. Before healthcare decision‐makers adopt hrHPV self‐sampling within their cervical screening strategy, they need evidence on different delivery strategies and on the impact of uptake.Since the 1980s, cervical cancer incidence rates have decreased for all ages worldwide by as much as 65%, particularly in countries with long‐established screening programmes (GLOBOCAN 2018;Jemal 2010). However, there has not been a similar decrease in women from socially deprived groups (Dos Santos 1997), and incidence rates amongst younger generations have increased in several countries, which may reflect increases in hrHPV prevalence and changing sexual practices (Bray 2005).Research has shown that cervical screening is effective for reducing cervical cancer incidence and mortality (Arbyn 2020;NCIN 2020), but the success of organised screening worldwide is strictly dependent on the programme's coverage. Therefore, researchers have made great efforts to understand factors that lead to poor uptake, such as cost, anxiety, embarrassment, and the stigma of disease.Women from ethnic minorities and deprived subgroups in the population have shown consistently lower uptake over decades of screening worldwide (Moser 2009;Webb 2004). This may be attributable to lower health literacy, especially since screening literature can include complex concepts. Because hrHPV is transmitted sexually, screening and cervical cancer itself can be perceived as a consequence of promiscuity and thus have negative connotations. Encouragingly, in a survey of Muslim Turkish women who mostly considered talking about sex as taboo, most respondents felt that recommendations from health workers had encouraged them more than any other factor to attend screening and accept HPV vaccination for their daughters (Ilter 2010).Given the complex nature of the factors involved, there have been many interventions based on theoretical models of health behaviour, such as the Health Belief Model (Kreuter 1996;Marcus 1992), and the Trans Theoretical Model (Rimer 1999). It is important to acknowledge that interventions that are effective in one setting may be less effective in another.hrHPV self‐sampling could change women's attitudes to screening. By removing practical obstacles (inconvenient clinic hours, transport to clinic, childcare issues) and personal‐level factors (e.g. embarrassment, fear of pain or social judgement), hrHPV self‐sampling may facilitate and encourage screening uptake. There is evidence to suggest that offering hrHPV self‐sampling may lead to higher rates of screening participation compared to a reminder invitation for cytology (Racey 2013;Verdoodt 2015), and mailing the self‐sampling kit appears to offer higher population coverage than opt‐in strategies (where women are sent the self‐sampler only if they agree;Broberg 2014;Giorgi 2011). Furthermore, the diagnostic accuracy of self‐collected samples analysed with PCR assays is comparable to that of clinician‐collected samples (Arbyn 2014;Arbyn 2018b).However, there is considerable heterogeneity between studies, and there is a need for further research into how hrHPV self‐sampling could work in practice and how it would impact on screening uptake in the non‐attenders group. In addition, primary HPV testing cannot discriminate between transient and clinically significant hrHPV infections, and women with a positive result need a triage assessment for the presence or absence of cervical lesions. At present, the recommended triage is by cytology, which is less effective on self‐collected samples (Arbyn 2015;Garcia 2003). Consequently, these women would need to attend an outpatient appointment for a cervical smear, with the consequent risk of loss to follow‐up. Different studies have investigated alternative triage strategies, including repeated self‐sampling and molecular methods, but these strategies require further validation (Castle 2011;De Strooper 2016;Gustavsson 2018;Luttmer 2016).Cervical cancer incidence decreases with increasing frequency of screening: by 93.5% in women who attend a screening appointment every year and have approximately 50 smear tests in their lifetime, 92.5% for those who attend every two years and have 25 tests, 90.8% for those who attend every three years and have 16 tests, 83.6% for those who attend every five years and have 10 tests, and 64.1% for those who attend every 10 years and have five tests (IARC 1986). Modelling analyses have shown that extending the re‐screening interval from every year to every three years results in an average excess risk of about 3 per 100,000 (Sawaya 2003). For this reason, in the UK, women aged 25 to 50 years are invited for screening every three years, and those aged 50 to 64 years are invited every five years. Each year, around 3.5 million women accept screening (NHS England 2019), and this response has prevented up to 3900 cases of cervical cancer annually in the UK (Peto 2004;Sasieni 1996;Sasieni 2018). However, despite its effectiveness, the uptake rate of cervical screening by eligible women is still only 75% in the UK (NHS England 2019). Globally, 65% of countries have introduced national cervical screening programmes. Amongst them, only 12% have achieved an uptake above 70% (WHO 2020).Several studies have shown that primary screening for hrHPV followed by cytology triage of HPV‐positive women (aged 30 years or older) is more effective than cytology‐based screening (Arbyn 2012;Koliopoulos 2017;Ogilvie 2018). In 2016, the UK National Screening Committee recommended that the National Health Service (NHS) Cervical Screening Programme adopt testing for hrHPV as the primary strategy, and as of December 2019, primary hrHPV screening has been fully rolled out and is being offered across England as part of the NHS Cervical Screening Programme (NHS CSP 2020).As information is needed to establish what can be done to increase screening uptake rate, it is important to assess if hrHPV self‐sampling could be an effective strategy.[Description of the condition]Cervical cancer is the fourth most common cancer and the fourth leading cause of cancer death amongst women worldwide, with an estimated 570,000 new cases and 311,000 deaths in 2018 (GLOBOCAN 2018). [Heliox for prevention of morbidity and mortality in ventilated newborn infants] [Objectives]This is a protocol for a Cochrane Review (intervention). The objectives are as follows:To determine the effect of heliox on the rates of mortality, neurodevelopmental outcome, and chronic lung disease in invasively ventilated infants.[Description of the condition]Helium, used in combination with oxygen (heliox), facilitates laminar flow in the airways, and offers less resistance to flow due to its low density (one‐seventh the density of nitrogen (Morgan 2014)). Heliox decreases the pressure and work of breathing to ventilate the lung, and may be a useful adjunct in the management of people with airway obstruction, respiratory syncytial virus bronchiolitis, and respiratory distress (Martinon‐Torres 2012).Respiratory distress syndrome is the commonest form of respiratory disease in premature neonates, and correlates with structural and functional pulmonary immaturity (Bancalari 2012). The term refers to preterm neonates with oxygen or respiratory support requirements after delivery (Gomella 2020). Bronchopulmonary dysplasia, or chronic lung disease, describes the ongoing requirement for oxygen or respiratory support at 36 weeks' corrected gestational age (Jobe 2001). Mainstays of treatment include oxygen supplementation and ventilation, both invasive and non‐invasive (Sweet 2019). Prolonged mechanical ventilation is associated with increased incidence of chronic lung disease, neurodevelopmental delay, and death (Jobe 1998;Nowadsky 2009). The advent of antenatal steroids, surfactant, and continuous positive airway pressure have improved respiratory outcomes, but further decreasing the duration of ventilation and inflammatory changes may improve neonatal outcomes (Dani 2016;Lopez 2013). In addition, minimising oxygen toxicity and the work of breathing using helium‐oxygen rather than nitrogen‐oxygen may allow the use of lower oxygen concentrations, reducing oxidative damage (Schulzke 2010).Routinely, supplemental oxygen is delivered as an air‐oxygen mixture. However, there are theoretical benefits of using a helium‐oxygen mixture as an alternative to air‐oxygen mixtures for respiratory support. Helium was first discovered by Janssen and Lockyer in 1868 (Kean 2021). It is a colourless, odourless, noble gas that does not react with biological tissues or compounds. Since helium is non‐toxic and biologically inert, it can safely be mixed with oxygen. The helium‐oxygen mixture may be superior to an air‐oxygen mixture. This systematic review will concentrate on the combination of helium and oxygen, known as heliox.The composition of air is 21% oxygen, 79% nitrogen, and trace amounts of other gases. Heliox is a mixture of 21% oxygen and 79% helium, which is lighter than air or oxygen. Carbon dioxide diffuses more rapidly through a helium‐oxygen mixture (heliox) than through a nitrogen‐oxygen mixture. When supplemental oxygen is inspired, there is a reciprocal effect on inspired nitrogen concentration. The higher the concentration of helium, the lower the fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2), and the less dense the gas mixture. Therefore, the major impediment to heliox’s use is hypoxia, because of the limited FiO2of 40% that can be achieved, due to a high concentration of helium versus oxygen. Generally, heliox is available in mixtures of 80% oxygen and 20% helium (80:20 heliox) or 70% oxygen and 30% helium (70:30 heliox); however, heliox can be blended with other gases (Hess 2006).Heliox has a similar viscosity to air but a significantly lower density. Flow of gas through the airway comprises laminar flow, transitional flow, and turbulent flow. The tendency for each type of flow is described by the Reynolds number, a dimensionless number used to determine the likelihood that a gas will develop a laminar or turbulent flow pattern. Heliox's low density produces a lower Reynolds number, and hence, a higher probability of laminar flow for any given airway. Laminar flow tends to generate less resistance than turbulent flow. Heliox generates less airway resistance than air, and thereby, requires less mechanical energy to ventilate the lungs. It does this by two mechanisms: (a) increased tendency to laminar flow; heliox facilitates laminar flow in the airways and offers less resistance to flow due to its low density (one‐seventh that of nitrogen), and (b) reduced resistance in turbulent flow; heliox is less likely to generate turbulent, inefficient flow in situations where airway size is reduced, such as the constricted airways seen in asthma. Indeed, helium‐oxygen gas mixtures have been used in the management of human respiratory disorders, such as asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, since 1935 (Barach 1935). Methods of administration have progressed, and heliox can now be delivered by several routes, including ventilator, incubator, nasal prongs, and head box (Myers 2003;Singhaus 2006).Animal models have shown evidence to support the use of, and effects of heliox. Long‐term heliox incubator exposure has been shown to be safe in a randomised controlled trial of neonatal rabbits. There were no differences in growth parameters between those rabbits nursed in heliox versus rabbits nursed in air (Singhaus 2007). In neonatal pigs, heliox was found to reduce tidal volumes with a concomitant therapeutic benefit of attenuating lung inflammation, by reducing mechanical and oxidative stress in the clinical management of acute lung injury (Nawab 2005). A study on ventilated rats showed that neutrophil infiltration, interstitial oedema and intra‐alveolar oedema were all reduced in the group treated with heliox when compared to the control group (Yilmaz 2013).Beneficial effects have been observed in adults and children with asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, bronchiolitis, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, and upper airway obstruction (Chevrolet 2001). In adults, the use of helium in the immediate post‐extubation period decreases inspiratory effort and improves comfort (Jaber 2001). In children, heliox has been described as a potentially useful adjunct in the management of children with airway obstruction (Myers 2003). In a consecutive series of children with acute upper airway obstruction, heliox reduced the need for intubation (Connolly 2001). However, although it has been shown to improve clinical scores in infants and children with upper and lower airway respiratory insufficiency, it did not obviate the need for non‐invasive or invasive mechanical ventilation (Iglesias‐Fern 2007).The properties of heliox provide advantages in situations where there is reduced airway size, as seen in the small airways of premature infants (Jolliet 2003). A pilot time‐series study showed heliox to be well tolerated in mechanically ventilated newborns with broncho pulmonary dysplasia (Szczapa 2014), and in neonates with meconium aspiration syndrome (Szczapa 2011). A multicentre, randomised, blinded controlled trial of 319 infants with bronchiolitis, showed that heliox was effective if delivered via a tight‐fitting, non‐rebreathing face mask or continuous positive airway pressure, but not via a nasal cannula at conventional flow rates (Chowdhury 2013).The practicalities of administering heliox therapy remained a significant barrier to both its use in NICU, and to studying its effectiveness in high‐powered randomised controlled trials (RCTs). Previously, one of the main issues was equipment, and methods to safely deliver the helium‐oxygen mix. With modern ventilators, this barrier has reduced, but the cost impact remains significant. In the USA, heliox is estimated to cost approximately 20% to 40% more than medical oxygen, which would usually account for less than 1% of the total NICU costs. When the authors looked internationally, this estimated increase in costs was significantly higher, for example, an increase in spending of more than 20‐fold compared to basic oxygen. (Szczapa 2022).[How the intervention might work]Heliox has been used in infant studies for the treatment of respiratory syncytial virus bronchiolitis (Cambonie 2006;Chowdhury 2013;Gross 2000;Martinon‐Torres 2003a;Panitch 2003), and respiratory distress (Elleau 1993), with variable success. [Interventions for improving adherence to amblyopia treatments in children] [Objectives]This is a protocol for a Cochrane Review (intervention). The objectives are as follows:To assess the efficacy and harms of various behavioral interventions, such as educational and reward systems, for improving children's objective adherence to amblyopia treatments.Secondary objective: to assess the subsequent treatment effects of improved adherence to amblyopia treatments and qualitatively explore equity and social determinants of health as factors affecting adherence.[Description of the condition]Amblyopia, commonly referred to as 'lazy eye', is a neurodevelopmental disorder that results from the abnormal processing of visual images in which the best‐corrected vision in one or, less often, both eyes is reduced in the absence of ocular disease (Cruz 2022). This condition is classified by cause and can be unilateral or bilateral. Causes of unilateral amblyopia include anisometropia (unequal refractive error between the eyes), strabismus (misalignment of the eyes), visual deprivation (e.g. cataract or ptosis), and/or mixed mechanism (more than one type, typically anisometropia and strabismus). Causes of bilateral amblyopia include significant isoametropia (high degree of refractive error in both eyes) and, much less commonly, bilateral visual deprivation. If one of these conditions is present to disrupt the child’s visual experience during the critical period of visual development from birth to six to eight years of age, amblyopia may develop.Amblyopia is a common cause of reduced vision in infants and young children, affecting 2% to 5% of the population (Chen 2016;Fu 2020;Hassan 2018;NEI 2022;Rouse 2004;Webber 2005). An increased prevalence has been reported in populations with lower socioeconomic status, with lower cognitive function, of Hispanic/Latinx ethnicity, and immigrant status (Fu 2020;Nitzan 2021). Meridional amblyopia affects the Hispanic/Latinx community at a higher rate, and the lack of timely treatment of bilateral amblyopia affects vision potential and perpetuates health disparities (MEPEDS 2008;Varma 2017).The incidence of amblyopia globally is 1% to 5% (Hu 2022). Based on a 2022 meta‐analysis by Hu and colleagues, countries in Africa, such as Nigeria and Egypt, have a prevalence of around 0.38%, whereas countries in Europe, such as Sweden and Spain, have a prevalence of around 2.7%. There appears to be a slight predilection towards males, and this appears to be unrelated to geographical location, economic status, or age (Hu 2022). Another meta‐analysis reported similar findings of increased prevalence in Europe and North America (Fu 2020). Additionally, in terms of ethnicity, the highest prevalence is in the Hispanic population, followed by Europeans, Africans, and Asians (Hu 2022).Diagnosis of amblyopia is often based on the interocular difference of best‐corrected visual acuity and amblyogenic factors (anisometropia, strabismus, combination of two conditions, deprivation) (Cruz 2022). However, amblyopia is typically associated with other conditions, such as binocular vision disorders (e.g. interocular suppression and poor stereopsis), as well as accommodative and oculomotor dysfunctions (Ghasia 2022).Amblyopia has been linked with poor performance on everyday vision‐reliant tasks involving fine motor coordination, such as writing (Bhutada 2022;Chen 2018;Grant 2011;Grant 2014;Kanonidou 2010;Kelly 2017;Kelly 2020;Niechwiej‐Szwedo 2010;Niechwiej‐Szwedo 2019) reading (Bhutada 2022;Kanonidou 2010;Kelly 2017), and visual search tasks (Chen 2018). Thus, amblyopia often has a lifelong impact on children's academic and physical abilities, with adverse psychosocial effects (Carlton 2011a;Carlton 2011b;Holmes 2003).The initial treatment for many forms of amblyopia is full‐time optical correction. However, additional treatments are often required. Historically, these include penalization of the fellow eye (e.g. patching, 1% atropine, or Bangerter filter). More recently, dichoptic treatments, utilizing a computer or tablet to display treatment software, have been explored as another viable treatment option (Levi 2020).Amblyopia treatment has been shown to be more effective in children under seven years of age compared with those aged seven to 12 years (Holmes 2011), although it can still be effective into the teenage years (PEDIG 2005). The success rates for amblyopia treatment using patching or atropine can be quite high (50% to 80%), with success being defined by visual acuity at study completion as either (1) at least 20/25 or better; or (2) better than or equal to that of the sound eye (Chen 2016;Repka 2004;Repka 2009a;Repka 2009b). But given the long‐term nature of amblyopia treatments, varying from months to years, the success of spectacles, patching, atropine, and binocular treatments is often limited by poor adherence (Levi 2020;Maconachie 2016;Wang 2015). Poor adherence to treatment may result in reduced treatment efficacy, limiting visual improvement and increasing the burden of visual function deficits.There are important public health consequences when amblyopia is left untreated; therefore, methods to improve adherence are essential. Untreated amblyopia can negatively impact school performance, self‐esteem, employment prospects, functional skills, quality of life, future social interactions, and overall risk of blindness (Birch 2019;Birch 2020;Carlton 2011a;Carlton 2011b;Hatt 2020;Rahi 2002;Tommilla 1981). Furthermore, vision loss, often from trauma, in the sound eye can impact quality of life and employment status if the impairment causes inadequate visual function (Rahi 2002;Tommilla 1981). Unfortunately, people with amblyopia have an increased risk of their sound eye becoming visually impaired, with the estimated lifetime risk of visual impairment being at least 1.2% to 3.3% (Rahi 2002). Improving adherence to amblyopia treatment could have a positive long‐term impact on visual function and quality of life.Adherence is critical for the successful treatment of amblyopia, particularly with patching (Stewart 2004;Wang 2015). Amblyopia treatment adherence is measured using subjective and objective methods. Commonly used subjective methods include caregiver‐reported adherence, as well as calendars, logs, or diaries filled out by the participant's caregiver (PEDIG 2002). Subjective methods are limited by caregiver forgetfulness and recall bias, in which the caregiver reports greater adherence than was actually achieved. However, these subjective methods are still commonly employed due to their low cost and ease of implementation.Objective methods of measuring adherence to amblyopia treatments vary depending on the type of treatment. For glasses/spectacle wearing, an objective method of adherence includes a type of sensor to track spectacle wearing (Maconachie 2016;South 2021). Similarly, during patching, occlusion dose monitors (ODMs) are a well‐known method for tracking adherence. These devices are able to track patching time based on sensing temperature contact with skin. This method of tracking adherence using an ODM has been utilized in many amblyopia studies (Stewart 2004). For atropine penalization (which entails the instillation of 1% atropine eye drops twice‐weekly into the sound eye), some have measured adherence indirectly using objective clinical findings, such as dynamic retinoscopy (Tejedor 2008) and pupil size (Foley‐Nolan 1997). Research studies outside of amblyopia have described eye drop bottles with dose‐use tracking devices, but this has not been utilized in amblyopia treatment research (Tapply 2021). Objective adherence to dichoptic treatment (where different stimuli are displayed to each eye) is measured by using a timer on the device.There are multiple reasons to focus on objective measures of treatment adherence. First, quantitative, objective adherence data are more precise than qualitative, subjective adherence data. Whereas subjective adherence is often estimated to the hour, or half‐hour, an objective measure of adherence, such as ODMs, can provide estimates as precisely as 5‐minute intervals, while computer logs can measure adherence to the nearest second (Januschowski 2013;Wang 2020;Xiao 2022). Second, previous patching studies have found that subjective diary data are often better matched to the prescribed regimen than the objective adherence assessed by an ODM (Fielder 1995), which suggests a biased assessment. Third, objective data are often reported electronically and provide data more reliably.Researchers have used a number of treatment modifications to improve adherence. These include educational cartoons, reward systems, and more engaging therapy techniques, such as video and virtual reality games. The assumption is that improved adherence to the amblyopia treatment will lead to improved treatment effectiveness. This assumption, however, has not been well‐studied. In addition, the effectiveness of interventions designed to improve adherence remains unknown.To improve adherence, behavioral interventions such as educational cartoons, reward systems, and caregiver educational pamphlets have been studied (Tjiam 2013;Tjiam 2016;Wang 2015). Educational pamphlets have been used to increase caregiver health literacy, which in turn may improve adherence outcomes. Other pediatric healthcare disciplines have described an increase in adherence when interventions are focused on family education (Uhl 2021;Yang 2018). Reward stickers and educational cartoon stories have also been designed to target children (Tjiam 2012;Tjiam 2013;Tjiam 2016).For recent new dichoptic treatments, novel and engaging stimuli, such as video games, movies, and virtual reality, have been employed to increase the engagement and motivation of children to improve adherence (Birch 2021;Falcone 2021;Levi 2020;Quoc 2023). However, the impact of these interventions on adherence to amblyopia treatment, and subsequent visual outcomes, remains poorly understood.A variety of studies have examined whether factors intrinsic to participants’ amblyopia and its treatment are associated with increased or decreased adherence, including age, gender, amblyopia type, severity, and treatment assigned (Le 2022). While many of these factors have mixed results, factors such as increased hours of prescribed patching may lead to decreased adherence (Stewart 2004). There are other factors, such as socioeconomic status (Tjiam 2012), psychological components (Loudon 2009), and health literacy (Loudon 2006;Newsham 2002), which also play a role in individuals' adherence. These numerous variables contribute to the challenges of measuring adherence.While we have well‐established treatments for amblyopia, a lack of adherence may negatively affect the duration of therapy and its effectiveness. Adherence may be one of the main determinants of success since it directly relates to treatment outcomes and duration. In turn, this affects healthcare resources (Carlton 2011b). When a participant fails to respond to amblyopia treatment, the provider looks at different factors that may contribute to this lack of response, including adherence as a highly probable cause. It is well‐documented that treatment is more effective when implemented earlier in life. However, treatment effectiveness – whether treatment consists of refractive correction, penalization of the better‐seeing eye, or dichoptic treatments – is largely limited by poor adherence (Newsham 2000;Newsham 2002). A Cochrane Review from 2019 compared conventional patching to pharmacologic penalization for amblyopia. While adherence between the two methods was discussed, interventions to improve adherence were not mentioned (Li 2019).The systematic review aims to investigate the effectiveness of different behavioral interventions in improving objectively‐measured treatment adherence. This review has the potential to provide evidence‐based guidance on which behavioral interventions are more effective. Understanding which interventions can reliably improve adherence to amblyopia treatment may help improve the effectiveness of amblyopia treatment. Improved adherence to treatment can also lessen the burden of amblyopia on pediatric and adult populations and save valuable healthcare resources. Furthermore, this review can guide future research in developing novel stimuli that can reliably improve adherence to treatment. [Invasive management for patent ductus arteriosus in preterm infants] [Objectives]This is a protocol for a Cochrane Review (intervention). The objectives are as follows:Primary objective: to assess the effectiveness and safety of invasive PDA closure strategies in preterm infants compared to medical management (pharmacotherapy or conservative) or no treatment.Secondary objective:to analyse subgroups based on the following.Postnatal age at intervention (less than four weeks versus late rescue)Initial mode of treatment versus after failed medical management (based on courses and timing of pharmacotherapy)Invasive closure following primary pharmacotherapy versus repeat pharmacotherapyWithin seven days versus after seven daysTCPC coil versus occluderGestational age (< 32 weeks versus 32 to 36 weeks)Birth weight (< 1500 g or < 1000 g)Weight at the time of the procedure (< 1000 g or > 1000 g)Postnatal age at intervention (less than four weeks versus late rescue)Initial mode of treatment versus after failed medical management (based on courses and timing of pharmacotherapy)Invasive closure following primary pharmacotherapy versus repeat pharmacotherapyWithin seven days versus after seven daysTCPC coil versus occluderGestational age (< 32 weeks versus 32 to 36 weeks)Birth weight (< 1500 g or < 1000 g)Weight at the time of the procedure (< 1000 g or > 1000 g)[Description of the condition]Ductus arteriosus is a vascular connection essential in fetal life and supports systemic circulation by diverting the right side of the heart's cardiac output. However, a persistent patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) after birth has been associated with many morbidities in preterm infants. The incidence of persistence of PDA is inversely proportional to the gestational age (Semberova 2017). More than 90% of infants born at ≥ 30 weeks' gestation spontaneously close PDA by the end of the first postnatal week, whereas in 50% to 70% of infants born at < 28 weeks' gestation, ductus arteriosus remains patent for weeks (Slaughter 2019;Su 2020). Furthermore, approximately 5% to 7% of ducti remain patent at discharge in infants born at 28 weeks' gestational age (Herrman 2009;Sung 2019). Patency of ductus is determined by a complex interplay of vasodilatory and vasoconstrictive forces governed by various physiological, structural, and molecular factors (Hamrick 2020;Hundscheid 2019). Sensitivity to these forces depends on gestational age. Preterm ductus arteriosus shows higher sensitivity to vasodilatory forces compared to near‐term ductus arteriosus (Hundscheid 2019).Multiple observational and epidemiological studies have demonstrated a significant association between a large left‐to‐right shunt through PDA and adverse neonatal outcomes (Kitterman 1980;Kluckow 2000;Marshall 1999). A large left‐to‐right ductal shunt during the transition period may contribute to pulmonary overcirculation, systemic hypoperfusion, and hypoperfusion‐reperfusion injury. A hemodynamically significant PDA (HS‐PDA) in the first week of life is associated with hypotension requiring treatment, intraventricular hemorrhage, and pulmonary hemorrhage (Deshpande 2018;Noori 2015). Beyond the first week, adverse effects related to PDA depend on the magnitude, duration of left‐to‐right shunt, and degree of prematurity and may contribute to pulmonary morbidities like increased oxygen requirement, need for invasive and noninvasive respiratory support, and bronchopulmonary dysplasia (Clyman 2018). Preterm infants with HS‐PDA in the setting of systemic hypoperfusion may have an increased risk of feeding intolerance, necrotizing enterocolitis, impaired renal function, intraventricular hemorrhage, and mortality (Dollberg 2005).The optimum management for HS‐PDA remains unclear. However, there is a secular shift in the management of HS‐PDA, from 'aggressive treat all' to 'selective treat few' regarding those who are at risk of complications, thus moving towards an individualistic approach (Bixler 2017). Management options for HS‐PDA include the following.Pharmacotherapy with nonsteroidal anti‐inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs; e.g. indomethacin, ibuprofen) or acetaminophen. Indomethacin, ibuprofen, and acetaminophen can be administered enterally or parenterally once a diagnosis of HS‐PDA has been made. The dosage regimens may vary across studies (Ferguson 2019;Hamrick 2020).Invasive management by surgical ligation or transcatheter PDA closure (TCPC): In the surgical approach, the PDA is ligated either surgically via posterolateral thoracotomy or video‐assisted thoracoscopic surgical (VATS) closure by using a clip or ligation (Valentik 2007). In the transcatheter closure approach, the placement of a device in the PDA closes it with arterial or venous access to achieve occlusion. Different devices are available to achieve closure via this approach (Almeida‐Jones 2019).Conservative management with interventions like “fluid restriction, diuretics, high peak end‐expiratory pressure, permissive hypercapnia and maintaining a higher hematocrit” (Smith 2018)No treatment, which entails the 'standard care' management of the premature neonate irrespective of PDA statusPharmacotherapy with nonsteroidal anti‐inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs; e.g. indomethacin, ibuprofen) or acetaminophen. Indomethacin, ibuprofen, and acetaminophen can be administered enterally or parenterally once a diagnosis of HS‐PDA has been made. The dosage regimens may vary across studies (Ferguson 2019;Hamrick 2020).Invasive management by surgical ligation or transcatheter PDA closure (TCPC): In the surgical approach, the PDA is ligated either surgically via posterolateral thoracotomy or video‐assisted thoracoscopic surgical (VATS) closure by using a clip or ligation (Valentik 2007). In the transcatheter closure approach, the placement of a device in the PDA closes it with arterial or venous access to achieve occlusion. Different devices are available to achieve closure via this approach (Almeida‐Jones 2019).Conservative management with interventions like “fluid restriction, diuretics, high peak end‐expiratory pressure, permissive hypercapnia and maintaining a higher hematocrit” (Smith 2018)No treatment, which entails the 'standard care' management of the premature neonate irrespective of PDA statusInvasive management modalities for HS‐PDA include surgical ligation and TCPC. Although surgical ligation eliminates a PDA shunt in 98% to 100% of preterm infants, improvement in long‐term outcomes has been equivocal. Multiple studies in the past decade showed that surgical ligation, when compared to medical treatment, was associated with reduced mortality but increased neurodevelopmental impairment, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, and severe retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) (Bourgoin 2016;Kabra 2007). However, survival bias and confounding by indication may be limitations of these data. Surgical ligation may lead to acute complications like postligation cardiac syndrome, alteration in cerebral perfusion, acute kidney injury, prolonged mechanical ventilation, vocal cord palsy, and thoracic scoliosis (Rodriguez 2018). [Plasma transfusion to prevent intraventricular haemorrhage in very preterm infants] [Objectives]This is a protocol for a Cochrane Review (intervention). The objectives are as follows:To assess whether plasma transfusion administered within the first 24 hours of life can prevent IVH in preterm infants born at gestation less than or equal to 34 weeks. To determine whether use of plasma transfusion is associated with adverse effects.[Description of the condition]Advances in treating preterm infants have led to improved survival of those with birth weight less than 1500 grams, but rates of long‐term neurodisability remain high in this group. Risks of neurodisability are highest for the smallest and sickest preterm babies, but it is not possible to determine precisely which infants will go on to develop significant neurological motor or cognitive problems. Germinal matrix intraventricular haemorrhage (IVH) is found most commonly in preterm infants and occurs in approximately 20% to 25% of infants weighing less than 1500 grams (Heuchan 2002;Volpe 2008); most cases are identified in the first 48 hours after birth (Brouwer 2012). It is known that the presence of IVH, particularly severe IVH, increases the risk of adverse neurological sequelae (Murphy 2002;Volpe 2008). The severity of IVH is assigned Grades I to IV according to Papile's classification (Papile 1978). Intraventricular haemorrhage of Grade III or IV is associated with the worst outcomes, including death from hypovolaemic shock, hydrocephalus and later disability (Klebermass‐Schrehof 2012). Healthcare providers have provided interventions to try to prevent or limit the extent of IVH in an effort to improve long‐term outcomes.Intraventricular haemorrhage originates in the germinal matrix in subependymal regions around the lateral ventricular horns (Roland 2003). The pathogenesis of IVH is most likely multifactorial, with contributions from fluctuations or acute increases in cerebral blood flow (Ment 1995;Whitelaw 2001), poor vascular integrity and extravascular factors around the germinal matrix capillaries (Brouwer 2012;Roland 2003). Abnormalities of coagulation have been suggested as part of the pathogenesis of newborn IVH (Beverley 1984).Concern about coagulopathy arises because very low birth weight (VLBW) infants have prolonged prothrombin time (PT) and activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) compared with older infants (Neary 2013). Evidence of maturation has been noted in haemostatic factors in preterm infants, including both quantitative and qualitative differences in components such as fibrinogen (Monagle 2011), compared with adults. Even term infant values differ from those of adults (Reverdiau‐Moalic 1996). Coagulation factors are synthesised by the foetus from approximately 10 weeks of gestation onwards and do not cross the placenta (Monagle 2011). Foetal studies reveal inverse relationships between gestation and standard measurements of PT and APTT at increasing gestation (Reverdiau‐Moalic 1996). A study from the 1980s examining preterm infants delivered after 30 completed weeks of gestation (Andrew 1988), reported differences in APTT and haemostatic factors versus older infants and adults. Reference ranges for infants born before 27 weeks have been published (Neary 2013). Transfer of vitamin K across the placenta is tightly regulated, with foetal values one‐tenth those of maternal vitamin K concentrations (Mandelbrot 1988;Shearer 1982). High levels of vitamin K are postulated to play a role in DNA mutagenesis in vitro. Therefore, low levels of vitamin K in foetal life could be beneficial in reducing mutagenic risk amongst rapidly proliferating cells (Israels 1995). Vitamin K‐dependent factors do not cross the placenta and are synthesised independently in the foetus from 10 weeks of gestation. Consequently, vitamin K‐dependent factors, prothrombin, protein C, protein S and factors VII, IX and X, as well as contact factors XI and XII, prekallikrein and high‐molecular‐weight kininogen, are present in very low concentrations in the foetus and do not achieve adult levels until later infancy to adolescence, as reflected in prolonged coagulation screening tests (Reverdiau‐Moalic 1996). Thus, vitamin K is administered to all infants at birth.Despite controversy over the role of coagulopathy in the development of IVH (Volpe 2008), treatment of preterm infants with coagulopathy, or perceived coagulopathy, has been advocated by some to prevent, or prevent extension of, IVH in VLBW infants. Cochrane Reviews have been undertaken with regard to administration of ethamsylate, indomethacin and maternal vitamin K. Ethamsylate is a non‐steroidal drug that reduces bleeding from small vessels by increasing capillary endothelial resistance while promoting platelet adhesion. However, observed reduction in IVH has had no impact on mortality nor on impairment of neurodevelopment (Hunt 2010). Indomethacin, another non‐steroidal anti‐inflammatory drug, has been found to decrease the frequency and severity of IVH, mainly by reducing baseline cerebral blood flow (Fowlie 2010). Total IVH incidence (for all grades) was significantly reduced in infants receiving prophylactic indomethacin, although indomethacin did not improve the neurodevelopment of treated infants compared with those given placebo (Fowlie 2010). Meta‐analysis of other interventions, such as maternal administration of vitamin K before preterm delivery, did not show a significant improvement in outcome amongst these infants (Crowther 2010). Of infants receiving plasma transfusion in a recent study, 63% were administered plasma prophylactically without bleeding episodes (Motta 2014).Stanworth 2011cited abnormal coagulation studies without clinical bleeding as an indicator for plasma transfusion in 58% of transfusion episodes, with an additional 14% of episodes involving prophylactic plasma transfusion without coagulation testing. The need to prevent extension of existing IVH was cited as an indicator for plasma transfusion in 18.6% of episodes (Motta 2014). This practice was supported by a randomised controlled trial (RCT) including infants at less than 32 weeks of gestation or with birth weight less than 1500 grams, which reported that infants who received plasma transfusions had a reduced incidence of IVH (Beverely 1985). In a more recent study, the relative risk of IVH was non‐significantly decreased in infants who received plasma transfusion in response to abnormal coagulation tests but with no evidence of bleeding compared with infants who received the plasma transfusion after a bleeding event (Dani 2009).In this Cochrane Review, we will evaluate the role of plasma transfusion in prevention of IVH among very preterm neonates, who are known to have a propensity to severe intraventricular bleeds along with prolonged standard laboratory measurements of coagulation. Plasma products such as fresh frozen plasma (FFP) contain plasma proteins including procoagulant and inhibitory components of the coagulation cascades, acute phase proteins, immunoglobulin, complement, transport molecules and albumin. Many factors have short half‐lives; in particular, FVII has a half‐life of three to five hours so that very little remains after eight hours. Plasma products can be produced from whole blood or through plasmapheresis, but are primarily produced from whole blood. The time after collection to time of freezing determines whether the product becomes FFP, which is frozen within six to eight hours of collection, or F24, which is frozen within the first 24 hours after collection. Both FFP and F24 can be stored at −18 °C or colder, and these products are virtually equivalent, albeit with slightly lower FVIII and Factor V (FV) levels in F24. In particular, the term 'frozen plasma' encompasses both of these products. Such variation among transfused units is less marked for pooled plasma components such as solvent detergent‐treated frozen plasma. This component is prepared from pools of 300 to 5000 plasma donations and is one of the pathogen‐inactivated preparations of plasma available for clinical use. Pathogen inactivation technology represents an additional safety measure to reduce the risk of transfusion‐transmitted infection. Methods generally applied to plasma include solvent detergent treatment, in which pooled plasma is exposed to a solvent and detergent; methylene blue treatment, in which single‐donor units are treated with methylene blue (a phenothiazine dye) and light; and amotosalen treatment, in which a group of compounds called psoralens (which have been developed for their virus‐ and bacteria‐killing properties) are added to plasma before exposure to ultraviolet A (UVA) light. Although these methods offer good virus protection and can reduce microbial infectivity, they are associated with altered or lost coagulation factor content. Frozen plasma is generally administered in doses of 10 mL/kg (although doses can range to 20 mL/kg), a volume that may impact haemodynamic status and overall fluid balance in preterm infants. Plasma products carry the risk of adverse transfusion reactions and infection, including possible infection with as yet unidentified pathogens.Prevention or early treatment of IVH could potentially improve long‐term disability‐free survival amongst very preterm infants. Currently, no treatment is available for IVH once it has occurred, and most strategies have been directed towards prevention or treatment of underlying risk factors (McCrea 2008). Very low birth weight infants are known to have prolonged PT and APTT times compared with term infants and adults. Plasma transfusions contain both procoagulant and anticoagulant components of the coagulation cascade and are used in adult, paediatric and neonatal patients to correct coagulopathy in those who are bleeding or are perceived to be at risk of bleeding (Stanworth 2011). Defects in haemostasis have been associated with the occurrence of IVH (Beverley 1984). Administration of plasma could reduce bleeding tendencies in these preterm infants, who are known to have prolonged laboratory measurements of coagulation. This could prevent the occurrence or extension of an established low‐grade IVH into more severe forms (Grades III and IV ‐Papile 1978). However, effects of frozen plasma may be exerted by a mechanism other than improvement in coagulation factor concentrations. Associations between unstable blood pressure traces, variable cerebral blood flow and IVH have been well documented (Ballah 2010;Perlman 1983;Van Bel 1987). The potential beneficial effect of plasma transfusion may be from stabilising the haemodynamic circulation and thus preventing rapid changes in blood pressure. If this is the mechanism, other fluids could have a similar effect without risk of adverse transfusion reactions. Fresh frozen plasma transfusion likely acts through two mechanisms: reversal of a coagulopathy, and prevention of fluctuations in blood pressure and consequent prevention of fluctuations in cerebral blood flow through pressure passive cerebral circulation. Through these mechanisms, FFP might prevent development or extension of a new haemorrhage (Fanaroff 2006;Julkunen 2008;Salonvaara 2005). Most often, IVH occurs in the first 72 hours of life, and infants are most unstable and at greatest risk in the immediate perinatal period. Infants will be deemed eligible for inclusion in this Cochrane Review only when plasma is administered before 24 hours of age.Severe IVH is a major cause of serious disability in preterm infants. Up to 50% of survivors with Grade III IVH and up to 75% of those with Grade IV IVH have definitive neurological sequelae (Volpe 2008). The aim of this review is to identify the efficacy of plasma transfusion in prevention of IVH, to provide clinicians with robust and balanced evidence on which they can base clinical decisions. This is the first systematic review undertaken to examine this topic. Despite the perceived benefit of frozen plasma in prevention of IVH, the actual benefit of this practice has not been clearly shown. Administration of plasma transfusions carries potential risks due to volume overload, infection and transfusion reactions. Careful evaluation of potential benefits of frozen plasma in relation to safety profile, dosing, route and duration of administration is needed. It is unclear at this time whether prophylactic administration of frozen plasma prevents neonatal IVH in all high‐risk patients. This component is prepared from pools of 300 to 5000 plasma donations and is one of the pathogen‐inactivated preparations of plasma available for clinical use. Pathogen inactivation technology represents an additional safety measure to reduce the risk of transfusion‐transmitted infection. Methods generally applied to plasma include solvent detergent treatment, in which pooled plasma is exposed to a solvent and detergent; methylene blue treatment, in which single‐donor units are treated with methylene blue (a phenothiazine dye) and light; and amotosalen treatment, in which a group of compounds called psoralens (which have been developed for their virus‐ and bacteria‐killing properties) are added to plasma before exposure to ultraviolet A (UVA) light. Although these methods offer good virus protection and can reduce microbial infectivity, they are associated with altered or lost coagulation factor content. Frozen plasma is generally administered in doses of 10 mL/kg (although doses can range to 20 mL/kg), a volume that may impact haemodynamic status and overall fluid balance in preterm infants. Plasma products carry the risk of adverse transfusion reactions and infection, including possible infection with as yet unidentified pathogens.[How the intervention might work]Prevention or early treatment of IVH could potentially improve long‐term disability‐free survival amongst very preterm infants. Currently, no treatment is available for IVH once it has occurred, and most strategies have been directed towards prevention or treatment of underlying risk factors (McCrea 2008). Very low birth weight infants are known to have prolonged PT and APTT times compared with term infants and adults. Plasma transfusions contain both procoagulant and anticoagulant components of the coagulation cascade and are used in adult, paediatric and neonatal patients to correct coagulopathy in those who are bleeding or are perceived to be at risk of bleeding (Stanworth 2011). Defects in haemostasis have been associated with the occurrence of IVH (Beverley 1984). Administration of plasma could reduce bleeding tendencies in these preterm infants, who are known to have prolonged laboratory measurements of coagulation. This could prevent the occurrence or extension of an established low‐grade IVH into more severe forms (Grades III and IV ‐Papile 1978). However, effects of frozen plasma may be exerted by a mechanism other than improvement in coagulation factor concentrations. Associations between unstable blood pressure traces, variable cerebral blood flow and IVH have been well documented (Ballah 2010;Perlman 1983;Van Bel 1987). The potential beneficial effect of plasma transfusion may be from stabilising the haemodynamic circulation and thus preventing rapid changes in blood pressure. If this is the mechanism, other fluids could have a similar effect without risk of adverse transfusion reactions. Fresh frozen plasma transfusion likely acts through two mechanisms: reversal of a coagulopathy, and prevention of fluctuations in blood pressure and consequent prevention of fluctuations in cerebral blood flow through pressure passive cerebral circulation. Through these mechanisms, FFP might prevent development or extension of a new haemorrhage (Fanaroff 2006;Julkunen 2008;Salonvaara 2005). Most often, IVH occurs in the first 72 hours of life, and infants are most unstable and at greatest risk in the immediate perinatal period. Infants will be deemed eligible for inclusion in this Cochrane Review only when plasma is administered before 24 hours of age.[Why it is important to do this review]Severe IVH is a major cause of serious disability in preterm infants. Up to 50% of survivors with Grade III IVH and up to 75% of those with Grade IV IVH have definitive neurological sequelae (Volpe 2008). The aim of this review is to identify the efficacy of plasma transfusion in prevention of IVH, to provide clinicians with robust and balanced evidence on which they can base clinical decisions. This is the first systematic review undertaken to examine this topic. Despite the perceived benefit of frozen plasma in prevention of IVH, the actual benefit of this practice has not been clearly shown. Administration of plasma transfusions carries potential risks due to volume overload, infection and transfusion reactions. Careful evaluation of potential benefits of frozen plasma in relation to safety profile, dosing, route and duration of administration is needed. It is unclear at this time whether prophylactic administration of frozen plasma prevents neonatal IVH in all high‐risk patients. It is not known whether infants identified as having prolonged PT and APTT benefit from administration of plasma transfusion to prevent IVH.. [Remote digital monitoring for selected chronic diseases in primary health care] [Objectives]This is a protocol for a Cochrane Review (intervention). The objectives are as follows:To assess the benefits and harms of remote digital monitoring for adults with selected chronic diseases (hypertension, type 2 diabetes, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, congestive heart failure, and asthma) in primary healthcare settings.[Description of the condition]Chronic disease (CD), also referred by the World Health Organization (WHO) as non‐communicable disease, are illness that persist for a long period (Bernell 2016), and are the result of a combination of genetic, physiological, environmental, and behavioural factors (WHO 2022). Each year, 41 million people die from CD‐related causes, equivalent to 71% of all deaths globally (WHO 2022). An estimated 80% (32.8 million) of all CD‐related deaths are due to cancer, chronic respiratory diseases, and diabetes (Benette 2018). However, the increasing burden of CD, due to an aging population and a shortage of healthcare providers (Beard 2016), imposes stress on the entire health care system (Murray 2020;Walker 2019). In an attempt to address these challenges, RDM is being steadily introduced into PHC, especially since the COVID‐19 pandemic (Muller 2022).Innovative use of technology needs to be integrated at the system level to meet the public health demands (Dinesen 2016). [Entecavir for children and adults with chronic hepatitis B] [Objectives]This is a protocol for a Cochrane Review (intervention). The objectives are as follows:To evaluate the benefits and harms of entecavir versus no treatment or placebo for chronic hepatitis B infection in children and adults with chronic hepatitis B infection, who are either HBeAg‐positive or HBeAg‐negative.[Description of the condition]Hepatitis B virus (HBV) is a virus that affects the liver. Chronic hepatitis B is still a major, worldwide, public health concern, though effective vaccination and antiviral drugs have reduced the infection (McMahon 2005;WHO 2022). According to the World Health Organization (WHO) report, there were 296 million people infected with chronic hepatitis B in 2019, and the estimated number of new infections each year was 1.5 million (WHO 2022). Nearly 90% of people are unaware of their infection and 78% of diagnosed people do not receive treatment (Hutin 2018;WHO 2022). The prevalence of chronic hepatitis B varies widely amongst different regions. The African region had the highest hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) seroprevalence (8.83%, 95% confidence interval (CI) 8.82% to 8.83%), followed by the Western Pacific region (5.26%, 95% CI 5.26% to 5.26%) (Schweitzer 2015). China does not have the highest prevalence (5.49%, 95% CI 5.47% to 5.50%) (Schweitzer 2015), but it has the largest population living with HBV, accounting for one‐third of chronic hepatitis B infections worldwide (Chen 2018;Wang 2017). Chronic hepatitis B can present as hepatitis B virus e antigen (HBeAg) positive or HBeAg negative. Based on one study from 2006, the proportion of HBeAg‐negative chronic hepatitis B was 72%, and it was particularly higher in people born in Europe, Middle East, and Africa (WHO 2015;Zarski 2006).HBV is commonly spread through horizontal transmission (such as injectable drug abuse, transfusion of infected blood, unhygienic tattooing practices, and encountering blood infected with HBV), unprotected sex, and vertical or perinatal exposure (mother‐to‐child transmission) (Nelson 2011). Chronic hepatitis B caused more than 800,000 deaths in 2019; cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma, related to chronic hepatitis B, were the leading cause of death (Marrero 2018;WHO 2022). HBV was responsible for 33% of liver cancer deaths in 2015 (Akinyemiju 2017;McGlynn 2021). One study from the US showed that adults with chronic hepatitis B had a two‐fold higher risk of death than uninfected adults (Zhou 2020).Mother‐to‐child transmission is one of the most common routes of HBV transmission due to direct infection or long‐term close contact, which is the main cause of familial HBV infection (Obayashi 1972). Data from the WHO have shown that in the absence of any preventive interventions, the risk of mother‐to‐child transmission is between 70% and 90% for HBeAg‐positive mothers, and that the risk reduces to 10% and 40% for HBeAg‐negative mothers (WHO 2020). In general, approximately 90% of infected neonates and infants will develop chronic hepatitis B infection, which is much higher than 5% for infected adults (Indolfi 2019). The risk of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma in infected offspring is significantly increased (Sun 2014).The goal of chronic hepatitis B treatment is to permanently suppress HBV replication, reduce hepatic complications, and improve long‐term survival (Lok 2009). Antiviral therapy is regarded as conventional therapy for chronic hepatitis B, including interferon‐α (IFN‐α) therapy and nucleos(t)ide analogues therapy. Entecavir is one option of a nucleos(t)ide analogue antiviral therapy, which was approved for chronic hepatitis B treatment in 2005 in the US and in 2006 in Europe (Dimou 2007).Entecavir has a high resistance barrier, and its cumulative genotypic resistance rate reaches only 1.2% after six years for nucleos(t)ide‐naïve people (Lok 2012). However, this number increases to 57% for people who are lamivudine‐refractory (Tenney 2009). Entecavir and tenofovir have equal effectiveness in HBeAg clearance (risk ratio (RR) 1.05, 95% CI 0.68 to 1.62) and HBeAg seroconversion (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.54 to 1.61) for people with nucleos(t)ide analogue‐naive chronic hepatitis B (Chen 2019;Sriprayoon 2017). The safety of entecavir is comparable with lamivudine and most of its adverse reactions are of mild‐to‐moderate severity. The frequency of serious adverse events in people with chronic hepatitis B, with a mean exposure to entecavir of 75 weeks was 8% (27/354), and the rate of discontinuation due to adverse events was less than 1% (Chang 2006). In addition, entecavir was at a lower cost when compared with other drugs for chronic hepatitis B such as lamivudine and telbivudine (Ruggeri 2017;Wiens 2013), which is critical for equity and long‐term adherence to treatment measures. Entecavir and tenofovir were recommended as first‐line drugs for children with chronic hepatitis B, but only entecavir can be used for children aged two to 11 years (Terrault 2018). One randomised clinical trial demonstrated that the rates of HBeAg seroconversion and HBV DNA less than 50 IU/mL in the entecavir group were significantly higher than placebo after 48 weeks (Jonas 2016). Although lamivudine was approved for children aged two years or older, its risk of resistance is higher than entecavir.Entecavir is phosphorylated to the active triphosphate form and has an intracellular half‐life of 15 hours. In healthy people, peak plasma concentrations of entecavir were reached within 0.5 to 1.5 hours and steady‐state was reached after 6 to 10 days of once‐daily dosing (Osborn 2011). The recommended dose of entecavir for adults with chronic hepatitis B infection is 0.5 mg daily; however, if that adult has decompensated cirrhosis or is refractory to lamivudine, a larger dose (1.0 mg daily) should be used (Terrault 2018).Entecavir has potent antiviral activity in multiple long‐term clinical studies (Ridruejo 2011;Seto 2011;Zoutendijk 2011), with HBV‐DNA response rates of approximately 95% (Pol 2012). Meanwhile, entecavir showed superior virological and biochemical benefits for the nucleoside‐naïve people. One global multicentre study showed, in the fifth year of entecavir therapy, 94% of HBeAg‐positive chronic hepatitis B people had HBV DNA less than 300 copies/mL and 80% reached normal alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels (Chang 2010). Another study demonstrated that more than 90% of nucleos(t)ide analogues‐naïve Chinese chronic hepatitis B people achieved undetectable HBV DNA after two years of entecavir treatment (Luo 2013).Entecavir is recommended as the first‐line drug for chronic hepatitis B in many clinical guidelines (EASL 2017;Terrault 2018;WHO 2015), but none of them have issued the recommendation based on the direct comparison of entecavir versus placebo/no treatment in a systematic review. The net effect of entecavir versus no treatment or placebo is still uncertain. Several randomised clinical trials on this topic are available (Jonas 2016;Tseng 2014). According to the World Health Organization (WHO), in 2020, cancer caused almost 10 million deaths globally (WHO 2022). In high‐income countries, haematological malignancies are amongst the 10 most common cancer types (Cancer Research UK 2020;Cronin 2018). Haematological malignancies arise from the myeloid or lymphatic system, and affect the peripheral blood, bone marrow or lymph nodes, with possible involvement of other organs. Lymphoid cancers include non‐Hodgkin lymphoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, acute and chronic leukaemia and multiple myeloma. Approximately 60% of cancer deaths are related to or directly caused by infection (Chang 1976;Hersh 1965). Compared with people with solid tumours, those with haematological malignancies usually exhibit higher levels of immunosuppression because neoplastic processes affect the host immune system and treatments usually cause prolonged neutropenia (Rolston 2017).
