[Physical therapy interventions for pelvic girdle pain (PGP) after pregnancy] [Description of the condition]According to European guidelines, pelvic girdle pain (PGP) is a specific form of low back pain that can occur separately or concurrently with low back pain (Vleeming 2008). The following definition has been proposed: “Pelvic girdle pain (PGP) generally arises in relation to pregnancy, trauma or reactive arthritis. Pain is experienced between the posterior iliac crest and the gluteal fold, particularly in the vicinity of the sacroiliac joints. The pain may radiate in the posterior thigh and can also occur in conjunction with/or separately in the symphysis. The endurance capacity for standing, walking and sitting is diminished. The diagnosis of PGP can be reached after exclusion of lumbar causes. The pain or functional disturbances in relation to PGP must be reproducible by specific clinical tests” (Vleeming 2008). There are a number of clinical tests available to verify PGP. The posterior pelvic pain provocation test and the active straight leg raise test are the two most evaluated tests (Ostgaard 1994;Mens 2001), and have been found to have acceptable reliability and validity (Ostgaard 1994;Gutke 2009;Albert 2000;Mens 2001;Gutke 2010). The point prevalence of PGP during pregnancy is close to 20% (Vleeming 2008).Most women recover from PGP after delivery, however, it is a serious problem for those young women for whom pain and disability persist after delivery (Wu 2004;Bjelland 2013a). A study of pregnant women showed that woman with PGP were significantly more afflicted than women with low back pain (Robinson 2010). Furthermore, it has been shown that women with pain located in all three pelvic joints (the symphysis and the two sacroiliac joints) were more disabled than other subgroups of pain locations in the pelvis (Albert 2001).Despite the fact that PGP is a common ailment, it is poorly described and understood. The aetiology and pathogenesis of PGP is unclear and most likely multifactorial. Possible underlying causes include hormonal and biomechanical aspects, stress on ligament structures, and inadequate motor control (O'Sullivan 2007;Aldabe 2012;Aldabe 2012a;Palsson 2012). Studies associating serum relaxing levels with PGP are few and conflicting, and since the evidence for the association between PGP and the hormone relaxin is low, no secure conclusion can be drawn (Aldabe 2012). The movements that occur in the pelvic joints have been traced (Mens 1999;Goode 2008). A recent study showed that the movement in the sacroiliac joints is small and almost undetectable by precise radiosteriometric analysis (Kibsgard 2014). Despite a large overlap in the range of the symphyseal motion, a review byMens 2009reports a larger motion of the symphysis during pregnancy and puerperium in patients with PGP than in those without.The pelvis transfers load from the trunk to the legs and for the load to be effectively transferred, and for the shear forces to be minimised across the joints, the pelvis needs to be optimally stabilised. Stability is obtained by ridges and grooves in the articular surfaces of the sacroiliac joints (form closure) and additional compression forces (force closure), which are generated by muscles, fascia, and ligaments. The self locking mechanism of the sacroiliac joints with the principles of form and force closure, based on a theoretical model from anatomical and biomechanical studies was introduced by Snijders et al (Snijders 1993a). Failure of the self locking mechanism and load transfer through the pelvis have been suspected in patients with sacroiliac pain (Hungerford 2003;Hungerford 2004), and asymmetric laxity of the sacroiliac joints has been shown to correlate with moderate to severe levels of symptoms in subjects with postpartum PGP (Damen 2001).An impaired load transfer may result in overload of the ligaments of the pelvis (Snijders 1993;Eichenseer 2011). Both the sacrospinous ligament and superficial sacroiliac joint structures (Torstensson 2009;Torstensson 2013), such as the long dorsal sacroiliac ligament, are reported to be a potential source of pain in PGP (Palsson 2012;Palsson 2015). It has been found that pain and hyperalgesia induced in the long dorsal sacroiliac ligament in healthy subjects has a negative influence on muscle activity with excessive muscle stabilisation, similar to that which is seen in patients with PGP (Palsson 2015). Furthermore, changes in spinal curvature and posture may be caused by pregnancy. Both increased lumbar lordosis (Franklin 1998), and a tendency for lumbar kyphosis is reported to be prevalent during pregnancy (Moore 1990,Okanishi 2012). Frequent or sustained pain‐provoking postures might influence the pelvic ligaments and in turn link to relevant symptoms.There is a moderate level of evidence that PGP is related to an altered pelvic mechanism and/or motor control (Aldabe 2012a). PGP disorders have been associated with an alteration in the strategy for lumbopelvic stabilisation with excessive as well as insufficient motor activation of the lumbopelvic and surrounding musculature (O'Sullivan 2007). Attention has been paid to motor control of local muscles, such as the transverse abdominals (Richardson 2002;Stuge 2006). Also the pelvic floor muscles are considered to be an important part of the local muscle system. Interestingly, a significantly smaller levator hiatus was found in women with PGP than in controls both at rest, during voluntary and automatic contraction of the pelvic floor muscle, indicating an increased muscle activity (Stuge 2012;Stuge 2013). Also, specific tests of muscle groups around the pelvic girdle have shown lower trunk muscle endurance and hip extension strength, underpinning the hypothesis of muscle dysfunction in women with PGP (Gutke 2008). A possible mechanism for ongoing pain and disability in patients with persistent PGP may be aberrant motor control patterns (Beales 2009;Beales 2010). Difficulties in walking as seen in women with PGP, might be a consequence of impaired motor control (Gutke 2008). Positive changes in motor control have been found to be associated with relief of pain and disability (Stuge 2004;O'Sullivan 2007). However, the knowledge about PGP and its underlying mechanisms is still limited and hampers our ability to treat and help women with postpartum PGP in an optimal manner.Treatment options vary widely. The physical therapy interventions we will focus on are: exercise therapy (individual or in groups, home‐based, land‐ or water‐based); physical conditioning; manual therapy (mobilisation and manipulation); pelvic belts; massage; and electrotherapy (therapeutic ultrasound and transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation). Education is often used as a supplement to these interventions.Exercise therapyis a management strategy that is supervised or ‘prescribed’ and encompasses a group of interventions ranging from general physical fitness or aerobic exercise to muscle strengthening, various types of flexibility, and stretching exercises (Hayden 2005). Exercises for optimal muscle function and motor control can be performed without provoking pain. Individualisation of exercise positions and dosage might easily be performed with sling suspensionStuge 2004.Physical conditioning,sometimes called 'work conditioning', 'work hardening' or 'functional restoration' and 'exercise programmes', may be a part of a return to work strategy to reduce sickness for workers with back pain (Schaafsma 2013). Physical conditioning can consist of existent or simulated work tasks, as well as addressing individual and work‐related psychosocial factors (Waddell 2001). Physical conditioning is characterised by progressively graded structured tasks, exercises, or advice about exercise (Schaafsma 2013).Manual therapy (joint mobilisation and manipulation)is a common intervention used to restore normal joint motion and involves hands‐on low‐velocity passive movements within or at the limit of range of motion for the joint, whereas manipulation is a high‐velocity manual thrust to a joint beyond the passive range of motion (Rubinstein 2012).Pelvic beltsor maternity belts have been worn for comfort and support for centuries (Carr 2003). The supports have been categorised into four main types: belts, briefs, cradles, and torso supports (Ho 2009).Massageis soft tissue manipulation using hands or a mechanical device (Vickers 1999). A natural reaction when experiencing pain is to rub the painful area, which may be seen as the simplest type of massage. Massage over a painful area is used to promote relaxation and well‐being and to decrease pain by distraction (Furlan 2008). A classification system has described four categories of massage based on the goal of treatment i.e. relaxation massage, clinical massage, movement re‐education, and energy work (Sherman 2006).Therapeutic ultrasoundis a treatment that uses the vibration of high frequency sound waves to deliver heat and energy to muscles, ligaments, tendons and bones, and the goal is to reduce pain and speed the healing process (Ebadi 2014).Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS)is widely used. TENS units deliver electrical stimulation to the underlying nerves via electrodes placed over the intact skin surface near the source of maximal pain. Several types of TENS applications, differing in frequency, amplitude, pulse width and waveform, are used in clinical practice (Khadilkar 2008).Patient educationprogrammes are designed to improve patients' understanding of their PGP problems and how to handle them.The working mechanisms of exercise therapy, are in general, improved muscle strength, range of motion, co‐ordination, motor control and cardiovascular fitness, and a decrease of muscle tension (Staal 2002). Exercises in slings are first of all used as an aid to prevent weight‐bearing pain during exercise (Stuge 2004).A deconditioning syndrome has been defined as inactivity due to avoidance of painful activities, resulting in disuse (Verbunt 2010;Schaafsma 2013). Physical conditioning is believed to increase physical, psychological, and emotional tolerance, and the hypothesis of the effect of such a programme is that as functional capacities improve, the capability of returning to work will increase (Schaafsma 2013).From a mechanistic approach manipulative therapy is thought to act on a manipulable lesion, and proposes that the manipulation can reduce the internal mechanical stresses, and thereby result in reduced symptoms (Triano 2001). From the neurophysiologic approach, spinal manipulative therapy is thought to act on reflex neural outputs to both muscle and visceral organs, producing excitatory and inhibitory effects (Pickar 2002).Pelvic belts, as treatment for PGP, are thought to increase the stability of the pelvis (Snijders 1993a). Both elastic and non‐elastic belts have been used in research (Ostgaard 1994;Noren 1997;Depledge 2005;Kalus 2008;Kordi 2013), without a clear hypothesis for differences in explained effect. The influence of pelvic belts on ligament load has been analysed by means of a computer model (Sichting 2014). The results suggests that pelvic belt application can provide increased sacroiliac motion around the sagittal axis but decreased motion around the transverse axis, and relieve strain of the sacroiliac joint ligaments, especially for the sacrospinous, sacrotuberous, and the interosseous sacroiliac ligaments (Sichting 2014).Soft tissue massage is believed to block the pain nociception (gate control theory;Melzack 1996) by stimulating large diameter nerve fibres, and by activating the parasympathetic nervous system, which may stimulate the release of endorphins and serotonin (Ernst 1999).It is proposed that therapeutic ultrasound delivers energy to deep tissue sites through ultrasonic waves, to produce increases in tissue temperature or non‐thermal physiologic changes. [Parenting programmes for incarcerated parents] [Description of the condition]There has been a substantial increase in incarceration rates worldwide. Recent figures indicate a 91% rise in the prison population in the UK between 1993 and 2014; the figure now stands at 84,372 (Prison Reform Trust 2015). In the USA over one and a half million people were held in prison at the end of 2014 (Bureau of Justice Statistics 2015). Consequently, the number of children affected by parental incarceration is significant (Purvis 2011). Approximately 65% of prisoners have children, and 7% of women who go into prison are pregnant (Bureau of Justice Statistics 2004). Annually, parents of over 200,000 children in the UK experience imprisonment; this is twice the number of children in care and six times the number of children subject to child protection plans (Burry 2012). The implications of rising incarceration rates reach far beyond the individual to the children, family and community (Murray 2012).Incarcerated parents may experience many life adversities before entering prison. Mental health problems are common in prisoners, many of whom experience more than one mental illness. A UK study revealed that 26% of women and 16% of men reported that they had received treatment for a mental health problem in the year before custody (Prison Reform Trust 2013). According to the US Bureau of Justice statistics, an estimated 56% of state prisoners and 45% of federal prisoners have a mental health problem (Bureau of Justice 2006). Incarcerated parents often report having little education; in 2013, a survey of prisoners in UK prisons found that 47% had no qualifications, compared with 15% of the working age general population (Prison Reform Trust 2013). Further, 53% of women and 27% of men in prison report having experienced sexual, emotional, or physical abuse as a child (Prison Reform Trust 2013).Parents who are incarcerated often experience stress, related to being separated from their children. Mothers in prison who reported higher levels of parenting stress were more likely to suffer from depression and anxiety (Houck 2002). Higher stress levels appear to be associated with an increased risk of violating prison rules and regulations, suggesting that those who experience parenting stress also have more difficulty adjusting to prison life (Loper 2006). Research indicates that incarcerated fathers feel powerless and personally devalued, and have lowered self‐esteem (Purvis 2011).Skar 2015found that incarcerated fathers, even after engaging in a parenting programme, suffered poor mental health and psychosocial functioning; the authors believed that this was due to an increased awareness of the negative consequences of being incarcerated on their child, and subsequent feelings of guilt.Children of incarcerated parents have been described as 'among the riskiest of the high risk children in [the USA]' (Myers 1999, p 11). One of the biggest concerns is the increased risk of emotional and behavioural problems amongst these children, including mental health problems (Turanovic 2015). This may not be directly attributable to incarceration per se, as children whose parents are sent to prison are more likely than others to have been exposed to such adverse events as parental substance abuse, parental mental ill health, domestic abuse and poverty (Johnston 2012;Shlafer 2012) Further, living in a household with a criminally‐involved parent can increase children's risk of exposure to such adversities as sexual or physical violence, witnessing the arrest of a parent, out‐of‐home placement and ‐ longer term ‐ more punitive sentences if brought before the court (McCrudden 2014;Rodriguez 2009). These experiences may account for the increased risk of social, emotional and behavioural difficulties encountered amongst children whose parents have been imprisoned (Murray 2012;Tasca 2014;Wildeman 2014).Nonetheless, parental incarceration can set in motion a cascade of negative consequences (Murphey 2015), beginning with adverse effects on parent‐child contact and attachment. Maternal incarceration may be especially hard on a child, given that mothers are most likely to be the primary caregivers (Murphey 2015;Wildeman 2014). Although babies and children are sometimes allowed to reside with their mothers in prison (depending on jurisdiction), the large number of mothers who are incarcerated limits the possibility of this being an option for all and, after a certain age, the prison environment is deemed unsuitable for children (O'Malley 2016). For older children or children unable to remain with their mother, the care they receive may be adversely affected, as they may experience changes in caregiver or in the quality of care provided. Visiting a parent in prison can also be a very stressful experience. It is not surprising that under these circumstances children may become sad, anxious and afraid, and worry incessantly about their parent’s wellbeing and safety in prison (Gilham 2012).As well as mental health risks, children of an incarcerated parent are more prone to cognitive delays and difficulties in school (Eddy 2010). They may be more likely to experience lower educational achievement and have an increased risk of truancy and school exclusion (Morgan 2013). Research also suggests that maternal incarceration decreases teachers' expectations of children, which is especially problematic at a time when children need as much support and encouragement as possible (Dallaire 2010). As the authors ofMurphey 2015note, the social stigma associated with having an incarcerated parent often brings disapproval, and is generally not supported by society. However, some research has revealed that maternal incarceration has no effect on children's test scores and can actually increase their attendance and retention in school (Cho 2009). Thus, in some cases, especially when children are being exposed to harmful situations or neglect, maternal incarceration may lead to improved outcomes in some aspects of their lives (Turanovic 2012). For example, using data from the Fragile Families and Wellbeing study,Wildeman 2014found that maternal incarceration was associated with less aggressive behaviour, less attention problems and less internalising and externalising problems, at least for white children, as reported by their caregiver. Thus, in some cases, maternal incarceration may improve child well‐being.Standard parenting programmes are usually short‐term interventions aimed at helping parents improve their parenting, their communication and their relationship with their children (Barlow 2011). Most also aim to increase parental skills, knowledge and understanding of their child, and some seek more specifically to improve child emotional and behavioural problems via improvement of parenting behaviours. Programmes usually last for between 8 and 12 weeks, and deploy a range of techniques such as discussion, role play, video vignettes and homework (Barlow 2011). Many are manualised, and most are delivered to parents in groups in a range of hospital or community‐based settings. They are underpinned by a number of theoretical approaches, including social learning theory, attachment theory, family systems theory and ecological theory.Programmes designed for incarcerated parents differ from other programmes in two significant ways. In addition to focusing on the development of parenting skills, they need to deal with the challenge of parenting within the context of incarceration, and provide parents with the skills and strategies needed for positive engagement with their children, families and communities after release. This means addressing those factors that might threaten successful reintegration. Additional topics critical for this population might include identifying and avoiding abusive or negative relationships, staying away from drug and alcohol misuse, dealing with past trauma, and life development skills, such as job skills training and gaining employment (Kjellstrand 2012). As the authors ofKjellstrand 2012note, these parents may only be able to parent effectively when these essential health and safety needs are addressed, and thus generic parenting programmes that focus solely on parenting skills without addressing such particular issues may be of little benefit.Many men and women who become incarcerated may also have experienced much childhood adversity, for example, violence in the home, substance abuse and physical or sexual abuse (Purvis 2011). Many may have lacked positive adult role models during their developmental years and, asPurvis 2011states, these early experiences will inevitability shape their own parenting style in later life. Hence, there is a real need for incarcerated parents to be offered education and training in effective parenting, given that most lack the knowledge necessary to demonstrate positive parenting. Research has indicated that parenting programmes can be successful in helping parents develop their skills and resources, which, in turn, help them to parent more effectively (Wilson 2011). Components within the programmes can enhance parental knowledge of child development and positive parenting styles, which, in turn, can lead to enhanced parenting skills and parental self‐esteem (Wilson 2011). Parenting programmes that improve the mental health of parents and their ability to regulate their emotions may also help parents in their parenting role (Barlow 2011). This seems particularly pertinent to incarcerated parents, given their risk of mental health and self‐regulation difficulties.Loper 2006cites the example of a mother who waits patiently for a visit from her children, only to have an uncontrollable anger display during the visit, leaving her wracked with guilt and the children not keen to visit again. Because these visits, whilst very beneficial, are so emotionally charged, prisoners would benefit from the opportunity to deal with past trauma and learn strategies that enable them to handle their own emotions and equip them to deal with the stresses they face more effectively (Loper 2006).Research also suggests that men’s attitudes and ideas about their relationship with their partners and children may be unrealistic and unclear, which can lead to conflict within the home (Day 2005;Purvis 2011). Parenting programmes provide the opportunity, within a safe environment, for fathers to explore their beliefs and attitudes towards issues such as discipline, affection and family roles, which can support their reintegration back into the family upon release (Purvis 2011). It is also possible that promoting healthy parent‐child relationships and responsive parenting may help break the cycle of intergenerational incarceration and improve the health and well‐being of their children (Newman 2011). It should be acknowledged here that whilst all of these components are important, the existing evidence base is somewhat limited, and thus it is difficult to know how many studies actually measure these issues. Similarly, most general parenting programmes assume that the parents attending have at least some contact with their children and thus have an opportunity to 'practice' the skills being taught, which may not be the case for incarcerated parents.The number of parenting programmes delivered to incarcerated parents has increased over recent years, and existing programmes designed for parents living in the community are often delivered to parents in prison, without modification (Eddy 2008). It is not clear what kinds of programme might be most effective for this population, and what changes, if any, are required to community‐based parenting programmes to render them suitable for incarcerated parents (Purvis 2011).Hoffman 2010has revealed that many programmes are being implemented without any knowledge of their impact as only a few institutions conduct evaluations. Indeed, we do not yet know whether parenting programmes for incarcerated parents have the potential to generate positive outcomes, or whether a universal, prison‐specific intervention can meet the needs of this particular population (Kjellstrand 2012), given that prisoners are not a homogenous group (McCrudden 2014).Loper 2006questions whether there are specific circumstances in which parenting programmes should not be used, as they may be harmful to the participants. [Dental filling materials for managing carious lesions in the primary dentition] [Description of the condition]Dental caries (more commonly known as tooth decay) develops when bacteria from food debris and sugar in the mouth release acids that demineralise and soften the tooth surface (Marsh 2006). The condition initially appears as white spot lesions of demineralised enamel. If the demineralisation process is not interrupted or reversed, carious lesions can progress further into the tooth structure and form cavities. Ultimately, untreated caries can lead to infection and tooth loss. Children who require extraction of decayed primary teeth also face an increased risk of developing orthodontic problems due to premature primary dentition loss (Law 2013).Dental caries is a chronic disease that is almost entirely preventable, and usually manifests from a combination of the following risk factors: poor oral hygiene, frequent sugar consumption, and lack of exposure to topical sources of fluoride, which is understood to have a cariostatic effect (Rošin‐Grget 2013;Rugg‐Gunn 2013;WHO 2010).Untreated caries in the primary dentition is the 10th most prevalent health condition worldwide, and is estimated to affect 621 million children (Kassebaum 2015). The World Health Organization's (WHO) geographical estimation of disease burden indicates that children in the Southeast Asian region suffered the greatest burden of caries in 2012 (36% of the total global caries disability‐adjusted life years (DALYs) burden from birth to 14 years), followed by children in the Western Pacific (19%) and African regions (18%), and to a lesser extent by children in the Eastern Mediterranean region (11%), the Americas (9%), and the European region (7%;WHO 2014a).According to the WHO's estimation of disease burden by World Bank region, children from high‐income countries collectively accounted for only 6% of the total global caries DALYs burden in 2012. Of the six low‐ and middle‐income World Bank regions, children in South Asia suffered the greatest DALYs burden of caries in 2012 (35% of global total), followed by East Asia and Pacific (25%), Sub‐Saharan Africa (19%), Latin America and the Caribbean (7%), the Middle East and North Africa (5%), and Europe and Central Asia (3%;WHO 2014b).Despite the fact that the European region suffered the lowest burden of disease from dental caries, 28% of children in the UK suffered from tooth decay at the age of five (Public Health England 2012), and dental caries was the most common cause of hospital admissions for children aged five to nine years (Royal College of Surgeons of England 2015). In low‐income countries, the problem of caries among children is of even greater concern, due to the combination of high prevalence and limited resources that present substantial access barriers to oral healthcare services. Consequently, it is clear that this chronic disease presents a significant global burden for health service resources (Rugg‐Gunn 2013).Dental caries can have a substantial impact on children's quality of life (QoL); not only causing pain and difficulties with eating, but also affecting school attendance and disrupting sleep patterns, potentially affecting growth and educational performance (Finucane 2012;Guarnizo‐Herreño 2012).The prevalence of dental caries is strongly associated with deprivation, whereby children from low‐income families suffer a greater burden of caries than children from more affluent backgrounds (Schwendicke 2015;Thomson 2012). This trend of social inequality continues into adulthood, and independent of deprivation level, children who suffer from caries are at increased risk of developing carious lesions as adults (Thomson 2004;Thomson 2012).Once carious lesions are identified in the primary dentition, dentists and dental auxiliaries have a range of options available to restore the decayed tooth's structure.Direct restorations allow dental professionals to place and shape a malleable filling material, which then hardens, during a single appointment. Depending on the choice of filling material, liners may be used to protect the pulp, or the use of enamel etching, adhesives, and light curing may be required (American Dental Assocation 2002). This review will not assess effectiveness of preformed metal crowns or cavity liners, as they are addressed by other Cochrane reviews (Innes 2015;Schenkel 2013).Direct filling materials can be categorised as non‐aesthetic or aesthetic. Non‐aesthetic filling materials are constructed from a combination of metal alloys (known as amalgam) and are perceived to provide dental professionals with a strong, well‐retained, and cost‐effective option (American Dental Assocation 2002;Rasines Alcaraz 2014;WHO 2010). It should be acknowledged that there has been a global decline in the use of amalgam as a dental filling material over the past decade as a result of the Minamata Convention, due to (largely environmental) concerns over toxicity relating to potential mercury release (American Academy of Pediatric Dentistry 2014;Rodríguez‐Farre 2016;United Nations Environment Programme 2013).At one end of the aesthetic restoration spectrum, resin composites (RC), which are made from a mix of plastic resin and powdered glass, are strong and resemble the natural colour of teeth, but they are more expensive to produce than amalgam, and require more time and greater expertise to fit (for example, ensuring moisture control;American Academy of Pediatric Dentistry 2014;DeRouen 2006;WHO 2010).An alternative is glass ionomer cement (GIC), which is made from a combination of acid and powdered glass. GIC also resembles tooth colour (although the appearance is reduced because it is more translucent than RC), but is more biocompatible as a material and claims to be able to release fluoride for up to a year after placement, although this is disputed (American Academy of Pediatric Dentistry 2014;American Dental Assocation 2002;Dionysopoulos 2014;WHO 2010). It is thought that the GIC fluoride‐release function also provides a mechanism whereby use of topical fluoride 'recharges' the GIC to maintain ongoing fluoride release (Dionysopoulos 2014;Gururaj 2013).Other chemical classifications of aesthetic filling materials are found along the spectrum between RC and GIC (WHO 2010). Polyacid‐modified RC ((PAMRC), also known as compomer) is a variation of RC that combines some of the acidic properties of GIC to release a smaller dose of fluoride (Nicholson 2007). Resin‐modified GIC (RMGIC) is a modification of GIC whereby resin is introduced to provide increased strength (Sidhu 2010).Different filling materials require different techniques for restoration placement and retention: amalgam requires preparation of retentive undercuts (known as macro‐retention) to mitigate the material's inability to adhere; RC use an adhesive system to forge a micro‐retentive bond with the tooth's structure, although the choice of bonding agent may require additional tooth surface pretreatment before placement; and GIC’s chemical adhesion bonds the material to the tooth structure without requiring additional adhesive or cavity pretreatment (Da Silva 2011).Cavitated carious lesions in primary teeth are frequently managed by placement of dental fillings. This treatment aims to replace missing dental tissue in order to aid plaque control, restore tooth function, and protect the pulp‐dentine complex by sealing the cavity (Schwendicke 2016a). The clinical success of such an intervention is dependent on the properties of the filling material and its integrity in the restored cavity, amongst other factors (Schwendicke 2016b). [Pulse oximetry sensor application for neonates during resuscitation] [Description of the condition]Neonatal resuscitation primarily depends on establishing effective ventilation. Excessive oxygen during resuscitation in the delivery room is associated with various short and long‐term morbidities. The recent neonatal resuscitation program (NRP) 2015 guidelines recommend initiating resuscitation in preterm neonates with low oxygen concentration (21% to 30%) (Perlman 2015). This and other similar recommendations make it more important to understand and identify the ideal and most feasible method of assessing the oxygenation in a reliable and continuous fashion in the delivery room to avoid unduly high oxygen delivery and associated morbidities. Studies have reported that color assessment, as a surrogate for oxygenation, is highly subjective and inaccurate. A newborn, despite a normal transition, may take close to 10 minutes to have a normal skin color on the central parts of the body (Dimich 1991;O'Donnell 2005b). Moreover, auscultation and palpation of heart rate (HR) are subjective, intermittent and of questionable accuracy (New Reference;Theophilopoulos 1998). Various authors have suggested that pulse oximetry in the delivery room can acquire continuous and accurate measurement of HR and pulse oxygen saturation (SpO₂) and can also help in achieving normoxia during resuscitation (Kattwinkel 2003). The Neonatal Resuscitation Program (NRP) guidelines advocate the use of pulse oximetry during resuscitation, especially when there is a need for providing positive pressure ventilation or supplemental oxygen (Perlman 2015). For pulse oximetry to be useful in the delivery room, the sensor has to be quickly applied to a suitable site on the infant after birth and then should be able to rapidly obtain a reliable signal. However, this can be quite challenging due to poor peripheral perfusion in the first few minutes of life, effects of transitional circulation, motion artifact, wet and slippery limbs, vernix and skin edema, all of which could delay the signal acquisition process (Dimich 1991;House 1987;Kopotic 2002;Meier‐Stauss 1990). After application of the pulse oximetry sensor, there is a delay before the display of SpO₂ and HR. During this lag period, the oximeter analyzes the signal, recognizes the pulse waveform and calculates the SpO₂ and HR, following which the values are displayed (O'Donnell 2005a).Pulse oximeters work on the basis of the Beer‐Lambert principle (Beer 1852). The visible red part and the invisible infrared part of the spectrum are specifically absorbed by the reduced hemoglobin fraction and the oxyhemoglobin fraction respectively. The relative proportional presence of these two fractions is calculated as the percentage of the oxyhemoglobin fraction to the total hemoglobin and is displayed as oxygen saturation percentage on the monitor (Aoyagi 2003;Sinex 1999). A standard pulse oximeter has three basic parts: the main equipment, an extension cable and a sensor. The extension cable connects the main equipment to the sensor. The sensor is applied to the patient’s body part, which is usually one of the limbs or the ear lobe, and once the communication from the sensor to the equipment is complete, the receiving part of the sensor starts sensing the pulse waveform and the signals are processed in the equipment. Depending on a function called averaging time, the pulse oximeter averages the signals acquired over the previous ‘x’ seconds and subsequently displays the heart rate and saturation. The technique of application of the pulse oximeter sensor has been proposed to be an important component of this delay in data retrieval and subsequent display of a reliable signal (O'Donnell 2005a;O'Donnell 2005b). When an oximeter is switched on with a sensor connected, the pulse oximeter immediately attempts to generate data. If the sensor is connected to a pulse oximeter but not applied to an infant, it may interpret the environmental 'noise' as pulses and may generate an artificial signal. When the sensor is then applied, the oximeter would tend to average this artificial signal with the true signal detected from the infant. This may lead to a delay in display of reliable data and may lead to an incorrect display. Attaching the sensor first to the infant before attaching to the pulse oximeter or applying an already in‐line sensor to another person’s finger before applying to the infant have been proposed as alternative methods of applying the sensor in order to avoid such delay and inaccuracies in data display (O'Donnell 2005a). Moreover, a significant number of babies in the delivery room failed to display saturation and heart rate data despite reapplication of the sensor (O'Donnell 2005a). Resuscitation guided by pulse oximetry using different techniques of sensor placement may have a potentially significant impact on various outcomes such as mortality, hypoxic‐ischemic encephalopathy as well as the time‐to‐display of reliable HR and SpO₂ data.Earlier acquisition of appropriate pulse signals and faster display of pulse saturations could expedite determining whether the target saturations have been achieved and in turn would help in titrating the oxygen concentration with respect to the target saturation for that postnatal age in minutes. This may help in reducing unnecessary exposure to additional concentrations of supplemental oxygen and in turn may reduce excessive oxygen‐associated morbidities such as chronic lung disease (CLD) and retinopathy of prematurity (ROP). On the contrary, in a preterm neonate whose resuscitation has been initiated with an oxygen concentration of 21% to 30%, a delay in signal acquisition can lead to potential hypoxemia and an associated increase in mortality. Apart from SpO₂, HR is another parameter which is the most important and objective clinical indicator of the health of newly born infants and the most reliable clinical indicator of effectiveness of resuscitation (Wyllie 2006). Heart rate also determines the need for changing interventions and escalating care during resuscitation of a newly born. Immediately after birth HR is usually counted by auscultation or palpation of the umbilical cord. Both of these are imprecise and systematically underestimate the true HR (Kamlin 2006). HR can be continuously measured and displayed by pulse oximetry provided there is a good plethysmographic signal and there are no indicators of poor signal (Kamlin 2006). A speedy and more precise determination of HR along with saturations using pulse oximetry, apart from the morbidities related to high and low oxygen, may potentially guide the resuscitation process, make the resuscitation efforts more effective and hence may reduce the risk of clinical outcomes such as hypoxic‐ischemic encephalopathy and mortality.A speedy pulse signal acquisition by pulse oximetry would help achieve an early and reliable estimation of the HR and SpO₂ and hence would avoid delay in management decisions. This is most crucial in a delivery room setting where a delay in reliable data acquisition of even a few seconds may lead to inaction and subsequent serious long‐term complications. A delay in identification of the correct saturation at any given postnatal age can potentially lead to an increase in risk of death (if the true pulse oxygen saturations fall below the target oxygen saturations) and CLD and ROP (if the true pulse oxygen saturations fall above the target oxygen saturations). Apart from certain human factors such as a delay in placing the pulse oximeter probe and the associated delay in signal acquisition, the technique of pulse oximeter probe placement on the neonate's limb is one of the major limiting factors for a timely signal acquisition. Various techniques and alternatives have been proposed with a hypothetical basis for such variations in the placement techniques (O'Donnell 2005a). Other than the placement technique of the probes, inter‐equipment differences in their algorithm and make could potentially play a role in the speed of data display. One small study reported that Nellcor monitors displayed data more quickly once the sensor was placed on the neonate even though placing the sensor was easier with the Masimo monitors (Pinnamaneni 2010). NRP 2015 guidelines recommend attaching the sensor first to the newly born infant and then to the extension cable of the oximeter (Level of Evidence Class IIb, Recommendation Level C) (Perlman 2015). However, the most appropriate technique of placement of the pulse oximeter sensor in neonates in a delivery room setting is not clear. [Cariprazine versus placebo for schizophrenia] [Description of the condition]Schizophrenia is a serious mental health disorder affecting more than 21 million people worldwide (WHO 2015). It amounts to about 1.8% of global years lived with disability (YLDs) (Vos 2013). The symptoms of schizophrenia can be categorised into positive symptoms (e.g. hallucinations, delusions. thought disorders), negative symptoms (e.g. blunted affect, lack of motivation, social withdrawal) and cognitive symptoms (e.g. decline in new learning) (NIMH 2014). People with schizophrenia have increased mortality rates (up to 50%) compared with the general population due to a variety of comorbid medical conditions, and suicide with an approximate lifetime risk of suicide for schizophrenia in adults at 5% (NICE 2014). Schizophrenia also leaves a debilitating impact on the quality of life, leaving people living with schizophrenia struggling to not only deal with their diagnosis, but also with resulting difficult social life, employment and housing conditions (Solanki 2008).Schizophrenia may be diagnosed using different diagnostic systems. The most widely used are the International Classification of Disease (WHO 1992) and the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual (APA 2013). According to the latter, the diagnosis of schizophrenia requires an illness duration of at least six months and at least one month of active symptoms.Schizophrenia is classified as a multifactorial disorder as no single cause has been linked to it. Those factors can include genetics (Gejman 2010), environmental factors such as obstetric complications (Picchioni 2007), social isolation and familial support, migrant status, and urban life (Boydell 2004).There are many pharmacological and psychosocial therapies effective for treating schizophrenia, but no cure. Most pharmacological interventions have targeted the dopamine pathways in the brain ever since people with schizophrenia were shown to have an overactivity of dopamine in the central nervous system (Miyamoto 2012).Cariprazine is an orally active atypical antipsychotic drug. It was approved In September 2015 by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the treatment of schizophrenia and for the acute treatment of manic or mixed episodes associated with bipolar I disorder (McCormak 2015). Its starting dose is 1.5 mg on the first day and may be increased to 3 mg on the second day. Further dose adjustments can be made in 1.5 to 3 mg increments depending upon clinical response and tolerability. The dosage range is 1.5 mg to 6 mg a day.Cariprazine is rapidly absorbed and its concentration peaks in three to four hours in the blood of a fasting patient. It accumulates with continued administration, but its concentrations stay dose proportional in the effective dose range (Caccia 2013;Citrome 2013). It significantly penetrates the blood brain barrier with a brain/plasma area under curve (AUC) ratio of 7.6:1 as shown by a study on rodents (Kiss 2010). Active metabolites of cariprazine (desmethyl‐cariprazine and didesmethyl‐cariprazine) are retrieved through the extensive hepatic metabolism of the parent compound by cytochrome P450 (CYP) (mainly by CYP3A4 and to lesser extent by CYP2D6) just like other lipophilic antipsychotics (Caccia 2013). Cariprazine's mean half‐life is long and it varies from two to five days for cariprazine, and two to three weeks for didesmethyl‐cariprazine, which makes patient exposure to didesmethyl‐cariprazine several times higher than their exposure to cariprazine (Caccia 2013).Cariprazine has been reported to be associated with improvements in negative and positive symptoms of schizophrenia. Cariprazine is generally well‐tolerated. Its common adverse events include akathisia, restlessness, tremor, back pain, and extrapyramidal side effects (Durgam 2016;Kane 2015).Current antipsychotic drugs mainly target D2 receptors and have clinical benefit in treating positive symptoms with no effect on negative and cognitive symptoms (Dunlop 2015). Cariprazine, on the other hand, is a potent partial agonist of dopamine D3 and D2 receptors with preferential binding to the D3 receptor. However, there are a significant number of survivors with morbidities, such as retinopathy of prematurity (ROP), necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) and bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) (Stoll 2010). Oxygen free radicals are one of the agents implicated in causing the tissue damage that results in many of such adverse outcomes. From conception, preterm infants are exposed to free radical oxidative damage from intrauterine infections, resuscitation, mechanical ventilation and postnatal complications (Poggi 2014). Preterm infants are at risk from oxidative damage due to their higher metabolic rate and low levels of antioxidant enzymes, as both endogenous and passively acquired exogenous antioxidant defence systems do not mature until late in the third trimester (Baba 2008;Frank 1996). Other factors that increase oxidative damage include impaired antioxidant defence mechanism and increased susceptibility to infection and inflammation (Saugstad 2005).ROP is a disease that almost exclusively affects preterm infants. The relationship between hyperoxia and the development of ROP was discovered in the 1950s (Campbell 1951). As ROP has been related to hyperoxia, reactive oxygen stress may be involved in this disease (Shweiki 1992). Present treatment for severe ROP is mainly laser retinal ablation of the avascular retina. Supplementation with antioxidants such as D‐Penicillamine, vitamin A and vitamin C have been tried but have not been proven to reduce the rate of severe ROP (Darlow 2005;Darlow 2011;Qureshi 2013).The pathogenesis of BPD is multifactorial. Risk factors such as chorioamnionitis, systemic infection, inadequate resuscitation, fluid overload, patent ductus arteriosus, high‐inspired oxygen concentrations, barotrauma, volutrauma and mechanical ventilation cause injury through oxygen toxicity and inflammatory mediators (Saugstad 1998). Nutrition plays a critical role in prevention of BPD and antioxidant nutrients, including inositol, glutamine, cysteine and methionine, as well as vitamins and some trace elements are thought to play a role in protection of lung parenchyma (Biniwale 2006).The pathogenesis of NEC is a result of several causative factors, including gastrointestinal immaturity, hypoxia/ischaemia, hyperosmolar feedings, bacterial colonization and oxidative stress (Hsueh 2003). Management of NEC consists of bowel rest and decompression, antibiotics and management of other haematological or electrolyte imbalances. Surgical intervention may be indicated if pneumoperitoneum is present. Breast milk, early initiation of trophic feeds and judicious advancement of enteric feeds are postnatal strategies to prevent NEC. Both have proven roles in reducing oxidative damage especially in decreasing the risk for developing age‐related macular degeneration (AREDS2 2013). [Erythromycin and related macrolides for gastroparesis] [Description of the condition]Patients with functional gastrointestinal disorders consume a large amount of time and resources in the ambulatory practices of gastroenterologists (Parkman 2004). One such chronic functional disorder is gastroparesis. This condition is characterized by the stomach failing to move its contents into the small bowel in the absence of luminal obstruction. Typical symptoms of delayed or abnormal gastric emptying include nausea, vomiting, bloating, early satiety and abdominal discomfort (Soykan 1998). Gastroparesis may be caused by a number of conditions including diabetes, connective tissue disorders, certain neurologic and autoimmune diseases, drug therapy, and previous surgery; in a substantial number of cases there is no clear etiology (Soykan 1998).There are few population‐based studies on the epidemiology and impact of gastroparesis, and only a limited number of case‐based studies are available. The only community‐based study was in patients with diabetes mellitus (DM), which found the cumulative 10‐year incidence of gastroparesis symptoms and delayed gastric emptying to be highest in type 1 DM patients (5.2%) vs type 2 DM patients (1%) and controls (0.2%) (Choung 2012). Many researchers believe that the overall incidence of gastroparesis‐related hospitalizations in the United States has increased in the last two decades, particularly after 2000, thereby increasing direct healthcare costs (Bharucha 2015).Treatment of gastroparesis is usually applied in a stepwise fashion, including education, dietary support, treatment with prokinetic or antiemetic agents, and more recently, direct neuro‐stimulation using implantable electrodes. Unfortunately, the clinical benefits of the various treatment options are unclear, and no consensus exists as to the optimal therapeutic approach (Patrick 2008).Erythromycin is a macrolide antibiotic that can activate the motilin receptor. Motilin is a polypeptide hormone secreted by M cells in the duodenum and distal stomach during the fasting state. Motilin plays an important housekeeping role by pushing remnant food and bacteria along the gut to prevent overgrowth and nutrient malabsorption. It initiates phase III of the migrating myoelectric complex (MMC), which causes strong rhythmic contractions beginning in the lower esophogeal sphincter and traveling through the stomach to the ileum, thereby expediting gastric emptying (Richards 1993;Sarna 1991).Erythromycin and drugs of the same family may increase motility by activating the secretion of motilin, whose purpose is to assist in emptying the stomach. Erythromycin is widely used in patients with gastroparesis because of its prokinetic and gastric emptying properties. It has been shown to increase emptying in both patients with normal and impaired gastric emptying (Kendall 1997). Although both oral and intravenous applications seem efficacious, tachyphylaxis is a potential limiter to long‐term use (Desautels 1995).Even though studies have evaluated erythromycin's (or other macrolides) ability to improve gastric emptying, it is unclear if it reduces symptoms of gastroparesis. We plan to systematically review the available literature to determine the safety and efficacy of erythromycin in improving symptoms of gastroparesis. The secondary aim is to assess its efficacy in improving gastric emptying.A previous review from 2003 on symptom improvement of gastroparesis using erythromycin was inconclusive (Maganti 2003). Included studies suffered from inadequate sample sizes, inappropriate follow‐up, uncontrolled trial design and incomplete symptom evaluations that limited appropriate analysis. Since then, there have been many randomized trials to assess symptom relief of gastroparesis through the use of erythromycin. It is timely to summarize this new information and revisit the previous review's conclusions.Another review conducted on gastroparesis claimed that a few studies using erythromycin showed promising results for bloating symptoms (Patrick 2008). However, there was no formal assessment that comprehensively incorporated studies relating to erythromycin or its derivatives, nor were there comparisons to other modes of therapy.The efficacy and symptom improvement of both metoclopramide and domperidone for gastroparesis are well documented (Davis 1988;Horowitz 1985;Patterson 1999;Rayner 2001), but both treatments have side effects (Patrick 2008). Metoclopramide can frequently cause central antidopaminergic side effects including restlessness, fatigue, headache, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting and hyperprolactinemia leading to breast tenderness and galactorrhea. Acute dystonic reactions are rare but can manifest as tremor, trismus and torticollis within days of treatment initiation. Late and possibly irreversible side effects of metoclopramide include parkinsonian syndrome and tardive dyskinesia. Domperidone has antidopaminergic properties but fewer central side effects than metoclopramide (Patrick 2008). However, it can cause hyperprolactinemia resulting in menstrual cycle irregularity, breast engorgement and galactorrhea, and recently, there have been safety concerns about its arrhythmogenic potential (Van Noord 2010). There is also evidence of tachyphylaxis for both domperidone and metoclopramide (Horowitz 1985).Common side effects of erythromycin include rash, anorexia, abdominal cramping, nausea and abnormal liver tests. Torsades de pointes may be a rare complication with long‐term treatment (Patrick 2008). Given the relatively tolerable side effect profile, which is comparable if not superior to other commonly used agents, the clinical utility of erythromycin in gastroparesis warrants further study.A number of studies have shown poor correlation between mechanical improvement in gastric emptying and symptom improvement following a given intervention in managing gastroparesis (Maganti 2003). [Antenatal corticosteroids for fetal lung maturation: an overview of Cochrane reviews] [Description of the condition]Up to 10% of all births globally are preterm (born less than 37 weeks' gestational age) (March of Dimes 2012). Over one million babies die each year as a direct consequence of being born preterm (Lawn 2013). Preterm birth can have significant effects on short‐term morbidity and mortality, and also long‐term health and disability. The short‐term sequelae of preterm birth include respiratory distress syndrome (RDS), intraventricular haemorrhage (IVH), necrotising enterocolitis (NEC), retinopathy of prematurity, patent ductus arteriosus and sepsis (Haram 2003;Saigal 2008). RDS develops as a consequence of immature lung development and is the major cause of early neonatal morbidity and mortality in preterm infants. Prematurity can also predispose to the development of chronic lung disease (bronchopulmonary dysplasia) which may be associated with impaired airway function into adult life (Doyle 2006;Saigal 2008). In those infants who do survive there are increased risks of long‐term neurodevelopmental disability (Saigal 2008), including cerebral palsy, and intellectual, visual and hearing impairment (Anderson 2003;Doyle 2001;Farooqi 2006;Wood 2000). Therefore prematurity and its associated sequelae has significant psychosocial and emotional effects on families caring for these infants (Saigal 2000;Singer 1999). Being born preterm also increases the risk of developing non‐communicable diseases such as diabetes and hypertension in later life (Hovi 2007).The rates of preterm birth are increasing in almost all countries with reliable data (Blencowe 2012). The greatest burden of preterm birth occurs in Africa and Asia (Blencowe 2012) where the use of interventions to mitigate the effects of preterm birth varies substantially (Vogel 2014). Reasons for preterm birth vary by geographical location. In high‐income countries the numbers of provider‐initiated preterm births has been rising (Blencowe 2012). In France and the United States, over 30% of all preterm births were medically indicated in 2000 (Blondel 2012;Davidoff 2006). It is difficult to differentiate the cause of preterm birth in low‐ and middle‐income countries due to the lack of population‐based studies. However medically‐indicated preterm births represent a much smaller proportion of all preterm births in low‐ and middle‐income countries when compared with spontaneous preterm birth (Alhaj 2010;Nkyekyer 2006).Overall, up to a third of all preterm births and up to half of very preterm births are provider‐initiated (encompasses urgent, discretionary, iatrogenic and social) (Goldenberg 2008;Menon 2008;Steer 2005). The main maternal/fetal indications for preterm delivery are maternal pre‐eclampsia, antepartum haemorrhage, and chronic or acute fetal compromise, including fetal distress and severe intrauterine growth restriction (Ananth 2006). The incidence of medically indicated preterm birth is likely to continue to rise due to increasing maternal disease, particularly in view of the world‐wide epidemics of diabetes and obesity (Lawn 2013).The aetiology of spontaneous preterm birth is not completely understood but it is likely to be multifactorial (Lawn 2013). In up to half of the cases the cause remains unknown (Menon 2008). Up to half of spontaneous preterm births occur following preterm prelabour rupture of membranes (Goldenberg 2008). Another important risk factor is multiple pregnancy, which is responsible for approximately 15% to 20% of all preterm births (Goldenberg 2008). A large contributor to the increasing incidence of multiple pregnancies has been advancing maternal age and the use of assisted reproductive techniques (Felberbaum 2007). Advancing maternal age has also been identified as an independent risk factor for spontaneous preterm birth (Goldenberg 2008).The incidence of preterm birth is not equally distributed across all gestational ages. Only 5% of preterm births occur at less than 28 weeks’ gestation, approximately 15% at 28 to 31 weeks’, 20% at 32 to 33 weeks’ and 60% to 70% at 34 to 36 weeks’ gestation (Goldenberg 2008). However, these figures can also vary depending on geographical location. Recent data from Australia reported an overall incidence of preterm birth of 7.7%, of which 10% occurred at 20 to 27 weeks’, 9% at 28 to 31 weeks and 81% at 32 to 36 weeks' gestation (Hilder 2014). Overall, the risks associated with prematurity are inversely related to gestational age (Saigal 2008).Marked improvement in survival rates of preterm infants in recent decades, particularly those born very preterm, has been attributed to administration of antenatal corticosteroids, surfactant use, the use of assisted ventilation and changing attitudes towards intensive care (Doyle 1999;Roberts 2006;Rojas‐Reyes 2012). However survival rates vary significantly depending on where preterm infants are born. The improvement in mortality in high‐income countries is most marked at extremes of gestation and in infants of extremely low birthweight (Saigal 2008). Population‐based cohort studies in Australia have demonstrated marked improvement in survival of extremely low birthweight infants from 25% in 1979, to 80% to 73% in 1997 (Doyle 2001). Similarly, a national cohort study in the UK demonstrated an increase in survival of infants born between 22 and 25 weeks’ gestation between 1995 and 2006 from 40% to 53% (Costeloe 2012). However this trend is not reflected in low‐income countries where more than 90% of very preterm infants (less than 28 weeks’ gestation) die within the first few days of life compared with less than 10% in high‐income settings (March of Dimes 2012).Uncertainty still exists around the use of antenatal corticosteroids at later gestations. This question has become increasingly important in view of increasing numbers of caesarean sections at both term and late preterm gestations (McClure 2007). Undergoing a caesarean section predisposes the neonate to respiratory complications including RDS and transient tachypnoea of the newborn (Hook 1997;Maisels 1977;Morrison 1995). Opinion is divided on the necessity of antenatal corticosteroids at term, as approximately only 5% of these babies will require admission for respiratory distress and serious morbidity is uncommon (Stutchfield 2005). There is also some concern about the potential for long‐term adverse effects of corticosteroid exposure in more mature fetuses (Aiken 2014;Steer 2005). [Melatonin for treating pre‐eclampsia] [Description of the condition]This protocol has been based on and further developed using the Cochrane Generic Protocol 'Interventions for treating pre‐eclampsia and its consequences' (Duley 2009) alongside the Cochrane Protocol 'Melatonin for preventing pre‐eclampsia' (Hobson 2015).Pre‐eclampsia is part of a spectrum of conditions known as the hypertensive disorders of pregnancy. Pre‐eclampsia itself is a multi‐organ syndrome unique to human pregnancy that manifests after 20 weeks' gestation with new‐onset hypertension (high blood pressure), alongside maternal end‐organ dysfunction and/or fetal growth restriction (Lowe 2015). It affects between 2% to 8% of all pregnancies and is associated with substantial maternal and perinatal morbidity and mortality, with a significant proportion of fetal complications due to the need for premature delivery (Ghulmiyyah 2012;Payne 2011). The majority of women with pre‐eclampsia are usually asymptomatic, however those with severe pre‐eclampsia, or very high blood pressure, may feel unwell with symptoms such as headache, upper abdominal pain or visual disturbances.At present, the pathophysiology of pre‐eclampsia is poorly understood, but early placental dysfunction plays a central role in all leading hypotheses (Roberts 2005;Steegers 2010). This placental dysfunction is thought to result in a local and systemic cascade of increasing oxidative stress in the mother, leading to endothelial (blood vessel) dysfunction and subsequent end‐organ consequences. Oxidative stress is essentially an imbalance between the production of free radicals and the ability of the body to counteract or detoxify their harmful effects through neutralisation by antioxidants.Placental hypoxia (low oxygen reaching the tissues) and reperfusion, as a consequence of abnormal placentation, generates profound oxidative stress which causes apoptotic (programmed cell death) and necrotic (injured cell death) disruption of the syncytial structure (the cellular interface between the mother and placenta). This disruption then results in the release of various factors and compounds from the intervillous space (where the placenta exchanges oxygen, nutrients and waste with the maternal blood vessels) into the maternal circulation that stimulate the production of pro‐inflammatory cytokines (cell signalling proteins), such as tumour necrosis factor alpha (TNF alpha), interleukin (IL)‐6 and anti‐angiogenic (anti‐blood vessel growth) factors, such as soluble fms‐like tyrosine kinase 1 (sFlt1) and soluble endoglin (sEng) (Steegers 2010). Together these result in further widespread oxidative stress with anti‐angiogenic compromise to the maternal vasculature (Hubel 1999).Dysfunction of the maternal vasculature leads to marked hypertension, increased vascular permeability in all maternal systems, along with the potential for fetal growth restriction and associated compromise leading to preterm birth. Approximately 10% of women will experience the potentially life threatening forms of severe pre‐eclampsia manifesting as HELLP (Haemolysis,ElevatedLiver enzymes andLowPlatelets) syndrome or eclamptic seizures (Fenton 2014). An estimated 10% to 15% of maternal deaths in developing countries are associated with pre‐eclampsia or eclampsia, as are 13% to 15% of the direct obstetric deaths in the UK and USA (Duley 2009). Perinatal mortality is also increased following pre‐eclampsia (Roberts 2005).Currently, there is no known curative treatment of the disease aside from delivery of the baby and placenta. For women with severe pre‐eclampsia before 32 to 34 weeks’ gestation, the optimal timing for delivery is a major dilemma, a precarious balance exists between the conflicting needs to protect the mother by ending pregnancy to limit further progression, and to maximise maturity for the baby by delaying the birth (Churchill 2013). While delivery may stop the release of the causal factors leading to maternal systemic disease, there is still a risk of new‐onset pre‐eclamptic complications during the postpartum period, including eclampsia. Close observation and supportive treatments are therefore warranted in the postpartum period with appropriate longer‐term follow‐up of patients to ensure resolution of signs of disease such as hypertension or proteinuria.There is a growing body of evidence that women who have pre‐eclampsia are at increased risk later in life of hypertension, stroke, and ischaemic heart disease (Bellamy 2007;Hannaford 1997;Wilson 2003), although it remains unclear whether this reﬂects a common pathway or whether having pre‐eclampsia increases this risk (Duley 2009). For the babies, pre‐eclampsia is an antecedent for up to 12% of those born small‐for‐gestational age (Kramer 2000) and 19% of those born preterm (Hewitt 1988). Such children are at an increased risk of developmental delay and chronic ill health in childhood (Duley 2009).Melatonin (5‐methoxy‐N‐acetyltryptamine) is an endogenous lipid‐soluble antioxidant hormone produced primarily by the pineal gland in humans, providing circadian and seasonal timing cues (Hobson 2015). In addition, melatonin is also a powerful antioxidant, acting both as a direct scavenger of oxygen free radicals, especially the highly damaging hydroxyl radical, and indirectly via up‐regulation of antioxidant enzymes including glutathione peroxidase, glutathione reductase, superoxide dismutase and catalase (Reiter 2000;Reiter 2003).Clinically, oral melatonin is an accepted and effective preventative measure and treatment for jet lag (Herxheimer 2002). A Cochrane review has demonstrated behavioural benefits when used in dementia patients (Jansen 2006). In the field of neonatology, melatonin treatment in asphyxiated newborns reduced oxidative stress and prevented an elevation of circulating markers of oxidative stress (malondialdehyde and nitrite/nitrate) (Fulia 2001), while in those with septicaemia, melatonin administration reduced oxidative stress and lead to an improvement in clinical outcomes (Gitto 2009).In human reproduction, melatonin has been studied in several clinical trials at varying gestations and for different purposes (Reiter 2009). It has been assessed in assisted reproductive technology where the quality of oocytes is important for the success of in‐vitro fertilisation (IVF). [Antiepileptic drugs for Tourette's syndrome] [Description of the condition]Tourette's syndrome (TS) is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterised by at least one phonic and several motor tics present for more than one year, which appear in childhood and are often accompanied by behavioural symptoms (Stern 2005;Pierce 2009). Tics are defined as repetitive, involuntary, sudden, rapid, non‐rhythmic movements (motor tics) and vocalisations (vocal or phonic tics) that can involve discrete muscle groups. The typical age of onset of tics is four to six years, with a male:female ratio of approximately 4:1 (Cavanna 2013;Dutta 2013). Epidemiological studies have found that TS affects between 0.3% and 1% of school age children (Robertson 2009;Scharf 2012). A meta‐analysis of the prevalence of TS is 0.77% (95% confidence interval (CI) 0.39% to 1.51%) in children, and 0.05% (95% CI 0.03% to 0.08%) in adults (Knight 2012).As well as the phonic or motor tics, TS is also associated with comorbid conditions such as attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), obsessive compulsive disorder, behavioural difficulties including self‐injurious/disinhibited behaviours, anxiety and depression (Roessner 2007;Pierce 2009;Wanderer 2012). Often, these comorbidities are more bothersome to patients than the tics. TS and associated problems can have a negative effect on patients' daily functioning across many domains (Roessner 2013). It is necessary to give timely intervention for patients with TS, otherwise TS can often lead to detrimental long‐term effects on social adaptation, academic success, self‐image, and self‐esteem. These risks are particularly important for children who have TS as well as one or more comorbid conditions (Sandor 2012).The exact mechanisms of TS remain unclear. However, the following may be important: (1) dysfunction of the dopaminergic pathways within the cortico‐striato‐cortico‐frontal circuitry (Felling 2011); (2) deficits in cerebral maturation, in particular at the level of striatal interneurone migration and genetic predisposition (Felling 2011); (3) environmental factors, including infections and autoimmune dysfunction, as well as prenatal and perinatal problems (Cavanna 2013).Psychotherapies and pharmacotherapies are widely used for the treatment of TS including the tics and comorbid symptoms, with pharmacotherapy currently the mainstay of treatment (Yang 2015). At present, the main treatments for tics are neuroleptic drugs (e.g. haloperidol, pimozide), atypical antipsychotics (e.g. risperidone, aripiprazole), substitute benzamides (e.g. sulpiride, tiapride) and presynaptic dopamine depletors (such as tetrabenazine) (Cavanna 2013;Waldon 2013;Weisman 2013). However, the use of neuroleptic drugs in TS and other psychiatric disorders has become less common due to their poor tolerability profile (e.g. extrapyramidal and metabolic side effects) (Robertson 2000). Atypical antipsychotics are better tolerated overall and have similar efficacy for tic control, with a lower risk of extrapyramidal side effects (Correll 2004). However, metabolic side effects, including weight gain and hyperlipidemia (an abnormally high concentration of fatty substances in the blood) have restricted their use (Fedorowicz 2005). Substitute benzamides also have serious metabolic side effects, especially hyperprolactinaemia and weight gain (Cavanna 2013). Clinical enthusiasm for alternative treatments is, thus, understandable, antiepileptic drugs might be promising therapies for TS. Recently, a multicentre double‐blind, placebo‐controlled trial reported that topiramate showed statistically significant improvements in suppressing tics (Jankovic 2010). Some prospective, open‐label studies showed patients with TS improved in the Yale Global Tic Severity Scale (YGTSS) or the scale of Modified Clinical Global Impression (MCGI) scores after treatment with levetiracetam (Awaad 2005;Fernández 2009).Antiepileptic drugs (AEDs) work by modifying different structures and processes such as ion channels, neurons, glia and inhibitory and excitatory synapses involved in seizure development (Deckers 2000;Wiffen 2013;Pandey 2014). The majority of AEDs are thought to have more than one mode of action and, although AEDs' precise mechanism of action for TS remains unclear, there are two main hypotheses of mechanisms which may be benificial for controlling tics:AEDs (such as levetiracetam, topiramate, clonazepam, valproate) enhance gamma‐aminobutyric acid (GABA) inhibition, bind to SV2a, a synaptic vesicle protein found in neurons, and have an GABAergic effect by enhancing chloride ion influx at the GABA‐A receptor complex (Poulain 2002;Rigo 2002;Toth 2005).AEDs (such as topiramate) also block the AMPA/kainate subtype of glutamate receptors without affecting the N‐methyl‐D‐aspartate (NMDA) subtype (Jankovic 2010).AEDs (such as levetiracetam, topiramate, clonazepam, valproate) enhance gamma‐aminobutyric acid (GABA) inhibition, bind to SV2a, a synaptic vesicle protein found in neurons, and have an GABAergic effect by enhancing chloride ion influx at the GABA‐A receptor complex (Poulain 2002;Rigo 2002;Toth 2005).AEDs (such as topiramate) also block the AMPA/kainate subtype of glutamate receptors without affecting the N‐methyl‐D‐aspartate (NMDA) subtype (Jankovic 2010).So far, the effects of AEDs on TS are controversial and there is currently no systematic review of antiepileptic agents for TS.
