[Non‐pharmacological treatments for improving memory in people with epilepsy] [Description of the condition]Epilepsy is a chronic neurological disorder affecting nearly 50 million people worldwide (WHO 2015), characterised by recurrent involuntary brain activity manifesting in seizures (Chang 2003). It is associated with several comorbidities including psychological and cognition difficulties (Bell 2011). Cognitive impairment is a major concern among people with epilepsy. A survey of over 1000 patients with epilepsy found that cognitive impairment was ranked as their greatest concern (Fisher 2000). Memory difficulties are the most commonly reported cognitive impairment in epilepsy (Hendriks 2002) with 20% to 50% of people with epilepsy complaining of memory impairments (Hendriks 2002). Memory problems are cited to have a marked adverse effect on quality of life (Hall 2009).Several factors may affect memory in people with epilepsy. The use of antiepileptic drugs (AEDs) seizure foci, interictal epileptiform activity (specific electrical abnormalities occurring in the brain between seizures), and seizure activity may disrupt the encoding of new information into memory and the retrieval of previously stored information (Hall 2009). Cognitive impairments in epilepsy are addressed indirectly by effective seizure control, careful selection and adjustment of AED doses, restructuring of antiepileptic drug polytherapy regimens, and treatment of co‐morbid depression (Shulman 2002). However, this systematic review will focus instead upon the non‐pharmacological interventions for the direct treatment of memory problems associated with epilepsy.Vagus nerve stimulation is a device, similar to a pacemaker, which generates regular electrical stimulation to the brain via the vagus nerve. It is a Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved add‐on therapy for reducing seizure frequency in medically refractory partial epilepsy. The efficacy of VNS in reducing and preventing medically refractory seizures is supported by a significant amount of clinical evidence. The use of VNS has been shown to reduce seizure frequency by 24.5% to 30.9% (Landy 1993;Ben‐Menachem 1994;Handforth 1998;Panebianco 2015). However, the effects of VNS on cognition are less established with some studies reporting memory enhancement (Cramer 2001;Ghacibeh 2006) and others describing no change or deterioration in memory (Helmstaedter 2001;Hoppe 2001;McGlone 2008). In addition, a small randomised clinical trial found that the administration of VNS following learning improved word‐recognition memory in people with epilepsy (Clark 1999).Deep brain stimulation is a device which generates regular stimulation to specific parts of the brain via implanted electrodes in the brain. It is an FDA approved treatment for Parkinson’s disease, dystonia and central tremor. Research has demonstrated the efficacy of DBS for reducing seizure frequency in epilepsy (Sprengers 2014). Several studies of DBS of the anterior nucleus of thalamus (ANT) reported 50% or greater reduction in mean seizure frequency in 16% to 100% of epilepsy patients (Hodaie 2002;Kerrigan 2004;Andrade 2006;Lim 2007;Osorio 2007). In addition, a multicenter randomised trial of bilateral stimulation of the ANT in refractory partial epilepsy found stimulated patients experienced a 40% reduction in seizure frequency compared with 14% of controls (Fisher 2010). Several recent studies have examined the effects of DBS on cognition in people with epilepsy; one study of bilateral ANT stimulation found that DBS was associated with significantly improved performance in verbal fluency and delayed verbal memory tasks (Oh 2012), and stimulation of the entorhinal region during learning significantly enhanced performance on a spatial learning task which required patients to navigate through a virtual environment (Suthana 2012).Transcranial magnetic stimulation is a non‐invasive procedure which uses electromagnetic induction to deliver a magnetic field across the scalp stimulating nerve cells in regions of the brain (Ališauskienė 2005). Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) has been studied extensively as a treatment for a variety of psychiatric and neurological conditions including depression, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, post‐traumatic stress disorder, Parkinson’s disease, dystonia, and epilepsy (Rossi 2009). A number of small studies and case reports have demonstrated the efficacy of rTMS for reducing seizure frequency in refractory partial epilepsy (Tergau 1999;Menkes 2000;Joo 2007) and epilepsia partialis continua (Graff‐Guerrero 2004;Misawa 2005;Rotenberg 2008). Currently, seven randomised controlled trials have examined efficacy of TMS for seizure reduction in epilepsy with four studies reporting significant results (Tergau 2003;Fregni 2006;Wang 2008;Sun 2012) and three studies reporting insignificant results (Theodore 2002;Cantello 2007;Joo 2007). One clinical trial (Fregni 2006), and one case report (Cotelli 2012) of rTMS in refractory epilepsy patients with malformations of cortical development found that this improved some aspects of cognition functioning.The ketogenic diet is a high‐fat, moderate‐protein, low‐carbohydrate diet used in the treatment of refractory epilepsy, primarily in children. The ketogenic diet is based on a 3:1 or 4:1 fat to protein and carbohydrate ratio imitating the biochemical effects of fasting (Neal 2010). A low‐carbohydrate, high‐fat diet causes the body to enter a ketotic state, which leads to a reduction in seizure frequency (Huffman 2006). Two systematic reviews of the ketogenic diet report about 16% of children achieve seizure freedom and 33% to 56% experience a greater than 50% reduction in seizure frequency (Lefevre 2000;Keene 2006). A randomised controlled trial found the ketogenic diet to significantly reduce seizure frequency in children, with 38% of those assigned to the diet having a greater than 50% reduction in seizures compared with 6% on the waiting list control group (Neal 2010). A recent Cochrane review (Levy 2012) identified four randomised control trials that assessed the efficacy of the ketogenic diet and concluded that there are short to medium benefits, but tolerability is low over a longer period of time (Bergqvist 2005;Seo 2007;Kassoff 2008;Neal 2008).Cognitive rehabilitation is a neuropsychological treatment program focused on the training of attention and memory functions in people with cognitive deficits due to brain injury. Although training strategies vary for each program, compensation, rather than restoration, is the primary aim of cognitive rehabilitation (Ponds 2006). Compensatory strategies can be either external or internal in nature. External memory strategies include methods of storing information externally and reminding oneself to complete a certain activity, such as the use of an electronic agenda (Koorenhof 2012). Internal memory strategies focus on the elaboration and visualization of information to facilitate later retrieval (Ponds 2006). Research has demonstrated the effectiveness of cognitive rehabilitation programs for the treatment of epilepsy‐related memory problems (Bresson 2007;Helmstaedter 2008;Radford 2011;Koorenhof 2012). However, methodologies and program characteristics varied significantly from study to study. A randomised controlled trial of two cognitive rehabilitation programs, the retraining method and the compensation method, found both treatment strategies to be effective in improving self‐reported cognitive outcomes and quality of life in people with epilepsy (Engelberts 2002).The mechanisms of action of vagus nerve stimulation and how it may affect memory are not completely understood. However, the presumed mechanism of action of VNS involves activation of upstream neural networks from the input of the vagus nerve into the medulla and deep brain structures (George 2000). Some functional imaging evidence has indicated that the thalamus and mesial temporal lobe, structures involved in aspects of memory, are activated during vagus nerve stimulation in patients with epilepsy and treatment resistant depression (Lomarev 2002;Henry 2004). Secondary benefits may occur through improved alertness and attentional capacities, as well as the prospect of a reduction in AEDs (Tatum 2001;Kostov 2009;Shahwan 2009).The mechanisms of deep brain stimulation are also not fully understood. However, mechanisms of action for improvement in seizure control and potential benefits for cognitive functioning likely depend upon the region in the brain selected for neurostimulation, as well as neural network interrelationships with targets of stimulation. Deep brain stimulation therapy in epilepsy thus far has most frequently targeted the anterior nucleus of thalamus (ANT). Three neuroanatomic circuits which are implicated in seizure propagation, the corticothalamic, mammillothalamic, and Papez circuits, involve the ANT (Mirski 1986;Takebayashi 2007;Lega 2010). Thus, DBS may exert a positive, indirect effect on cognition by decreasing abnormal, epileptic activity within these pathways (Zhong 2011). In addition, recent research has found that electrical stimulation during preoperative intracranial recording of another neuroanatomical target, the entorhinal cortex, improved spatial memory in patients with epilepsy (Suthana 2012).In transcranial magnetic stimulation, an alternating electric current passes through a coil of wire, creating a rapidly changing magnetic field which is concentrated to a specific area, depending on coil shape (Hallett 2000). When a TMS device is positioned, the magnetic field passes through the skull and causes neurons near that area to generate action potentials which may have excitatory or inhibitory effects (Hemond 2007). More specifically, low‐frequency rTMS has been shown to reduce the excitability of neurons in the motor cortex (Chen 1997;Muellbacher 2000;Modugno 2003), which are hyperexcitable in medically refractory epilepsy (Macdonell 2002;Tassinari 2003;Cantello 2007). Research has demonstrated that rTMS may improve cognitive performance by affecting electrical activity of the brain (Klimesch 1999;Jensen 2002;Klimesch 2003;Hamidi 2009).The mechanisms of action of the ketogenic diet and seizure reduction are not completely understood. The ketogenic diet may reduce seizure frequency through a variety of metabolic changes, including ketosis (Huffman 2006). Acetone, which is elevated during ketosis (Seymour 1999;Likhodii 2002), has been shown to have anticonvulsant properties (Likhodii 2003). Some evidence suggests that certain ketone bodies may protect neurons in structures implicated in learning and memory (Massieu 2003). Only one prospective study, which included 65 children being treated with ketogenic diets, has reported benefits in cognitive functioning (Pulsifer 2001). However, many other studies suggest that this intervention may positively affect cognition through seizure reduction and neuroprotection.Cognitive rehabilitation is different from other potential treatments for epilepsy‐associated memory problems as it does not target a neurochemical or structural problem within the brain, but rather improves memory by training patients in a variety of compensatory strategies. These behavioural strategies require practice and aim to reduce patients’ reliance on impaired cognitive faculties, thereby reducing anxiety when faced with a memory task (Engelberts 2002). Mnemonic strategies, such as name‐face associations and the method of loci, use visual elaboration to facilitate memory by providing patients with additional relational cues that may serve to enhance recall (Ponds 2006). In addition, the use of an electronic agenda or other device provides patients with a way to store information externally and prompt themselves to complete a particular task (Koorenhof 2012).Cognitive impairments are common in people with epilepsy, especially complaints of memory problems. Currently, few therapies exist for the direct treatment of memory problems in people with epilepsy and few studies have examined the efficacy of specific treatments for memory impairment in epilepsy. [Transfusion of fresh versus non‐fresh (older) red blood cell in neonates] [Description of the condition]Red blood cell transfusions are often administered to neonates, in particular to preterm infants, primarily to treat anaemia of prematurity, blood loss and cardiopulmonary diseases (Kasat 2011;Kelly 2013;Ohlsson 2014). Despite the benefits of this treatment, there are many risks associated with this intervention including iron overload, hyperkalaemia, hypocalcaemia, dilutional coagulopathy, transfusion reactions and infection (Abdelghaffar 2012;Kasat 2011;Sloan 2011). Additionally, frequent red blood cell transfusions have been associated with numerous adverse outcomes including chronic lung disease (CLD), retinopathy of prematurity, necrotising enterocolitis, intraventricular haemorrhage and impaired mental development (Christensen 2014;Kasat 2011;Mohamed 2012). Furthermore, there remains uncertainty regarding possible differences in morbidity and mortality in neonates who have received fresh versus non‐fresh red blood cell transfusions (Wagner 2014).For the purpose of this review, we will consider red blood cells transfused within seven days of donationfresh, whilenon‐freshred blood cells will refer to those that have been stored for up to 42 days following donation (D'Alessandro 2010). Improvements in preservative solutions and storage techniques have made it possible to store red blood cells for this duration (Sparrow 2012). However, such longer‐term storage results in the progressive accumulation ofred blood cell storage lesions(see:How the intervention might work) and an altogether reduction of in vivo survival time of the red blood cells when transfused (D'Alessandro 2010;Hod 2010;Sparrow 2012). In comparison, fresh red blood cells are believed to have longer in vivo survival times (Hod 2010).Neonatal red blood cell transfusion practices vary between health facilities and clinical situations, and according to the expert opinion of the healthcare team. However, common indications for transfusion include severe anaemia, cardiopulmonary disease and blood loss (Kasat 2011). Neonates who are administered red blood cells may be transfused with fresh or non‐fresh units, with the rate of transfusion dependent on body weight. As previously mentioned, 'fresh' and 'non‐fresh' solely refer to the age of the cells, with both types being preserved in an anticoagulant solution with or without a nutrient additive solution and stored in a similar manner. Commonly used anticoagulant solutions include citrate‐phosphate‐dextrose‐adenine (CPDA), citrate‐phosphate‐dextrose (CPD) and citrate‐phosphate‐double dextrose (CP2D), and commonly used additive solutions include additive solutions 1, 3 and 5 (AS‐1, AS‐3, AS‐5), mannitol‐adenine‐phosphate (MAP), phosphate‐adenine‐glucose‐guanosine‐saline‐mannitol (PAGGSM) and saline‐adenine‐glucose‐mannitol (SAGM) (Hess 2006;Sparrow 2012).Differences between the morbidity and mortality of neonates who have received fresh versus non‐fresh red blood cell transfusions may be attributable to age‐related changes of the stored red blood cells, the additive solutions, the number of transfusions required by the neonate, or a combination of these (D'Alessandro 2010;Flegel 2012;Hod 2010;Sloan 2011). Longer‐term storage of red blood cells results in the progressive accumulation of red blood cell storage lesions including intracellular potassium leakage, altered metabolism, morphological changes and variations to cell membrane structures (Abdelghaffar 2012;D'Alessandro 2010).At storage temperatures of approximately 4°C, the activity of Na+/K+pumps on the red blood cell membranes is significantly impaired, resulting in the passive leakage of potassium ions out of the cells and into the plasma or additive solution. Karon et al. have observed that extracellular potassium concentration rapidly increases with cold storage of packed red blood cells up to 42 days (Karon 2012). These ionic changes impact upon cellular physiology and pose a risk of hyperkalaemia in neonates who are rapidly transfused with older red blood cell units. This risk is superimposed in infants with impaired renal function (Abdelghaffar 2012;D'Alessandro 2010). In addition, the production of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) is reduced with prolonged red blood cell storage due to general slowing of cellular metabolism, and there is an increase in the number of morphologically variant red blood cells, including echinocytes and sphero‐echinocytes up to 42 days of storage (Karon 2012). Furthermore, oxidative and apoptotic changes to the red blood cell membranes and lipid vesicles accumulate with the duration of storage (D'Alessandro 2010;Tinmouth 2006). Altogether, these lesions accumulate throughout the duration of red blood cell storage and are postulated to reduce in vivo oxygen‐carrying capacity of the cells or induce inflammatory responses (or both) in transfused patients (Tinmouth 2006). This could result in differences between the morbidity and mortality of neonates who have received fresh versus non‐fresh red blood cell transfusions.The additive solutions in which red blood cells are stored are significantly acidic (pH 5.6 to 5.8) compared to the physiological pH of human blood (pH 7.35 to 7.45) (Sparrow 2012), with these differences potentially contributing to differences in morbidity and mortality. The acidity of the additive solutions impairs the production of 2,3‐diphosphoglycerate (2,3‐DPG) in stored red blood cells, with a decline in levels occurring within the first seven days of storage (D'Alessandro 2010;Sparrow 2012). The reduced levels of 2,3‐DPG in older red blood cells leads to an increased affinity of haemoglobin for oxygen, with a consequent reduction in oxygen availability at metabolic sites after transfusion. Notably, this drop in 2,3‐DPG and concomitant reduction in oxygen availability is generally reversed within 72 hours of transfusion (D'Alessandro 2010). However, the reduced oxygen availability due to transfusion of older red blood cells could pose a risk to seriously ill neonates within this 72‐hour window. In addition, the acidity of the additive solutions further reduces the production of ATP by stored red blood cells (D'Alessandro 2010;Sparrow 2012). These changes may contribute to differences in morbidity and mortality between neonates receiving fresh versus non‐fresh red blood cells.Difference in morbidity and mortality between neonates receiving fresh versus non‐fresh red blood cells may be associated with the number of transfusions required by the neonate. In vivo survival time of transfused red blood cells is reduced according to the length of storage (Hod 2010). The aforementioned morphological changes that occur with storage may account for the reduced in vivo survival time of non‐fresh red blood cell units compared to fresh units (Hod 2010;Karon 2012). As such, the utilisation of fresh red blood cell units could potentially lead to a reduction in the number of transfusions required by chronically ill neonates, with a parallel reduction in the risks associated with these transfusions (Flegel 2012).Seriously ill neonates, in particular preterm infants, are frequently administered red blood cell transfusions (Kelly 2013). There is uncertainty as to whether transfusing non‐fresh red blood cell units, as compared to fresh units, results in differences in morbidity and mortality of the treated neonate. Given the frequent use of red blood cell transfusions, it is pertinent to investigate the effects of fresh versus non‐fresh (older) red blood cell transfusions on infant morbidity and mortality to inform clinical practice guidelines. This will be the first systematic review of randomised controlled trials (RCTs) pertaining to this research question. Longer‐term storage of red blood cells results in the progressive accumulation of red blood cell storage lesions including intracellular potassium leakage, altered metabolism, morphological changes and variations to cell membrane structures (Abdelghaffar 2012;D'Alessandro 2010).At storage temperatures of approximately 4°C, the activity of Na+/K+pumps on the red blood cell membranes is significantly impaired, resulting in the passive leakage of potassium ions out of the cells and into the plasma or additive solution. Karon et al. have observed that extracellular potassium concentration rapidly increases with cold storage of packed red blood cells up to 42 days (Karon 2012). These ionic changes impact upon cellular physiology and pose a risk of hyperkalaemia in neonates who are rapidly transfused with older red blood cell units. This risk is superimposed in infants with impaired renal function (Abdelghaffar 2012;D'Alessandro 2010). In addition, the production of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) is reduced with prolonged red blood cell storage due to general slowing of cellular metabolism, and there is an increase in the number of morphologically variant red blood cells, including echinocytes and sphero‐echinocytes up to 42 days of storage (Karon 2012). Furthermore, oxidative and apoptotic changes to the red blood cell membranes and lipid vesicles accumulate with the duration of storage (D'Alessandro 2010;Tinmouth 2006). Altogether, these lesions accumulate throughout the duration of red blood cell storage and are postulated to reduce in vivo oxygen‐carrying capacity of the cells or induce inflammatory responses (or both) in transfused patients (Tinmouth 2006). This could result in differences between the morbidity and mortality of neonates who have received fresh versus non‐fresh red blood cell transfusions.The additive solutions in which red blood cells are stored are significantly acidic (pH 5.6 to 5.8) compared to the physiological pH of human blood (pH 7.35 to 7.45) (Sparrow 2012), with these differences potentially contributing to differences in morbidity and mortality. The acidity of the additive solutions impairs the production of 2,3‐diphosphoglycerate (2,3‐DPG) in stored red blood cells, with a decline in levels occurring within the first seven days of storage (D'Alessandro 2010;Sparrow 2012). The reduced levels of 2,3‐DPG in older red blood cells leads to an increased affinity of haemoglobin for oxygen, with a consequent reduction in oxygen availability at metabolic sites after transfusion. Notably, this drop in 2,3‐DPG and concomitant reduction in oxygen availability is generally reversed within 72 hours of transfusion (D'Alessandro 2010). However, the reduced oxygen availability due to transfusion of older red blood cells could pose a risk to seriously ill neonates within this 72‐hour window. In addition, the acidity of the additive solutions further reduces the production of ATP by stored red blood cells (D'Alessandro 2010;Sparrow 2012). These changes may contribute to differences in morbidity and mortality between neonates receiving fresh versus non‐fresh red blood cells.Difference in morbidity and mortality between neonates receiving fresh versus non‐fresh red blood cells may be associated with the number of transfusions required by the neonate. In vivo survival time of transfused red blood cells is reduced according to the length of storage (Hod 2010). The aforementioned morphological changes that occur with storage may account for the reduced in vivo survival time of non‐fresh red blood cell units compared to fresh units (Hod 2010;Karon 2012). As such, the utilisation of fresh red blood cell units could potentially lead to a reduction in the number of transfusions required by chronically ill neonates, with a parallel reduction in the risks associated with these transfusions (Flegel 2012).[Why it is important to do this review]Seriously ill neonates, in particular preterm infants, are frequently administered red blood cell transfusions (Kelly 2013). There is uncertainty as to whether transfusing non‐fresh red blood cell units, as compared to fresh units, results in differences in morbidity and mortality of the treated neonate. Given the frequent use of red blood cell transfusions, it is pertinent to investigate the effects of fresh versus non‐fresh (older) red blood cell transfusions on infant morbidity and mortality to inform clinical practice guidelines. This will be the first systematic review of randomised controlled trials (RCTs) pertaining to this research question. Previous Cochrane reviews have investigated partial, single or double volume exchange transfusion (Mills 2001;Thayyil 2006;Özek 2010), but not fresh versus non‐fresh (older) red blood cell transfusions.. [Tests for screening for hearing loss in children about to start school] [Target condition being diagnosed]Early identification of significant hearing loss is essential to enable timely intervention to safeguard against the effect of hearing loss. Hearing loss can be temporary or permanent but, depending upon the severity, both can have a significant impact on a child's speech and language development, educational achievement and general development, with a longer‐term risk to mental health and quality of life (Davis 1986;Holm 1969;Moeller 2000;Pimperton 2012;Yoshinaga‐Itano 1998;Yoshinaga‐Itano 2000).Hearing screening programmes are undertaken to identify hearing loss and thereby enable active intervention to provide children with access to sound. Timing of the screen has been tried at two points: newborn and school entry. Several countries now have both newborn hearing screening programmes (WHO 2010), and school entry screening programmes (Skarżyński 2012). This makes it possible to identify and address hearing loss in a timely manner and thereby minimise its negative impact on speech and language development, education and general development. In the UK, school entry hearing screening has been in place since the 1950s, with universal newborn hearing screening being introduced between 2002 and 2006. A recent presentation reports that eight countries screen over 90% of newborns, 10 countries screen between 25% and 89% of births and a further 54 countries have small‐scale newborn hearing screening practices in place (White 2012).As newborn hearing screening programmes have become established the age of diagnosis of hearing loss present from birth and subsequent hearing aid fitting has decreased. In the UK there are approximately 900 children born each year with significant, permanent hearing impairment likely to affect their own and their family's quality of life. Prior to the introduction of newborn hearing screening about 400 of these children would have been missed by the age of 1½ years, and about 200 by the age of 3½ years. The median age of confirmation of permanent bilateral moderate to profound hearing loss was 18.1 months and hearing aid fitting was 23.6 months. For the 2012/13 birth cohort this had reduced to 49 days and 82 days, respectively (Davis 1996;NHS 2015).This has raised a question as to the relevance of school entry hearing screening. However,Fortnum 2001estimated that the prevalence of bilateral permanent hearing loss rises from 0.91 (95% confidence interval (CI) 0.85 to 0.98) for three‐year olds to 1.65/1000 (95% CI 1.62 to 1.68) for children aged 9 to 16 years andWatkin 2010showed a prevalence of 1.51 (95% CI 1.11 to 1.92)/1000 at the end of the first year in primary school. The UK National Screening Committee review on hearing screening for newborns states that the incidence of hearing loss almost doubles by 10 years of age because of acquired hearing loss from meningitis, mumps, measles, trauma and other causes (UK NSC 2006). Glue ear has been shown to have a bimodal prevalence of 20% at two years of age and 16% at around the age of five years (Zielhuis 1990), thereby highlighting the potential need for the school entry hearing screen. The Child Health Subgroup of the UK National Screening Committee recommendation from July 2006 currently still stands, which is that hearing screening in school age children should continue while further research is undertaken. This is due to be reviewed in 2015/16.Some countries, such as New Zealand, have a nationally defined protocol for the school entry hearing screen (Ministry of Health 2014), but in others, such as England, it is only recommended that a screen should take place, not how it should be performed. Within the UK, this has resulted in variable practice, with no national approach to data collection, audit or quality assurance (Bristow 2008). This study found that the yield from screening ranged from 0.05% to 0.59% for permanent sensorineural hearing impairment and from 0.07% to 0.44% for permanent conductive hearing impairment. Temporary conductive hearing loss was not reported on.The age of school entry screening varies across countries due to differences in school entry age, which ranges from age four (Northern Ireland) to seven (Sweden, Finland, China, Bulgaria and the Baltic states). In Western Australia, targeted screening audiometry is performed on any child where there is parental or professional concern from the age of three and on all children from the age of 3.5 years (DoH 2007). The nature of school age screening also varies.In New Zealand, the national protocol defines a sweep frequency audiometry method, where the child responds to low, mid and high‐frequency sounds at defined sound levels. The Australian protocol defines mid and high‐frequency sounds. The American Academy of Audiology defines sweep frequency audiometry and tympanometry screening (Bright 2011). Sweep frequency audiometry is used in many areas within the UK and across Europe, the USA and China, but there are also alternative techniques available such as questionnaires, tympanometry (a test of middle ear function that can identify glue ear, but not a sensorineural hearing loss), transient or distortion product otoacoustic emissions (an objective test used to assess the auditory pathway to the outer hair cells of the inner ear by measuring a response from the inner ear when stimulated by a sound), auditory evoked response tests (an objective test used to assess the auditory pathway to areas in the brain using recording electrodes applied to the head) and speech tests. Knowing the accuracy of these tests (sensitivity and specificity) is an important consideration in deciding which test to employ.Wide variation in practice of the school hearing screen in the UK has been identified, such as differing frequencies being used, different pass criteria and re‐test protocols, and tests being performed in less than ideal test conditions and with limited resources to ensure good staff training and maintenance of skills, and this has called into question the accuracy of the screen (Bamford 2007;Fonseca 2005).The target condition being diagnosed is temporary conductive or permanent conductive or sensorineural hearing loss of a mild nature or worse. However, it is important to note that the purpose of the screen is to detect hearing loss, rather than the cause of it. A mild hearing loss is defined as hearing thresholds between 20 dB HL and 40 dB HL (BSA 2012). A temporary conductive hearing loss, such as glue ear (otitis media with effusion), is one that can resolve with time and hearing can return to normal, but the time course of recovery cannot be predicted and natural resolution of the condition is not definite. A permanent conductive hearing loss, such as otosclerosis, or a permanent congenital or acquired sensorineural hearing loss, does not improve with time and is likely to deteriorate further with time. At school age these conditions can be identified by pure tone audiometry using both air conduction and bone conduction, with tympanometry used to confirm middle ear status. Temporary conductive hearing losses are included in this review due to the high incidence of glue ear at around the age of five years (Zielhuis 1990), and the influence glue ear may have on speech and language development in children aged five to nine years (Holm 1969;Shriberg 2003;Teele 1990).We will include studies evaluating any of the following tests: audiometry, tympanometry, transient or distortion product otoacoustic emissions and auditory evoked response tests. Each ear is tested separately and the child referred for further assessment if either ear is impaired. [Decision aids for the management of menopausal symptoms] [Description of the condition]Menopause is clinically defined as amenorrhoea of 12 months' duration(Bruce 2009). Primary amenorrhoea is the result of the complete depletion of ovarian follicles and the cessation of estrogen secretion by the ovaries. The mean age of menopause is 51.3 years (Col 2009), but most women will undergo a transition to menopause in their mid‐ to late forties referred to as the perimenopausal period, during which women may experience menstrual irregularity (Tong 2013). Menopausal symptoms last on average for between two and five years (NICE 2015). The most common symptoms are hot flushes and night sweats. Women may also experience one or more of the following symptoms: sleep disturbances, sexual dysfunction, vaginal dryness, urinary tract infections, incontinence, depressive symptoms and mood disturbance, memory deficits, joint pain, and longer‐term health issues such as osteoporosis and coronary artery disease (Judd 2012;NICE 2015;Tong 2013). It is estimated that 35% to 55% of women will experience vasomotor symptoms (hot flushes and night sweats) associated with the menopause (Col 2009).A significant number of women will experience menopause prematurely, defined by the World Health Organization as cessation of menses before the age of 40 years occurring either spontaneously or as a result of oophorectomy or chemotherapy/radiotherapy‐induced ablation of ovarian function (WHO 1996). Some women will experience early menopause, a term used to describe menopause that occurs between the ages of 40 and 45 years (The North American Menopause Society 2010).In the next 10 years, about 50 million American women will experience menopause, although not all women experience troubling symptoms of menopause (The North American Menopause Society 2010). Australian and New Zealand women now have a life expectancy of about 84 years and 82 years, respectively, so menopause can span up to 30 years (Australian Bureau of Statistics 2006;Statistics New Zealand 2012). This is of particular importance because women can expect to spend a significant proportion of their lives after menopause, where quality of life and functional ability are vital (Utian 2005). Thus the physiological and psychological changes that occur at menopause can negatively impact on overall quality of life for a substantial number of women.The mainstay of treatment for troublesome menopausal vasomotor and vaginal symptoms is the supplementation of circulating levels of estrogen with hormone therapy (HT) (Schmidt 2012). However, despite its efficacy at controlling these symptoms, HT use has declined sharply worldwide because of concerns related to safety of its use long term (Marjoribanks 2012). The Women’s Health Initiative (WHI) trial, published in 2002, was stopped early when results indicated that risks of treatment with HT for healthy postmenopausal women outweighed the benefits over an average follow‐up of 5.2 years (Rossouw 2002). Combined estrogen plus progestin was linked to an increased risk of breast cancer, stroke, thromboembolism, and gallbladder disease (Rossouw 2002). However, the WHI trial did show that HT was associated with a reduction in fractures and colorectal cancer (Rossouw 2002). A secondary analysis of the WHI data published in 2007 showed that risks are influenced by the age of the woman, the time since menopause, and whether the HT was combined with or consisted only of estrogen (Rossouw 2007;Schmidt 2012). [Iloperidone versus placebo for schizophrenia] [Description of the condition]Schizophrenia is a major psychiatric disorder (or cluster of disorders) with an estimated lifetime prevalence of about 0.3% to 0.7% (DSM‐5 2013). The symptoms and experiences associated with schizophrenia are the result of important alterations in perceptions, thoughts, mood, and behaviour. These symptoms are unique to each patient (NICE 2014), and are usually divided into three broad categories: positive symptoms (such as hallucinations, delusions, thought and movement disorders), negative symptoms (like flat affect and lack of pleasure), and cognitive symptoms (including poor executive functioning, problems with focusing and memory) (NIMH 2014). Schizophrenia usually starts between the late teens and the mid‐30s, with a peak age of onset for the first psychotic episode in the early‐ to mid‐20s for males and in the late‐20s for females (DSM‐5 2013).Schizophrenia is generally associated with social and occupational impairment (DSM‐5 2013), and it is counted among the top fifteen medical disorders associated with dysfunction and disability (Murray 2013;NICE 2014). Schizophrenia is also accompanied by an elevated mortality rate, which can be up to 50% above that of the general population. This is partly because of an increased risk of a variety of physical diseases (NICE 2014), and partly because of an increased incidence of violent death and suicide. The approximate lifetime risk of suicide for psychosis and schizophrenia in adults is 5% (Hor 2010;NICE 2014).Many pharmacological and psychosocial therapies are effective for schizophrenia (Chien 2013a;Chien 2013b). The earlier the treatment is initiated, the more effective it will be (Chien 2013b). However, while many antipsychotics are effective in treating schizophrenia, most patients with chronic schizophrenia do not receive treatment, which contributes to the chronicity (WHO 2014).Iloperidone is a second‐generation antipsychotic drug which was approved by the US Food and Drug administration (FDA) for the acute treatment of schizophrenia in adults in May 2009 (Crabtree 2011). The benzisoxasole chemical structure and D2/5HT2A receptor affinity profile of Iloperidone places it in the “[xyz]done” family (Risperidone, Ziprasidone, Paliperidone) (Weiden 2012).It has been shown to work for both the positive and negative clusters of symptoms of schizophrenia, and improves all tested rating scales compared to placebo (Caccia 2010).Iloperidone is currently available only in oral formulation (Weiden 2012). It seems to be well tolerated, and to have an acceptable propensity to cause antipsychotic‐induced movement disorders (Weiden 2012). For iloperidone to reach its recommended target dose range, it requires four days of titration (Citrome 2011); so there is a relative disadvantage for choosing iloperidone as a treatment when there is an urgent need to start at full therapeutic dose (Weiden 2012).Iloperidone prescribing information states that side effects are reported in at least 5% of patients taking the drug. The most common side effects of iloperidone include orthostatic hypotension, dizziness, dry mouth, fatigue, nasal congestion, somnolence, weight gain, and tachycardia (Fanapt 2013).Iloperidone acts as an antagonist to serotonin (5HT2A) and D2 dopamine receptors (Crabtree 2011). Its recommended starting dose is 1 mg twice daily with a recommended target dose ranging between 12 to 24 mg/d in two divided doses (Weiden 2012). Oral tablet formulation of Iloperidone is well absorbed in the gastrointestinal tract, and takes about two to three hours to reach the peak plasma concentration (Sainati 1995). Iloperidone is essentially metabolised in the liver and subsequently yields four known metabolites. The Iloperidone parent compound and the reduced metabolite termed P88‐8991 (P88) are considered to be the major components identified in human plasma (Mutlib 1998).Iloperidone is a relatively new atypical antipsychotic drug which appears to be effective for the negative symptoms of schizophrenia, as well as against the more responsive positive symptoms. Some trials of its use in the treatment of schizophrenia have been published, but there is no systematic review summarising them. This review is important to do because it will summarise best available evidence and aims to provide a benchmark about the efficacy, safety and adverse effects of iloperidone compared to placebo. [Cardiac resynchronization therapy for dilated cardiomyopathy] . [Folate supplementation in women of reproductive age] [Objectives]This is a protocol for a Cochrane Review (intervention). The objectives are as follows:To assess the benefits and the potential adverse effects, including cancer, of folate supplementation, either in folic acid form or in 5‐methyltetrahydrofolate form, alone or in combination with other micronutrients, on folate status and health outcomes (physical, psychological, and neurocognitive) among women of reproductive age.[Description of the condition]Folate or vitamin B₉ is a generic term used to describe a B vitamin necessary for cell division. It helps produce the building blocks of both DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) and RNA (ribonucleic acid) as well as several amino acids (IOM 1998). Dietary folate is found in legumes, leafy green vegetables (such as turnips and spinach greens), and some citrus fruits. It is susceptible to heat and cooking losses. In contrast, folic acid (pteroyl‐L‐glutamic acid), the synthetic form of folate, is commonly used in vitamin supplements and food fortification, as the bioavailability of folate ranges from about 100% for folic acid supplements taken on an empty stomach to about 50% for food folate (IOM 1998). The dietary folate equivalents (DFEs) adjust for this difference of bioavailability, since 1 µg of DFE is equivalent to 1 µg of food folate but to 0.6 µg of folic acid from fortified food and to 0.5 µg of a supplement taken on an empty stomach (IOM 1998).In the human body, serum or plasma folate is a representation of recent usual intake, whereas red blood cell folate is a reflection of folate storage over a 120‐day period (WHO 2012a). Although there is limited information regarding the use of urinary folate as a biochemical indicator, there is literature that suggests that in steady‐state conditions there is a positive correlation with plasma and red blood cell folate (Niesser 2013).Low folate intake is reflected in a decrease in serum folate concentrations (IOM 1998). A continued low intake will result in a decrease in red blood cell folate concentrations. This is followed by enlargement of red cells and a reduction in their ability to divide appropriately, a condition known as megaloblastic anaemia (IOM 1998). Other symptoms of clinical deficiency include fatigue, headache, pallor and sore mouth and tongue (Hamrick 2008), and usually appear when concentrations are lower than 3 ng/mL (< 6.8 nmol/L) in serum, or lower than 100 ng/mL (< 226.5 nmol/L) in red blood cells (WHO 2012a).Inadequate folate intake in women during the periconceptional period can lead to an increased risk for serious birth defects of the brain and spine, called neural tube defects (NTD;Berry 1999). The mechanisms through which this occurs are still unknown. Though less well documented than NTD risk, the literature suggests that other birth defects, such as cardiovascular defects, Down syndrome, limb defects, cleft lip, urinary tract defects, and congenital hydrocephalus, may also be related to low folate status (Eskes 2006;Goh 2006;Wilcox 2007;Coppede 2009). Although the folate concentration in women of reproductive age associated with a low risk of NTDs is not yet determined, it has been reported that the lowest risk of NTDs occurs at a red blood cell folate concentration of about 906 nmol/L (Daly 1995).Low folate intake is also associated with an increase of homocysteine concentrations (which are a functional biomarker of folate levels), vitamin B₁₂, and other vitamin deficiencies. High values of homocysteine are associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular diseases (Zhou 2011), and cognitive impairment in the elderly (Ho 2011). In 2005, additional cut‐offs, developed using data from the US National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) 1988 to 1994, were suggested to define folate deficiency based on homocysteine as a metabolic indicator (Selhub 2008). [Subcutaneous or intramuscular methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis] [Description of the condition]Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is an autoimmune disease characterized by systemic inflammation (Lee 2001;Szekanecz 2007). The prevalence of RA has been estimated to be 0.5% to 1.0% in the Western world (Helmick 2008;Kvien 2004). RA often presents with signs and symptoms of joint pain, swelling, tenderness and stiffness, and joint deformities, which are due to the inflammation of the synovial lining of the joints, tendons and periarticular structures (Lee 2001). RA also leads to systemic inflammation characterized by premature atherosclerotic disease and other inflammatory sequelae such as interstitial lung disease, pneumonitis, mononeuritis multiplex, subcutaneous nodules and vasculitis (Ku 2009;Prete 2011;Snow 2005). RA can lead to joint destruction, and has a significant impact on health‐related quality of life (HRQoL) (Kvien 2005;Lubeck 2004). RA can lead to severe functional limitation and short‐ and long‐term disability (Odegard 2005;Reisine 1989;Rupp 2006;Yelin 1990;Yelin 2007), often with loss of worker and at‐home productivity (Burton 2006;Kessler 2008;Ozminkowski 2008;Strand 2010a;Strand 2010b), and significant societal cost (Birnbaum 2010). Thus, RA is a disease with major public health impact.The treatment of RA includes various pharmacological options such as nonsteroidal anti‐inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) (Garner 2002), glucocorticoids (Kirwan 2007), traditional disease‐modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs; e.g. methotrexate (MTX;Lopez‐Olivo 2014), sulfasalazine (Suarez‐Almazor 1998), hydroxychloroquine, leflunomide (Osiri 2002), cyclosporine (Wells 1998) and gold (Clark 1997)); biologic DMARDs (Singh 2009;Singh 2011;) e.g. etanercept (Lethaby 2013), infliximab (Blumenauer 2002), adalimumab (Navarro‐Sarabia 2005), abatacept (Maxwell 2009), anakinra (Mertens 2009), rituximab (Lopez‐Olivo 2008), certolizumab pegol (Ruiz Garcia 2011), golimumab (Singh 2010a) and tocilizumab (Singh 2010b); and new oral small molecule drugs such as tofacitinib (Lopez‐Olivo 2013).DMARD use is associated with an improvement in pain and function, reduction in disability, improvement in HRQoL, and reduction in radiographic destruction and disability (Cash 1994;Finckh 2006;Pincus 2002;Strand 2008;Strand 2010a;Strand 2010b). Guidelines for the treatment of RA have been published by the leading organizations, the European League Against Rheumatism (EULAR) in 2010 (Smolen 2010), and the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) in 2008 (Saag 2008), updated in 2012 (Singh 2012). An algorithm for RA treatment that incorporates the use of various pharmacological drugs, primarily focused on traditional and biologic DMARDs is suggested based on the disease activity and the prognostic factors at periodic evaluations of the person. The use of traditional DMARDs and biologics is the cornerstone of RA treatment, supplemented by the use of NSAIDs and glucocorticoids, and other non‐pharmacological modalities such as mobility aids and physical and occupational therapy.MTX is the most commonly used traditional DMARD in people with RA and is very effective in controlling its signs and symptoms (Cronstein 2005;Lopez‐Olivo 2014;Weinblatt 1985). It is usually the first line of therapy for RA (Cipriani 2014;Lopez‐Olivo 2014). MTX is used alone or in combination with other DMARDs or newer biologic therapies (Katchamart 2010;Lopez‐Olivo 2014;Singh 2012;Smolen 2010), or both, to enhance treatment response. Failure of MTX could be due to lack of efficacy or suboptimal response.MTX is prescribed either as oral or parenteral (subcutaneous or intramuscular) therapy (Cipriani 2014). Oral MTX use is much more common than parenteral due to the ease of use.Subcutaneous MTX and intramuscular MTX have similar pharmacokinetics but the subcutaneous injection is easier to perform and less painful (Brooks 1990;Jundt 1993). Studies have demonstrated increased bioavailability and decreased gastrointestinal intolerance in favor of subcutaneous over oral MTX, especially at higher doses such as 25 mg (Bingham 2003;Braun 2008;Hoekstra 2004;Kurnik 2003;Schiff 2014;Wilson 2013). Some people may respond better to parenteral treatment than oral MTX. However, the clinical significance is uncertain.RA is characterized by an activation and interaction of various immune cells (T cells, B cells, mononuclear cells, etc.) and other host cells in the joints such as fibroblasts, osteoclasts and chondrocytes (Brennan 2008;Connell 2006). This leads to overexpression of chemokines, metalloproteinases and inflammatory cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor‐alpha (TNF‐alpha) and various interleukins (IL)) (Brennan 2008;Choy 2001). Bone and cartilage destruction results from these cytokines and chemokines, a hallmark of RA. MTX affects the inflammatory cascade initiated by pro‐inflammatory cytokines (IL‐1, IL‐6, TNF), which play a major role in RA pathogenesis (Segal 1990).MTX is a derivative of folic acid and aminopterin. The exact mechanism of action of oral or parenteral MTX in RA is not known. Several mechanisms of action for its anti‐inflammatory action have been proposed, including the inhibition of: 1) T‐cell proliferation due to its effect on purine and pyrimidine metabolism; 2) glutathione metabolism leading to less recruitment of inflammatory cells; 3) transmethylation reactions required for the prevention of T‐cell cytotoxicity (Cronstein 2005); and 4) increased release of adenosine: MTX undergoes intracellular polyglutamation, which interferes with the action of dihydrofolate reductase and other folate‐dependent enzymes, such as 5‐aminoimidazole‐4‐carboxamide ribonucleotide (AICAR) transformylase. The accumulation of AICAR leads to the release of adenosine, an endogenous anti‐inflammatory autocoid, into extracellular space that interacts with receptors on neutrophils and mononuclear cells, likely contributing to the anti‐inflammatory effects of MTX (Cronstein 1997). Thus, several potential pathways have been proposed to explain the anti‐inflammatory action of MTX in people with RA and other inflammatory disorders.MTX is the cornerstone of RA management. Due to its favorable benefits versus toxicity profile, it is still the gold standard for the treatment of RA. As monotherapy, its benefits seem similar to biologic DMARDs such as etanercept and adalimumab (Breedveld 2006;Genovese 2002). It is frequently the first medication used in people with RA and, when people have inadequate response, it is used in combination with other DMARDs or biologics as combination therapy. People can be started on oral or subcutaneous MTX, which is usually titrated rapidly to the target weekly dose of 25 mg or higher. In people who do not respond to oral MTX, physicians may also try subcutaneous MTX, since pharmacokinetics have previously shown that MTX bioavailability is lower and somewhat unpredictable with higher oral MTX doses. To our knowledge, no Cochrane systematic review exists for subcutaneous MTX in people with RA. Given the much higher cost of treatment with biologics compared with MTX and MTX combinations, we need a better understanding of the role of subcutaneous MTX in the management of RA. MTX is used alone or in combination with other DMARDs or newer biologic therapies (Katchamart 2010;Lopez‐Olivo 2014;Singh 2012;Smolen 2010), or both, to enhance treatment response. Failure of MTX could be due to lack of efficacy or suboptimal response.MTX is prescribed either as oral or parenteral (subcutaneous or intramuscular) therapy (Cipriani 2014). Oral MTX use is much more common than parenteral due to the ease of use.Subcutaneous MTX and intramuscular MTX have similar pharmacokinetics but the subcutaneous injection is easier to perform and less painful (Brooks 1990;Jundt 1993). Studies have demonstrated increased bioavailability and decreased gastrointestinal intolerance in favor of subcutaneous over oral MTX, especially at higher doses such as 25 mg (Bingham 2003;Braun 2008;Hoekstra 2004;Kurnik 2003;Schiff 2014;Wilson 2013). Some people may respond better to parenteral treatment than oral MTX. Bone and cartilage destruction results from these cytokines and chemokines, a hallmark of RA. MTX affects the inflammatory cascade initiated by pro‐inflammatory cytokines (IL‐1, IL‐6, TNF), which play a major role in RA pathogenesis (Segal 1990).MTX is a derivative of folic acid and aminopterin. [Impact of entertainment media smoking on adolescent smoking behaviours] [Description of the condition]The public health burden of tobacco use is well documented in the scientific literature. According to the recent Global Burden of Diseases (GBD) study, smoking is the largest behavioural risk factor for mortality and morbidity, and second only to hypertension among all risk factors (Lim 2012). There is a strong association as well as causal links between tobacco use and lung cancer (Doll 1950;Doll 1953;Doll 1978;Jindal 1982), oral cancers (Sadri 2007), urinary bladder cancer (Staszewski 1966;Morgan 1974), pancreatic cancer (Wynder 1975;Iodice 2008), colorectal cancer (Cheng 2014;Walter 2014), cervical cancer (Gadducci 2011) and breast cancer (Gaudet 2013;Chen 2013), as well as cardiovascular (Wynder 1958;Friedman 1982;Huxley 2011) and respiratory diseases (Forey 2011;Wang 2014), which have been conclusively proven (US Department of Health and Human Services 2014) with many epidemiological studies, systematic reviews and meta‐analyses. Studies have also documented that tobacco use is associated with poor perinatal and child health (Treyster 2011;Been 2014). Tobacco is therefore the leading cause of preventable death in the world, and more so in low‐ and middle‐income countries (LMICs) where the tobacco industry continues to grow unregulated. The economic costs of tobacco have been documented in high‐income nations (WHO 2011a) and found to be as high as 3.4% of the gross domestic product. The scenario is probably worse in LMICs where data are scarce on the impact of smoking and other forms of tobacco use on economic burdens.For more than two decades now it has been apparent that images of tobacco smoking portrayed in the media appeal to adolescents who remember them (IOM 1994). Between 80,000 and 100,000 young people initiate smoking everyday globally, with half of them living in Asia (WHO 2002). In 2008 the United States National Cancer Institute's monograph on the role of the media in promoting or reducing tobacco use reported that adolescents with higher exposure to smoking in movies at baseline are 2.0 to 2.7 times more likely to try cigarette smoking in future; these effect estimates were consistent with evidence from cross‐sectional studies (NCI 2008). The evidence indicates that even after the Master Settlement Agreement (MSA) between the United States Attorney General and major tobacco manufacturers, in which the latter agreed on the prohibition of paid tobacco advertisements, the incidence of smoking in movies has increased (WHO 2011b). A review of tobacco industry documents (WHO 2011b) has demonstrated that the tobacco industry conducts extensive research to target youth and adolescents, aiming to associate a product with social and psychological needs including peer approval, autonomy, masculinity, and the quest for adventure. Because of their financial interests and the fact that entertainment media such as movies have a global appeal, the tobacco industry uses entertainment media to promote smoking (WHO 2011b). A strong influence on adolescents in the visual media is watching actors smoke (role‐modelling) (Sargent 2005); this is an important area of concern, because actors and the characters they play can be familiar to adolescents world‐wide.In terms of entertainment media; the media or medium means a channel of communication through which people share and exchange information. Entertainment media comprise (but are not limited to) print (books and magazines), audio (radio and music), and audio‐visual media (television, cinema, web‐based media, and video/computer games) (NCI 2008). The most important channels through which adolescents are likely to be exposed to smoking behaviour are television, movies and videos (Rideout 2010). This USA‐based study reported that children and adolescents distribute their time for entertainment media in the following proportions: television 46%; compact discs (CDs) and tapes 12%; movies and videos 11%; print media 11%; radio 10%; video games 5%; and 5% for computers. This provides an opportunity for the entertainment industry to generate revenue by using celebrities to promote a product or a behaviour to large segments of the population using mass media (NCI 2008).Exposure to media can impact both positively and negatively on tobacco use, depending on how the behaviour is presented (NCI 2008). One heuristic model (Sargent 2005) proposes that media exposure can have several influences on the likelihood that an adolescent will start smoking. Based on social learning theory, media content is expected to shape cognitive beliefs about tobacco and expectancies (what the individual thinks will happen if he or she uses it). In this model, media are one social influence (in addition to family and peers) that shapes expectancies (how adolescents perceive tobacco use will affect them), identity (how adolescents perceive themselves in the context of tobacco), and prototypes (how adolescents view other tobacco users). These cognitions affect intentions to use tobacco and willingness to try it in the context of a social cue to engage in the behaviour. One of the key aspects of the heuristic model is that media, peers and family influence identity formation. In search of identity, adolescents tend to adopt behaviours that are consistent with the self image they wish to convey to others ‐ the process of identity formation. According to social learning theory, children and adolescents form their own identities by adopting parts of the identities of the people they admire. Just as the behaviour of friends and families can affect this process, so media personality preferences and behaviours (e.g. tobacco use) can also affect it (Kobus 2003).On the basis of empirical studies of predictors for transition from one stage of smoking to another,Mayhew 2000proposed a staged approach to modelling smoking progression from no smoking to first puff, to first whole cigarette, various levels of experimental smoking to established smoking. They proposed key variables which uniquely predict transition, depending on smoking stage. It is an open empirical question whether media influence only the onset of tobacco use, or also the various transitions individuals go through as they move from early experimenter to monthly or weekly tobacco user, to daily regular use.Perhaps the most intensively studied medium is cinema. Multiple studies have shown that USA and European adolescents who have viewed smoking in films are more likely to initiate smoking (Hanewinkel 2008;Dal Cin 2013;Morgenstern 2013). Bollywood (a metonym for the Hindi film industry in India), which is the largest movie industry in the world in terms of the number of films released and the number of viewers (Arora 2012), is also notorious for depicting tobacco imagery, with more than 14.3 billion tobacco images being delivered from just 15 top box‐office hits within a single year (Bhaumik 2013). Based on studies to date, smoking in films has been proposed as a causal risk factor for smoking in the USA by the National Cancer Institute (NCI 2008).Our logic model is that exposure to tobacco use in entertainment media increases favourable associations with different tobacco products, cognitions (expectancies and prototypes) regarding tobacco use, increases the likelihood that an adolescent will adopt the identity of a tobacco user, and positively influences intentions and susceptibility towards initiation of tobacco use. This process could affect progression along the tobacco uptake continuum among adolescents. The levels of the tobacco uptake continuum model include progression from a 'non‐susceptible never‐smoker' to any progression in the smoking uptake continuum, including 'susceptible never‐smokers', 'experimental smokers' and 'established smokers' (Pearce 1998).Expectancies are the anticipated outcomes associated with a future behaviour. Expectancies are reported to be a strong predictor of future behaviour and to influence the decision whether or not to initiate a behaviour. Expectancies towards tobacco use will provide an insight on what adolescents perceive regarding the effects of smoking.Our hypotheses are:a) Exposure to tobacco use in the entertainment media is associated with more favourable attitudes, including positive affective response, to tobacco products; positive expectancies and prototypes, and identity as a tobacco user.b) Exposure to tobacco use in entertainment media will predict susceptibility or willingness to use tobacco among never‐users.c) Exposure to tobacco use in the entertainment media will predict transition from non‐susceptible never‐tobacco‐user, susceptible user and experimental user to established tobacco use behaviour among adolescents.Litigation against and opposition to public health interventions to prohibit tobacco advertising through entertainment media are on the rise in many countries, e.g. in India where the government has introduced stringent measures to regulate any form of tobacco depiction in television and films in 2005, but has faced strong protests from allies of the tobacco industry, as well as representatives of the entertainment media who questioned the evidence in support of a causal effect for this exposure (Reddy 2004). Film makers and artists sometimes claim that the use of smoking imagery is a 'dramatic necessity' and that banning it amounts to a lack of free speech protection (WHO 2011b). It is therefore necessary to have strong empirical evidence to justify public health interventions against smoking imagery in the entertainment media.The WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (WHO FCTC 2005) makes it an obligation on its 179 parties to enact comprehensive bans on tobacco promotion and advertisements, with Article 13 specifically targeting the entertainment media, including movies (WHO 2011b). A previous Cochrane review on the impact of tobacco advertising and promotion on increasing adolescent smoking behaviours (Lovato 2011) highlighted the gap in collated evidence on the role of tobacco use in entertainment media and its impact on adolescent tobacco behaviours. [Episodic therapy for recurrent genital herpes in non‐immunocompromized adults] [Description of the condition]This is the protocol for a review and there is no abstract.The objective is to assess the effectiveness and safety of episodic therapy for the treatment of recurrent genital herpes in non‐immunocompromized adults.Genital herpes simplex virus (HSV) is a recurrent disease that can occur throughout life and has no known cure (Beauman 2005). The virus consists of a viral DNA core, capsid, tegument, and an envelope (Whitley 1998). The two types of HSV (HSV‐1 and HSV‐2) have antigenic differences in their envelope proteins (Beauman 2005). HSV‐1 is normally associated with orolabial infections while HSV‐2 with genital disease, but cutaneous infections at other body sites may occur (Beauman 2005). Genital herpes is a prevalent condition in United States adults, with a trend towards an increase in diagnosed cases in the last decades (Xu 2002). The number of lifetime sexual partners, for both men and women, and a history of a different sexually transmitted disease are important associations with genital HSV‐2 infection (Wald 1997).Herpes is a very common infectious disease and its genital form is globally recognized as a major sexually transmitted disease. Genital herpes affects millions of people worldwide and its estimated prevalence is increasing, similar to the AIDS epidemic. The seroprevalence of HSV‐2 in the world is as low as 10% in Asian countries to as high as 80%, in some sub‐Saharan African countries (WHO 2007). The infection affects adolescents and adults after initiation of sexual intercourse, with a global peak incidence of HSV‐2 during middle and late adolescence (15 to 19 years of age) of 6.9 million per year in 2003 (Looker 2008).In the United States, the average age of sexual debut is 16.5 years (Shafii 2009). The majority of cases of genital herpes are caused by HSV‐2, however, HSV‐1 is becoming increasingly prevalent in young adults and women (Ross 1993;Samra 2003;Tran 2004). Genital herpes negatively affects the quality of life and work productivity of patients (Patel 2001), and in the United States is a major public health problem with high direct medical costs caused by diagnostic testing, drug treatments, and outpatient and hospital care (Chesson 2000).Almost all patients experiencing an outbreak of HSV‐2 subsequently suffer at least one recurrence, about 38% experience more than six recurrences per year (Azwa 2009). The median number of recurrences are four episodes per year (Benedetti 1994). Although recurrences of genital herpes tend to be less severe and shorter compared to the primary outbreak, they can be very painful and emotionally distressing (Swanson 1999). Besides clinical symptoms, persons who suffer from genital herpes worry about the social implications of a recurrent disease, the possibility of transmission to their partner, and fear of disclosing the truth about their health status to a new sexual partner (Brentjens 2003).Pregnant women and any immunocompromized population are also adversely affected by the infection and have different clinical outcomes. About 22% of pregnant women are seropositive to one of the herpes simplex viruses and 2% are diagnosed with a new infection during pregnancy (Brown 2005). Vertical transmission occurs mainly after a primary episode of genital HSV in the third trimester, through virus contact with active HSV lesions at time of delivery, with a high morbidity and mortality in neonates, if not treated (Brown 2005).Immunocompromized patients have more severe and atypical progression of the disease (Fatahzadeh 2007). HSV‐2 increases the risk of HIV infection (Wald 2002), enhances both HIV susceptibility and infectiousness, promoting a susceptible environment in genital mucosa with an increase in HIV target cell population (Rebbapragada 2007). Enhanced transmission occurs due to more frequent clinical and subclinical shedding in HIV infected women, and subclinical shedding in HIV positive men (Røttingen 2001).Acute infection starts as HSV enters the body through the skin or mucosa by direct sexual contact with secretions or mucosal surfaces of an infected person (Whitley 1998). Replication of HSV occurs at epidermic tissue, causing cellular damage. Subsequent inflammation of the dermis, passage to peripheral nerves, and retrograde transport to the nervous system (where the virus remains in a latent state) finishes the first stage of natural history (Gupta 2007). Clinical manifestations present four to seven days after sexual contact and vary in presentation. Classical signs and symptoms can be both local and systemic, although subclinical presentation is common (Kimberlin 2004). Patients complain of redness and bumps that advance to fluid‐filled blisters and ulcers over the next one to two weeks. These lesions crust and then heal with no visible scarring. Pain in adjacent areas to the lesion and tenderness in regional swollen glands are the main local symptoms. Fever, headache, muscle pain, and urinary symptoms are regular complaints (Corey 1993). Patients with primary infection (no pre‐existing antibodies to the other serotype of HSV, usually HSV‐1) have harsher symptoms (Beauman 2005;Schiffer 2009).During the latent stage, patients are asymptomatic but HSV transmission is possible through viral shedding (Schiffer 2009). Although risk is greater when ulcers are present, subclinical viral shedding is considered the most common means of transmission. Reactivations occur when the latent virus in peripheral nerve cells migrate to the skin and mucous membranes, causing clinical recurrences (Whitley 1998). In this stage, symptoms tend to be of milder severity and shorter duration than in acute infections. Fewer days of viral shedding with lower concentration of the virus are typical (Corey 1993). Prodromal symptoms may precede the advent of lesions. Altered sensation or pain around buttocks, thighs, hips, or the perineum, are characteristic 30 minutes to 48 hours before new lesions appear (Kimberlin 2004). Persisting stressors or high levels of anxiety may be required to increased risk of recurrences (Cohen 1999). Compared with HSV‐1, HSV‐2 infected patients present six times more frequently with outbreaks and more severe symptoms (Beauman 2005).There are three available methods for the diagnosis of genital herpes. Viral culture can be used and is useful when distinguishing between serotypes (Patel 2011). However, it has less sensitivity in recurrences (lower viral load) and in the healing stages of the outbreak (Workowski 2010); in addition culture is slow (7 to 10 days for a negative result) (Patel 2011). Polymerase chain reaction testing is a faster option than viral culture and has greater sensitivity, particularly during ulceration and crusting of the acute episode (Kimberlin 2004;Patel 2011). Type specific serologic testing (TSST) targets IgG of glycoprotein G of HSV‐1 or HSV‐2. TSST have acceptable accuracy (Wald 1997), but false‐negatives could be common in the first stages of the disease (Workowski 2010). TSST might be useful in recurrent genital symptoms or atypical symptoms with negative HSV cultures (Workowski 2010).Therapy for recurrent genital herpes includes nucleoside analogues: aciclovir, valaciclovir, and famciclovir. These drugs compete with nucleosides in infected cells. Their main antiviral action mechanisms are the incorporation of the phosphorylated molecule to the viral DNA chain and the inhibition of viral polymerase, blocking viral genome replication without affecting non‐infected human cells (Nath 2009). Valaciclovir and famciclovir are prodrugs and, as such, their antiviral activity depends on metabolism before targeting virus infected cells. Once targeted, activation is completed (De Clercq 2006;Simpson 2006).Aciclovir is highly active against HSV‐1 and less against HSV‐2. [Beta adrenergic antagonists for hospitalized burned patients] [Description of the condition]Burn injuries represent a common type of trauma injury and have a significant impact on public health worldwide. Burn injuries affect 1% of the world population annually, with an estimated 6 million people seeking medical help for burns per year. In a systematic review of 76 studies of burns in 22 countries in Europe, the annual incidence of severe burns was between 0.2 and 2.9 per 10,000 inhabitants. The incidence of burns was higher in children, who represented 40‐50% of the severe burn patients across the studies. In these studies flames and scalds were among the top three causes of severe burns, with mortality rates ranging between 1.4% and 18% in most studies (Brusselaers 2010).Burn severity is determined by several factors, including the burn size measured as the proportion of the total body surface area (TBSA), burn depth, the area affected (hands, legs, face), and other injuries (for example, inhalation injury). Risk factors for mortality after burn injury include burn size, age and inhalation injury. For example, the expected mortality rate in a 20 year old man and a TBSA of 40% is about 8%, as opposed to the same area of burn in a 70 year old man, with an expected mortality rate of 94% (Muller 2001). In a systematic review in Europe, mortality increased considerably with higher TBSA, reaching on average 30% for TBSA of 20% (Brusselaers 2010).Severe burn injuries, which cover more than 30% of the TBSA, result in stress, inflammation and hypermetabolic state. Several studies showed that the postburn period starts immediately after the injury and can last for at least 3 years. This period consist of two phases called the 'ebb' and 'flow' phases (Wilmore 1977;Kulp 2010). In the ebb phase which begins immediately postburn, patients have low cardiac output, low oxygen consumption and decreased metabolic rate, characteristic of early shock (Latenser 2009;Williams 2009), and impaired glucose tolerance associated with hyperglycemia (Pereira 2005). The ebb phase reaches a plateau after 5 days when enters the second phase, called also the 'flow' phase. The flow phase is characterized by a hyperdynamic state (tachycardia, fever) and hypermetabolism. Increased energy expenditure is associated with muscle protein catabolism, alternations in hepatic protein synthesis, and wasting of peripheral fat stores by inducing degradation of lipids to free fatty acids (FFAs) and glycerol (peripheral lipolysis). This increase in the FFAs concentration eventually leads to their accumulation in the liver or in peripheral muscle. There is also aberration in ATP consumption which contributes to increased gluconeogenesis and insulin resistance (Pereira 2005). This hypermetabolic state, though biologically borne to compensate for the injury, might become a source of morbidity in burn patients if left untreated (Kraft 2012). Prospective studies in children showed that these catabolic changes were associated with immunodeficiency, impaired wound healing, infections, decreased lean body weight and bone density, weakness and delayed rehabilitation, with potential impact on survival (Finnerty 2013).Over the past several decades, the knowledge on burn pathophysiology has been translated into therapeutic measures. In addition to surgical techniques dealing with wound closure and improvement in resuscitation, pharmacologic measures have been proposed to attenuate the hypermetabolic state. As catecholamines are the main mediators of the hypermetabolic state, it is logical that blocking their effect will attenuate the response (Wilmore 1974). Thus, beta‐blockers such as propranolol, metoprolol, atenolol have been proposed as a therapeutic measure for burn patients. It reduces tachycardia and hypertension by preventing catecholamine binding to beta adrenergic receptors. Propranolol use decreased tachycardia, reduced cardiac work and resting energy expenditure in children with severe burns (Herndon 1988). For example, a recent systematic review and meta analysis of nine randomized controlled trials including 10,529 patients showed that perioperative treatment of patients undergoing non‐cardiac surgery with beta‐blockers resulted in significantly increased mortality (risk ratio 1.27, 95% confidence interval 1.01 to 1.60) (Bouri 2014).The American Burn Association consensus statements do not provide specific guidance for beta adrenergic blocker use or the optimal duration of their use (Gibran 2013). The Spanish Society of Intensive Care Medicine and Coronary Units recommend the use of beta adrenergic blockers in critically ill patients (Garcia 2011). The ESPEN guidelines recommend the use of beta adrenergic blockers at the end of the first week after the burn injury, but the duration of treatment is not defined (Rousseau 2013).The primary mediators of the hypermetabolic phase after burn injury are endogenous catecholamines, along with corticosteroids and inflammatory cytokines (Wilmore 1974). [Interventions for the prevention of postoperative grommet (ventilation tube) obstruction] [Description of the condition]The insertion of a grommet (ventilation tube, tympanostomy tube) into the tympanic membrane is one of the most common operations performed in high‐income countries (Cullen 2009;Sood 2007). The two main indications for this operation are chronic otitis media with effusion (chronic OME; 'glue ear') associated with conductive hearing loss and recurrent acute otitis media (AOM). Other indications include acute mastoiditis and middle ear atelectasis.The primary aim of grommet insertion in chronic OME is to improve hearing by equalising pressure between the middle ear and external ear canal, allowing the release of middle ear negative pressure and encouraging the natural drainage of middle ear fluid down the Eustachian tube (Browning 2010). In recurrent AOM, the aim is to reduce the number and severity of AOM recurrences by the above mechanism and by allowing the middle ear effusion during any AOM episodes to drain through the grommet to the external ear canal. These benefits are lost when the lumen of the grommet is obstructed.Grommet obstruction is typically encountered prior to grommet extrusion, which, on average, occurs after around six to eight months (Yaman 2010). Early grommet obstruction, which can be defined as occurring within four weeks of surgery (Van Dongen 2013), prevents the intended benefits and is frustrating for patients, families and clinicians.Postoperative grommet obstruction has been attributed to middle ear effusions (if present at the time of surgery) or blood solidifying within the lumen of the grommet (Westine 2002). Later obstruction may be caused by otorrhoea, wax or granulation tissue.A meta‐analysis of ventilation tube sequelae estimated that the cumulative incidence rate of grommet obstruction at any stage of follow‐up was 6.9% (95% confidence interval (CI) 6.1 to 7.7, range 0% to 37.3%) in a mixed population undergoing grommet placement for otitis media (Kay 2001).
