[Melatonin for preventing pre‐eclampsia] [Description of the condition]Pre‐eclampsia, one of the hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, remains a leading cause of maternal death worldwide, with the majority of deaths occurring in developing countries (Lo 2013). Pre‐eclampsia is a multi‐organ syndrome of pregnancy that manifests after 20 weeks' gestation with new‐onset hypertension alongside maternal end‐organ dysfunction and/or fetal growth restriction (Lowe 2009). There is currently no effective treatment for pre‐eclampsia, and as such it remains a significant burden of disease for both mothers and their babies worldwide.There is no widely accepted definition of 'severe' pre‐eclampsia however the recent ISSHP (The International Society for the Study of Hypertension in Pregnancy) statement suggested there was general consensus that factors determining severity include difficulty in controlling blood pressure and deteriorating clinical condition including HELLP syndrome (characterised by breakdown of red blood cells (Haemolysis),ElevatedLiver enzymes andLowPlatelets), impending eclampsia, worsening thrombocytopenia (low platelets) or worsening fetal growth restriction while there is less concern regarding increasing proteinuria (Tranquilli 2014). Symptoms of HELLP syndrome may include pain in the upper right part of the abdomen, fatigue, a general feeling of being unwell, nausea, vomiting and increased oedema (swelling). Importantly, pre‐eclampsia poses serious health risks for the baby, is implicated in 12% of cases of fetal growth restriction (Kramer 2000) and is a known antecedent in up to 19% of preterm births.The exact pathogenesis of pre‐eclampsia is unknown but it is likely that it its evolution is multi‐factorial involving a complex interplay between the mother, fetus and the placenta. Most salient contemporary theories surrounding the development of pre‐eclampsia, embrace the fundamental contribution of the physiological mechanisms that underlie the establishment of the pregnancy and the process of placentation (Roberts 2005), during which the immature embryo (blastocyst) attaches onto the uterine lining (endometrial decidua) and begins the process of embedding into the underlying uterine vasculature. Subsequently, in order for optimal placentation to occur, the outer (extra villous trophoblast) layer of the blastocyst is able to infiltrate and remodel the maternal spiral arteries within the uterine walls. This invasive process transforms the spiral arteries into large conduits of low‐resistance vessels that are capable of accommodating adequate fetal‐placental blood flow during the evolution of pregnancy. Should the modification to the spiral arteries be disturbed, placental development may be impaired; a reduction of blood flow ensues ultimately generating a state of uteroplacental hypoxia, as witnessed with pre‐eclampsia and fetal growth restriction. Various hypotheses have been put forward to support interventions that might delay or reverse this process (Fenton 2014).The observation that women with pre‐eclampsia have decreased plasma and placental concentrations of antioxidants (Hubel 1999) has recently led to the proposal that placental hypoperfusion may induce a state of oxidative stress. This includes overproduction of highly reactive oxygen molecules or free radicals, depleting the body’s stores of antioxidants. Oxidative stress, coupled with an exaggerated inflammatory response, may cause the release of maternal factors that result in inappropriate endothelial cell activation and endothelial cell damage. Endothelial cells line the inside surfaces of blood vessels and their impairment results in the clinical signs of pre‐eclampsia, such as hypertension and proteinuria. A woman’s risk of, and response to, oxidative stress depends on various factors. These include the propensity for small low‐density lipoproteins, hyperhomocysteinaemia, a genetically determined poor resistance to oxidative stress, and a dietary deficiency of antioxidants (Roberts 2001).Screening for women at risk of pre‐eclampsia is an important part of antenatal care in order to triage higher‐risk women for more intensive antenatal surveillance and prophylactic interventions (Meher 2005). Most current strategies for risk assessment are based on the general medical and obstetric history, alongside clinical examination. However, there is surprisingly little reliable evidence on the actual risk associated with individual factors, and how they might interact (Meher 2005).Routine screening for pre‐eclampsia is based on measurement of blood pressure and urinalysis for proteinuria. Overall, 15% to 25% of women with gestational hypertension progress to pre‐eclampsia (Saudan 1998). Numerous physiological and biochemical screening tests and algorithms have been developed, however, none so far none have proved to be of good predictive value and few are used in clinical practice (Akolekar 2011;Oliveira 2014;Poon 2013). Increased resistance of the uterine arteries measured through Doppler ultrasound is a commonly used safe and non‐invasive test to assess for abnormal blood flow to the placenta, and at present holds some promise (Papageorghiou 2004).As the cause of pre‐eclampsia is not well understood, and screening tests remain unreliable, it is difficult to develop appropriate strategies for prevention of pre‐eclampsia. Current strategies for prevention focus on antenatal surveillance, modification of lifestyle, nutritional supplementation, and pharmacological therapy (Meher 2005). To date, the following pharmacological strategies to prevent pre‐eclampsia have found some merit:the use of antiplatelet agents such as aspirin is associated with a 17% reduction in the risk of pre‐eclampsia in high‐risk women (Duley 2007);calcium supplementation (≥ 1g/day) is associated with a significant reduction in the risk of pre‐eclampsia, particularly for women with low calcium diets (Hofmeyr 2014).antithrombotic therapies (such as low molecular weight heparin) may decrease the risk of pre‐eclampsia in women at high risk of placental dysfunction (Dodd 2013).the use of antiplatelet agents such as aspirin is associated with a 17% reduction in the risk of pre‐eclampsia in high‐risk women (Duley 2007);calcium supplementation (≥ 1g/day) is associated with a significant reduction in the risk of pre‐eclampsia, particularly for women with low calcium diets (Hofmeyr 2014).antithrombotic therapies (such as low molecular weight heparin) may decrease the risk of pre‐eclampsia in women at high risk of placental dysfunction (Dodd 2013).Supplementing women with melatonin, a potent antioxidant, may increase their resistance to oxidative stress and subsequently limit the systemic and uteroplacental endothelial damage that is observed in pre‐eclampsia (Hobson 2013). In addition, melatonin is also a powerful antioxidant, acting both as a direct scavenger of oxygen free radicals, especially the highly damaging hydroxyl radical, and indirectly via up‐regulation of antioxidant enzymes including glutathione peroxidase, glutathione reductase, superoxide dismutase and catalase (Reiter 2003).Clinically, oral melatonin is an accepted and effective preventative measure and treatment for jet lag (Herxheimer 2002). It has been assessed in assisted reproductive technology where the quality of oocytes is important for the success of in‐vitro fertilisation (IVF). Melatonin is present in the follicular fluid, is important for oocyte maturation and quality, and is thought to improve pregnancy outcomes with IVF (Rizzo 2010;Tamura 2008;Unfer 2011). Babies born from melatonin‐treated pregnancies have not been shown to have any increase in abnormalities (Unfer 2012). Melatonin freely crosses the placenta (Okatani 1998) and blood‐brain barrier (Welin 2007), and has an excellent safety profile with no known adverse effects (Fulia 2001;Gitto 2009). Reduced levels of melatonin are found in pregnant women with pre‐eclampsia (Lanoix 2012). In another published experiment they administered melatonin shortly before and during a short period of severe fetal asphyxia induced by umbilical cord occlusion at late gestation. Animal studies have supported its role in reducing fetal hypoxia and damage from oxidative stress when administered maternally. Animal and human studies to date have not shown melatonin treatment causes any harm. [Overview of ventilation strategies for the early management of intubated preterm infants] [Description of the condition]Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) is a chronic lung disease affecting preterm infants requiring respiratory support during the first days of life. More than 30% of infants less than 27 weeks gestation will have BPD (Fanaroff 2007;Stoll 2010). Mechanical ventilation is known to be one of the main factors contributing to BPD. Alternative modes of ventilation and respiratory support have been studied in the hope of reducing lung injury in preterm infants with respiratory distress (Greenough 2007;Greenough 2008a). Recently, non‐invasive respiratory support strategies such as nasal continuous positive airway pressure (NCPAP) and nasal intermittent positive pressure ventilation have been used in order to avoid endotracheal intubation and to protect the preterm infant’s lungs (De Klerk 2001;Jobe 2002;Kugelman 2007;Morley 2008;Patel 2008;Sai Sunil Kishore 2009;Subramaniam 2005;Thomson 2004). Despite efforts to offer less invasive respiratory support, many infants still need to be placed on mechanical ventilation via endotracheal tube due to worsening respiratory insufficiency. Evidence from a recent trial conducted in preterm neonates of 26 to 29 weeks gestational age has shown that 52% to 59% of the infants initially managed with NCPAP in the delivery room required endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation at some point in the neonatal period (Dunn 2011), and 45% of infants receiving NCPAP required intubation and ventilation within the first week of life (Dunn 2011). While the current research is mainly focused on non‐invasive respiratory support strategies, the relative benefits and safety of more invasive ventilation techniques and different ventilation modes frequently used in clinical practice remain unclear (Van Kaam 2010).Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD), also known as chronic lung disease, has been described as a series of radiological, clinical and histological changes in the lungs of premature infants with respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) who are treated with oxygen and mechanical ventilation (Northway 1967). Infants suffering from BPD are at increased risk of death and long‐term pulmonary and neurodevelopmental morbidities (Anderson 2006;Bhandari 2006). Children who have had BPD have higher hospital readmission rates during the first year of life (Eber 2001;Landry 2011) and are more likely to have impairment in development, cognitive function and language than children who have not had BPD (Karagianni 2011;Lewis 2002;Martins 2010;Short 2003). The impact of a respiratory disorder such as BPD on the overall health of the population is not only due to its high incidence and cost of hospital management, but also to its increased long‐term morbidity and mortality and the subsequent care due to associated disability (Karagianni 2011;Landry 2011;Short 2003).As first described by Northway in 1967, BPD (now known as 'classical BPD') was characterized by inflammation, necrotizing bronchiolitis and interstitial fibrosis that significantly compromised the process of blood oxygenation in the alveoli (Northway 1967). The definition of 'classic' BPD was proposed by Bancalari and colleagues (Bancalari 1979;O'Brodovich 1985) to include infants 28 days of age who required intermittent positive pressure ventilation during the first week of life and had an oxygen requirement and clinical signs of respiratory disease at 28 days of age or greater.In the late 1960s and early 1970s, few infants less than 30 weeks gestation survived. Therefore, the expected course for their repair of lung injury was in the 4 week (28 day) time frame. As a greater number of extremely preterm infants survived, 28 days became a less consequential outcome. Shennan and colleagues reported on outcome at 36 weeks postmenstrual age (PMA) and correlated that to poor pulmonary outcome at follow‐up (Shennan 1988). That definition at 36 weeks is now the standard definition. For all trials conducted in the past decade, if they involve preterm infants less than 32 weeks gestation, the 36 weeks PMA cut point is routinely used. It is not really an issue of standardization in the field ‐ more an issue of the historical use of these two outcome measures. As the population has changed, the definition has changed. In their time, both definitions were appropriate.Today, with the advent of pulmonary surfactant replacement therapy and the development of less aggressive modes of ventilation, it is rare to find necrotizing lesions of the bronchioles or alveolar fibrosis. [Homeopathy for reducing blood loss in the third stage of labour] [Description of the condition]Postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) is a leading cause of maternal mortality worldwide, especially in Africa and Asia (Khan 2006). Among causes of maternal death, the proportion of PPH (around 15%) has not changed between 1990 and 2013 (Kassebaum 2014). PPH is generally defined as blood loss from the genital tract greater than or equal to 500 mL within 24 hours after birth, while severe postpartum haemorrhage (SPPH) is blood loss greater than or equal to 1000 mL (WHO 2012). PPH also contributes to maternal morbidity such as blood transfusions, renal failure, and coagulation deficiencies. The prevalence of PPH and SPPH was reported to be around 6% and 2% respectively, although this varied widely across regions of the world (Carroli 2008). Inadequate measuring of blood loss during and after delivery has resulted in underestimates and thus variations in the reported prevalence of PPH (Duthie 2006;Stafford 2008). When blood loss was measured objectively, the overall prevalence of PPH and SPPH increased to 11% and 3% respectively (Carroli 2008). Common causes of PPH include hypotonic myometrium (uterine atony), retained placental tissue, genital tract trauma or coagulation defects (Cunningham 2014), with atonic PPH as the most prevalent among these conditions (Bateman 2010). Although some risk factors for PPH have been identified, such as previous PPH (Henry 2005;Magann 2005), pre‐eclampsia, chorioamnionitis (inflammation of the fetal membranes) (Wetta 2013), prolonged third stage of labour, retained placenta (Bais 2004), multiple gestation and macrosomia (large baby) (Sosa 2009), PPH can occur in women with no known risk factors.In order to prevent atonic PPH, active management of the third stage of labour is required, including controlled cord traction and administration of uterotonics, as recommended in various clinical guidelines (ACOG 2012;NICE 2014;WHO 2012). Several systematic reviews have assessed the effect of interventions to prevent PPH during the third stage of labour including: prophylactic oxytocin (Westhoff 2013), prostaglandins (Tunçalp 2012), ergot alkaloids (Liabsuetrakul 2007), carbetosine (Su 2012), uterine massage (Hofmeyr 2013) and umbilical injections (Mori 2012). Although prophylactic oxytocin, prostaglandins, and ergot alkaloids were reported as effective, the others have yet to be validated for effectiveness because of lack of evidence. At the same time, the prophylactic use of uterotonics, especially prostaglandins and ergot alkaloids, were reported to have unpleasant side effects. Moreover, alternative prophylactic interventions such as homeopathy for PPH are provided in clinical practice (Oberbaum 2005), but there are no systematic reviews that have examined its efficacy and safety.Complementary and alternative medicine (CAM) is incorporated into medical systems and practices, and is widely used, particularly by women. Several reviews reported that pregnant women use CAM therapies worldwide (Adams 2009;Hall 2011;Pallivalappila 2013). Pregnant women use CAMs to maintain or improve health and to obtain relief from pregnancy‐related symptoms (Adams 2009;Hall 2011). In addition, recommendations by healthcare professionals may influence their use of CAMs (Hall 2012). Women who used CAMs were characterised as older, with higher education and income and more physical symptoms (Adams 2009). Homeopathy, although controversial, is one of the popular CAM therapies among women in the prenatal period; other CAM therapies commonly used were acupuncture, aromatherapy, massage and yoga (Adams 2009). In the UK, 14.4% of pregnant women had used homeopathic medicine (Bishop 2011), 18.5% in Germany (Kalder 2011) and 4.3% in Norway (Nordeng 2011). Homeopathic medicine is gradually increasing in popularity outside of Europe. In Australia, 6.5% of pregnant women had used it (Skouteris 2008) and 2.3% in the US (Furlow 2008).Samuel Hahnemann originally developed homeopathy in the 18th century in Germany. Homeopathy is based on the fundamental principle of 'like with like', in which a substance that gives rise to symptoms in a healthy individual can be used to treat patients who present with similar symptoms. This is also described as the law of 'similars'. Homeopathic medicines are manufactured using a unique process in which the source material is serially diluted and alternated with violent agitation or 'succussion' (Peckham 2013). This is referred to as 'potentisation' or 'dynamisation', which is repeated many times until, theoretically, no molecules of the original substance remain. This process is thought to imprint information from the diluted substance to the solvent (Heirs 2007). Homeopathic medicines, their dilution and dosage, might change depending on the patient's condition.Treatments in this review will include homeopathic remedies, with single or multiple components, whose use is initiated by homeopaths, healthcare providers and/or women themselves. Some remedies may have a preventive effect on PPH.Arnica montana(leopard's bane) andBellis perennis(the common daisy) are commonly used in homeopathic treatments.Arnica montanais used to improve wounds and injuries on account of its abilities to control bruising, reduce swelling, and promote recovery, particularly for soft tissue damage (Robertson 2007), whileBellis perennisis used in the treatment of bruises, broken bones, and wounds (Karakaş 2012). Both remedies are regarded as anti‐haemorrhagic and analgesic, so are often employed to address problems that arise during labour (Oberbaum 2005). In addition,Thlaspi(Shepherd's purse) is used as a prophylactic treatment immediately after the delivery of the placenta (Brucker 2001). Inadequate measuring of blood loss during and after delivery has resulted in underestimates and thus variations in the reported prevalence of PPH (Duthie 2006;Stafford 2008). When blood loss was measured objectively, the overall prevalence of PPH and SPPH increased to 11% and 3% respectively (Carroli 2008). Common causes of PPH include hypotonic myometrium (uterine atony), retained placental tissue, genital tract trauma or coagulation defects (Cunningham 2014), with atonic PPH as the most prevalent among these conditions (Bateman 2010). Although some risk factors for PPH have been identified, such as previous PPH (Henry 2005;Magann 2005), pre‐eclampsia, chorioamnionitis (inflammation of the fetal membranes) (Wetta 2013), prolonged third stage of labour, retained placenta (Bais 2004), multiple gestation and macrosomia (large baby) (Sosa 2009), PPH can occur in women with no known risk factors.In order to prevent atonic PPH, active management of the third stage of labour is required, including controlled cord traction and administration of uterotonics, as recommended in various clinical guidelines (ACOG 2012;NICE 2014;WHO 2012). Several systematic reviews have assessed the effect of interventions to prevent PPH during the third stage of labour including: prophylactic oxytocin (Westhoff 2013), prostaglandins (Tunçalp 2012), ergot alkaloids (Liabsuetrakul 2007), carbetosine (Su 2012), uterine massage (Hofmeyr 2013) and umbilical injections (Mori 2012). Although prophylactic oxytocin, prostaglandins, and ergot alkaloids were reported as effective, the others have yet to be validated for effectiveness because of lack of evidence. At the same time, the prophylactic use of uterotonics, especially prostaglandins and ergot alkaloids, were reported to have unpleasant side effects. Moreover, alternative prophylactic interventions such as homeopathy for PPH are provided in clinical practice (Oberbaum 2005), but there are no systematic reviews that have examined its efficacy and safety.[Description of the intervention]Complementary and alternative medicine (CAM) is incorporated into medical systems and practices, and is widely used, particularly by women. Several reviews reported that pregnant women use CAM therapies worldwide (Adams 2009;Hall 2011;Pallivalappila 2013). Pregnant women use CAMs to maintain or improve health and to obtain relief from pregnancy‐related symptoms (Adams 2009;Hall 2011). In addition, recommendations by healthcare professionals may influence their use of CAMs (Hall 2012). Women who used CAMs were characterised as older, with higher education and income and more physical symptoms (Adams 2009). Homeopathy, although controversial, is one of the popular CAM therapies among women in the prenatal period; other CAM therapies commonly used were acupuncture, aromatherapy, massage and yoga (Adams 2009). In the UK, 14.4% of pregnant women had used homeopathic medicine (Bishop 2011), 18.5% in Germany (Kalder 2011) and 4.3% in Norway (Nordeng 2011). Homeopathic medicine is gradually increasing in popularity outside of Europe. In Australia, 6.5% of pregnant women had used it (Skouteris 2008) and 2.3% in the US (Furlow 2008).Samuel Hahnemann originally developed homeopathy in the 18th century in Germany. Homeopathy is based on the fundamental principle of 'like with like', in which a substance that gives rise to symptoms in a healthy individual can be used to treat patients who present with similar symptoms. This is also described as the law of 'similars'. Homeopathic medicines are manufactured using a unique process in which the source material is serially diluted and alternated with violent agitation or 'succussion' (Peckham 2013). This is referred to as 'potentisation' or 'dynamisation', which is repeated many times until, theoretically, no molecules of the original substance remain. This process is thought to imprint information from the diluted substance to the solvent (Heirs 2007). Homeopathic medicines, their dilution and dosage, might change depending on the patient's condition.[How the intervention might work]Treatments in this review will include homeopathic remedies, with single or multiple components, whose use is initiated by homeopaths, healthcare providers and/or women themselves. Some remedies may have a preventive effect on PPH.Arnica montana(leopard's bane) andBellis perennis(the common daisy) are commonly used in homeopathic treatments.Arnica montanais used to improve wounds and injuries on account of its abilities to control bruising, reduce swelling, and promote recovery, particularly for soft tissue damage (Robertson 2007), whileBellis perennisis used in the treatment of bruises, broken bones, and wounds (Karakaş 2012). Both remedies are regarded as anti‐haemorrhagic and analgesic, so are often employed to address problems that arise during labour (Oberbaum 2005). In addition,Thlaspi(Shepherd's purse) is used as a prophylactic treatment immediately after the delivery of the placenta (Brucker 2001). Treatments from this plant may contribute to the constriction of blood vessels, thereby reducing blood flow as an astringent agent, and is also thought to cause the uterine muscles to contract.[Why it is important to do this review]Although the popularity of homeopathic medicines for preventing PPH is growing worldwide, its effectiveness and potential side effects are not known.. [Beta‐3 adrenergic receptor agonist for adult with overactive bladder] [Description of the condition]Overactive bladder (OAB) is a clinical condition characterised by the presence of bothersome urinary symptoms including urgency, frequency and nocturia. If urinary incontinence is also present, it is known as OAB‐wet, while if not, it is termed OAB‐dry. OAB has a negative impact on quality of life (Gormley 2012).The International Continence Society defines OAB as the presence of urinary urgency, usually accompanied by frequency and nocturia, with or without urgency urinary incontinence, in the absence of urinary tract infection or other obvious pathology (Haylen 2010). Some conditions are commonly associated with OAB, such as neurologic injuries and diseases, urinary tract infection, bladder inflammation and bladder outlet obstruction. Urinary symptoms occur as a result of spontaneous detrusor contractions increasing the intravesical pressure during bladder filling. This may be caused by disturbances in nerves, smooth muscles or urothelium (Steers 2002). Among the different urinary symptoms, subjective symptom of urgency is the main symptom or parameter that should be measured in the diagnosis and monitoring response to treatment for patients with OAB (Abrams 2012;Yamaguchi 2009).According to the report of the 5thInternational Consultation on Incontinence, the worldwide estimated prevalence of OAB is between 12% and 17% (Altman 2013). The prevalence of OAB increases with age; in addition, it has been confirmed that OAB in general is prevalent among population over 40 years of age in both sexes (Abrams 2012). In the United States, the National Overactive Bladder Evaluation (NOBLE) program conducted a study which showed a prevalence of 16.9% in women and 16% in men (Stewart 2003). In Europe, the overall prevalence is 16.6% with similar rates in men and women (Milsom 2001).Abrams 2012included four population‐based surveys including the Epidemiology of LUTS (lower urinary tract symptoms) (EpiLUTS) study, storage symptoms were reported more frequently in women compared to men: urgency (35.7% vs 22.4%), frequency (24.6% vs 20.5%), and nocturia (75.8% vs 69.4%).Behavioral therapy is the first‐line therapy for patients with OAB. Patients are educated regarding bladder training, bladder control strategies, pelvic floor muscle training and fluid management.The current first‐line pharmacologic treatment for OAB is antimuscarinic drugs such as darifenacin, fesoterodine, oxybutynin, solifenacin, tolterodine, trospium or propiverine (Athanasopoulos 2011;Gormley 2012). These agents affect the efferent control of the detrusor muscles by antagonising the cholinergic muscarinic receptors. This blocks the parasympathetic impulses and inhibits detrusor muscle contraction. However, antimuscarinic agents can cause adverse effects such as dry mouth and constipation.Other treatment options are intermittent catheterisation, sacral neuromodulation and posterior tibial nerve stimulation (Gormley 2012). Onabotulinumtoxin A was also recently approved by regulatory authorities as a treatment for OAB among patients who do not respond or has inadequate response to anticholinergics (FDA 2013).Cochrane systematic reviews are available covering many of the treatment options mentioned above: anticholinergics (Madhuvrata 2012), pelvic floor muscle training (Hay‐Smith 2011), bladder training (Wallace 2004), intermittent catheterisation (Moore 2007), sacral neuromodulation (implanted) (Herbison 2009), and onabotulinumtoxin A (Duthie 2011).In June 2012, the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved the new drug class, beta‐3 adrenergic receptor agonists, for the treatment of OAB. This emerging drug class is represented by mirabegron, ritobegron, and solabegron (Igawa 2013). It acts by relaxing the detrusor muscle during the storage phase of the urinary bladder by activation of beta‐3 adrenergic receptors, thereby increasing bladder capacity (FDA 2012). The effect of beta‐3 adrenergic receptor agonists is through inhibition of the bladder afferent nerves, thereby improving the symptom of urgency, which, as mentioned, is the key symptom in the diagnosis and monitoring response of OAB.Beta‐adrenergic receptors are classified into three subtypes (beta‐1, beta‐2 and beta‐3) (Nomiya 2003). Cellular and messenger RNA expression studies have identified that majority of the beta‐adrenergic receptors in the human detrusor muscle are of the beta‐3 subtype, which was also found to promote detrusor relaxation and aid urine storage (Fujimura 1999;Takeda 1999). Hence, it was postulated as a novel drug class stimulating this receptor may have therapeutic potential, particularly in patients with storage symptoms (Kumar 2003).Several randomised controlled trials have shown significant reduction of OAB symptoms among patients with moderate to severe symptoms over at least an eight‐week treatment period with beta‐adrenergic receptor agonists (Ohlstein 2012). Dose‐dependent improvement (reduction) in the number of micturition episodes have been reported with good safety and tolerability (Chapple 2013a;Chapple 2013b;Chapple 2013c;Khullar 2013). Moreover, Its efficacy and safety in controlling OAB symptoms on outcomes such as frequency and incontinence, showed fewer incidences of the antimuscarinic side effects such as dry mouth and constipation compared to placebo and other drugs (Medscape 2013;Sacco 2012). However, adverse effects such as hypertension, nasopharyngitis, urinary tract infection and headache have been reported in some particular types of beta‐3 adrenergic receptor agonists (FDA 2012;Nitti 2013).Beta‐3 adrenergic receptor agonists is a new drug class that has a promising effect and potential for use in the treatment of OAB. As mentioned, a number of randomised controlled trials (RCTs) have been conducted using these drugs. However, only a small difference in the efficacy of such agents was noted when compared to anticholinergics and other treatment options. Furthermore, inconsistencies in the associated adverse events related to its use were also noted in the trials. A meta‐analysis of these trials may provide a clearer picture of the efficacy and tolerability profile of beta‐3 adrenergic receptor agonists, particularly when compared to other treatment options. [Ayurveda interventions for rheumatoid arthritis] [Description of the condition]Ayurveda is an ancient indigenous medical system that has been practiced in the Indian subcontinent for many centuries. Ayurveda is still a popular and widely used treatment system in India and other parts of the world (Acharya 2000;Valiathan 2003;Sharma 2007). Ayurveda derives its name from the Sanskrit'ayu'(life) and'veda'(knowledge), and Ayurveda is translated to mean the science of life (Valiathan 2006). The doctrine of Ayurveda is based on three'doshas'(energy forces):Vata,Pitta, andKapha.They are believed to be present everywhere in the body and govern all physiological functions. In healthy individuals, all of thedoshasare believed to be in balance and functioning adequately in appropriate proportions and positions; an imbalance of thedoshasis believed to result in disease (Hankey 2001;Prasher 2008;Chopra 2010). Some basic concepts of Ayurveda in health and disease are detailed inAppendix 1.Ayurveda uses a holistic approach to health and disease and aims to restore the delicate balance betweendoshas, tissues (dhatu), and wastes (mala) (Chopra 2002a). Ayurveda advocates a unique set of principles and individually customized guidelines on diet and exercise in daily healthy living, and uses an extensive pharmacopeia of natural remedies derived from medicinal plants and minerals documented in ancient texts. These remedies are now available in modern texts and from online sources (Frawley 1994;Acharya 2000;AyuSoft 2006;Samy 2008). These herbal and mineral remedies are prescribed as individualized therapy, based on the basic Ayurveda perspective that individuals with the same disease may differ, and hence the treatments given to individuals with the same disease can also be different.While Ayurvedic therapies were initially based on experience, they are increasingly being subjected to experimental validation in pre‐clinical laboratory studies and in clinical studies (Ziauddin 1996;Patwardhan 2005;Sumantran 2007;Prasher 2008;Narahari 2010;Sarmukaddam 2010). This validation is particularly evident in the use of Ayurveda in the treatment of chronic conditions such as degenerative disorders (Ven Murthy 2010), arthritic conditions such as osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis (Thabrew 2001;Chopra 2004a;Sumantran 2008;Chopra 2010), and as a promising anti‐cancer agent (Wadhwa 2013). Ayurveda is considered to be an important source of innovative drug discovery for safe, effective, and affordable medicines (Mashelkar 2008;Patwardhan 2009).Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic, progressive, systemic, autoimmune, inflammatory condition, affecting around 0.5% to 1% of the adult population in developed countries (Gabriel 2009). The prevalence of rheumatoid arthritis in low and middle‐income countries varies but is generally lower than in the developed world (Dans 1997;Chopra 2001a;Muirden 2005;Joshi 2009). Rheumatoid arthritis is characterized by inflammation of the synovia of flexible joints leading to joint swelling, stiffness, and tenderness, which can eventually result in cartilage damage, bone erosions, and joint destruction; this may lead to disability, decreased productivity, and increased health expenditure (Puolakka 2005;Odegard 2008;CDC 2011). Rheumatoid arthritis affects women predominantly in the perimenopausal age group and the sex ratio of females to males with rheumatoid arthritis is 3:1. The disease is dichotomously characterized by two auto‐antibodies: rheumatoid factor and anti‐cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti‐CCP). Rheumatoid factor is present (seropositive) in about 70% of people with rheumatoid arthritis and is often associated with rheumatoid nodules, more extra‐articular complications, and poor prognosis in terms of erosive and destructive bone disease and deformities. However, seronegative rheumatoid factor disease can be as disabling as seropositive rheumatoid arthritis in terms of articular deformities. Anti‐CCP antibodies are considered to be more sensitive and specific compared to rheumatoid factor; they play a central pathogenic role, and seropositivity to rheumatoid factor and anti‐CCP antibodies can exist for many years prior to the onset of rheumatoid arthritis (Sokolove 2014). An association has also been described between tobacco use (including smoking), premature atherosclerosis, and rheumatoid arthritis (Ruiz‐Esquide 2012). Though there are ethnic differences in the genotyping characters of rheumatoid arthritis polymorphisms all over the world, several studies unequivocally demonstrate the association of rheumatoid arthritis with human leukocyte antigen (HLA) D alleles and in particular HLA DRB 1, DR4, and 10 (Scally 2013;Zhou 2013).In around 40% of people, rheumatoid arthritis can also affect other systems over their lifetime and produce anaemia, vasculitis, kidney disease, diffuse inflammation in the lungs, cardiovascular complications, and eye disorders (Turesson 2003;Myasoedova 2011;Cavagna 2013). People with rheumatoid arthritis also have a higher risk of increased morbidity and mortality due to cardiovascular disease (Gabriel 2009;Meune 2009;Sodergren 2009).The diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis is based on clinical criteria, with laboratory and radiology findings helping to establish the diagnosis. The American College of Rheumatology/European League Against Rheumatism (ACR/EULAR) diagnostic criteria are the most commonly used operational standards for the diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis (Arnett 1988;Aletaha 2010). The revised 2010 criteria enable identification of early disease and the early initiation of aggressive therapy to protect against joint destruction. However, these are classification systems and they do not accurately differentiate between rheumatoid arthritis and other conditions in the early stages of disease, or those with atypical presentations (Chopra 2011).Conditions equivalent to rheumatoid and musculoskeletal diseases are described in detail inCharaka Samhitaor the 'Compendium of Charaka' (Sharma 1994). There are two schools of thought in Ayurveda regarding the diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis, depending on the preference of Ayurveda practitioners for the diagnostic guidelines in two Ayurveda texts,Madhava NidanaandAshtanga Hridaya.Madhava Nidana(a treatise of diagnostic guidelines from the 9th century) describes a clinical condition known as'Amavata'that is considered to be similar to rheumatoid arthritis (Srikantha Murthy 1993). The majority of Ayurveda practitioners considerAmavatato be equivalent to rheumatoid arthritis (MOHFW 2001).Amavatais linked to the gut and is considered to be the result of the production of'ama'(a toxic and pro‐inflammatory waste‐product of disturbed metabolism) and vitiatedVata dosha.According to this model, joints and soft tissues are affected by'ama', produced in the gut due to weakenedagni, food indiscretions, or disturbed'dosha'equilibrium, resulting in inflammatory and obstructive processes (Srikantha Murthy 1993;Sharma 1994;Chopra 2010). This model of etiopathogenesis is depicted inFigure 1. According to Ayurveda postulates, in general people withVata prakritiare more prone to develop joint diseases with severe pain (Srikantha Murthy 1993). Recent investigations utilizing inflammatory and oxidative stress pathway genes have provided evidence that the development of rheumatoid arthritis differs according toprakritisubgroups (Juyal 2012).Events in the pathogenesis of Amavata (Ayurveda equivalent of rheumatoid arthritis); based onAcharya 2000;Chopra 2002a.InAshtanga Hridaya, another ancient compendium of the Ayurvedic system, the clinical condition considered similar to rheumatoid arthritis is calledVatarakta(Manohar 2014).A smaller proportion of Ayurveda practitioners, particularly those from states in southern India, considerVataraktato be equivalent to rheumatoid arthritis, while those who considerAmavatato represent rheumatoid arthritis equateVataraktawith gouty arthritis (MOHFW 2001).Vataraktais considered to be the result of faulty lifestyle and dietary habits that lead to vitiatedRaktaand aggravation ofVatathat further aggravates the vitiatedRakta, leading toVidhanain the blood (similar to inflammation).Vataraktamanifests as the insidious onset of stiffness, inflammation of the joints of the fingers and toes that is often symmetrical, sometimes associated with cutaneous manifestations in the prodromal stages, and is characterized by flare ups and remissions (Manohar 2014).The diagnosis ofAmavataorVataraktais entirely clinical and depends on the Ayurveda physician's training and experience in examination (of the pulse, the tongue, hair, etc), and assessment of the individual's responses to questions about (or scores on questionnaires collecting information on) body constitution (prakriti), bodily energies (dosha), tissues (dhatu), metabolic waste (mala), metabolic fire (agni), toxicity (ama), body parts (avayava), vital body parts (marma), and life style, diet, and quality of life (Juyal 2012). These assessments are subjective and influenced by the experience of the practitioner, as well as the particular tradition of Ayurveda practiced. Attempts to improve the inter‐rater reliability ofprakritiassessments based on questionnaires and computer‐based assessments have met with some success, though this agreement is less evident for Ayurvedic diagnoses, or diagnosis of the state ofdoshasby examination of the pulse or on examination of the tongue (Kurande 2013a;Kurande 2013b). No commonly agreed set of criteria exist that have been evaluated to ensure the reliability of diagnoses made by different Ayurveda practitioners forAmavataorVatarakta; or to ensure that all those considered to haveAmavataorVataraktawill also show concurrence with modern definitions of rheumatoid arthritis, or to the extent of concurrence between these definitions. However, in some experimental clinical studies, the expected degree of improvement based on Ayurveda's stage‐wise classification, and predictions that patients of a certain constitution type would be more prone to developing the disease, were supported and the equivalence of the classical Ayurvedic diagnosis ofVataraktaand the modern medical diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis was also demonstrated (Kumar 2011).The treatment of rheumatoid arthritis includes analgesics and non‐steroidal antiinflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) for symptomatic relief. The non‐biological disease‐modifying anti‐rheumatic drugs (DMARDs) (hydroxychloroquine, leflunomide, methotrexate, minocycline, sulphasalazine) are used to slow disease progress, induce remission, and improve quality of life. Steroids are used for symptomatic relief, anti‐inflammatory actions, and to reduce joint damage. Biological agents inhibit specific steps in inflammatory processes and include those that do not target tumour necrosis factor (TNF) such as abatacept, rituximab, and tocilizumab, and those that are anti‐TNF such as adalimumab, etanercept, inﬂiximab, certolizumab pegol, and golimumab. Indications for their use as monotherapy and in combination are detailed in the 2012 update of the 2008 American College of Rheumatology (ACR) recommendations (Singh 2012), and in the guidance provided by the National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence and the National Collaborating Centre for Chronic Conditions in the UK (NCCCC 2009;NICE 2009). Guidance on the management of early rheumatoid arthritis is also provided by the Scottish Intercollegiate Guidelines Network (SIGN 2011). These guidelines are similar in their recommendations for a multidisciplinary approach to managing people with rheumatoid arthritis, and a step‐wise approach to the use of monotherapy with DMARDs before considering combination treatments. The ACR 2012 recommendations are more aggressive than other management approaches and also differ in the duration of symptoms required for definitions of acute and chronic rheumatoid arthritis (Singh 2012). Opinion is divided on the safety and effectiveness of early initiation of aggressive treatments, especially in community settings and in developing countries with their paucity of rheumatologists, and given the variable course of rheumatoid arthritis (Epstein 2003;Chopra 2011).These interventions have been recommended based on evaluation of their efficacy and safety. Low‐dose oral corticosteroids have been shown to be effective when used in combination with DMARD therapy for the short‐term relief of signs and symptoms, and to minimize radiological damage in the medium to long term (Gøtzsche 2005;Kirwan 2007). There is also limited evidence to indicate that moderate‐term prednisone treatment of rheumatoid arthritis is superior to placebo and similar to aspirin or chloroquine in improving several common rheumatoid arthritis disease activity measures (Criswell 1998).Methotrexate is substantially more beneficial than placebo in the short‐term treatment of people with rheumatoid arthritis, although its use is associated with a high withdrawal rate due to adverse events (Lopez‐Olivo 2014). Trials in DMARD‐naive patients and in those with inadequate response to methotrexate or other DMARDs showed no significant advantage for methotrexate given in combination with non‐biological DMARDs versus methotrexate monotherapy; withdrawals for lack of efficacy or toxicity were similar in both groups (Katchamart 2010). Significant reductions in pain and improvement in physical function (measured by the Health Assessment Questionnaire or HAQ) were found with the combination in a Cochrane review in those who had responded inadequately to methotrexate (Katchamart 2010). However, the balance of efficacy and toxicity from the moderate level of evidence in the systematic review showed no statistically significant advantage for the methotrexate combination over methotrexate monotherapy, prompting the authors of the Cochrane review to call for trials comparing currently used methotrexate doses and combination therapies (Katchamart 2010).An overview of Cochrane reviews of biologicals provided indirect evidence to show that anakinra was less efficacious than etanercept and adalimumab, and that etanercept caused fewer withdrawals due to adverse events than adalimumab, anakinra, and inﬂiximab (Singh 2009). Another overview of Cochrane reviews found that in the short term, biologicals were associated with statistically significantly higher rates of serious infections (opportunistic infections as well as bacterial infections), tuberculosis (TB) reactivation, total number of adverse events and withdrawals due to adverse events (Singh 2011). A Cochrane review in progress is evaluating the efficacy and safety of methotrexate monotherapy and methotrexate combination therapy with traditional and biologic disease‐modifying anti‐rheumatic drugs for rheumatoid arthritis using network meta‐analysis (Hazlewood 2013).Thus, while DMARDs have demonstrable benefits in people with rheumatoid arthritis, they are not devoid of adverse reactions; many patients experience only partial benefits. Adverse effects, especially the risk of infections and of reactivation of TB, and their high cost, limit use of biologicals, particularly in low‐ and middle‐income countries with a high burden of TB, latent TB, and HIV infections.Rheumatoid arthritis continues to be a major therapeutic challenge despite several advances in modern medicine.Classical Ayurvedic interventions utilize 'whose systems' and 'personalized' approaches that consider causative factors and pathogenic process and do not specifically target only the symptoms of rheumatoid arthritis. Ayurvedic interventions for people with rheumatoid arthritis are based on the individual's disease status and attempt to restore the imbalance of the threedoshas, and thereby attempt to reduce symptoms, arrest disease progression, and improve functioning and quality of life. Ayurvedic formulations invariably target the gut, joints, and immune system. Ayurvedic texts describe the role ofRasayana(adaptogenic, tissue strengthening, and rejuvenating) therapy with specific medicinal herbs and minerals, several of which are used to treat arthritis (Srikantha Murthy 1993;Sharma 1994).Ayurvedic formulations are often complex, with several herbal‐mineral ingredients. Their preparation is governed by well‐described pharmacological principles of compatibility and administration. The various formulations prescribed in combination in Ayurveda practice forAmavataare detailed inAppendix 2, and forVataraktainAppendix 3.Ricinus communis(Erand/castor oil) and Guggul extracts (Commiphora mukul,Boswellia serrata) are examples of potent anti‐arthritic medicinal plants listed in Ayurvedic texts (Sharma 1994). Numerous otherRasayanaplants, especiallyWithania somnifera(Ashwagangda), are common components of anti‐rheumatic medications. Other well‐standardized and commonly used formulations areDashamool,Mahayograj Guggul,Vatavidhwansa,Suvarna Bhasma,Yograj Guggul,and Triphala Churana. Several of these have a potent laxative action. The non‐biological disease‐modifying anti‐rheumatic drugs (DMARDs) (hydroxychloroquine, leflunomide, methotrexate, minocycline, sulphasalazine) are used to slow disease progress, induce remission, and improve quality of life. Steroids are used for symptomatic relief, anti‐inflammatory actions, and to reduce joint damage. Biological agents inhibit specific steps in inflammatory processes and include those that do not target tumour necrosis factor (TNF) such as abatacept, rituximab, and tocilizumab, and those that are anti‐TNF such as adalimumab, etanercept, inﬂiximab, certolizumab pegol, and golimumab. Indications for their use as monotherapy and in combination are detailed in the 2012 update of the 2008 American College of Rheumatology (ACR) recommendations (Singh 2012), and in the guidance provided by the National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence and the National Collaborating Centre for Chronic Conditions in the UK (NCCCC 2009;NICE 2009). Guidance on the management of early rheumatoid arthritis is also provided by the Scottish Intercollegiate Guidelines Network (SIGN 2011). These guidelines are similar in their recommendations for a multidisciplinary approach to managing people with rheumatoid arthritis, and a step‐wise approach to the use of monotherapy with DMARDs before considering combination treatments. The ACR 2012 recommendations are more aggressive than other management approaches and also differ in the duration of symptoms required for definitions of acute and chronic rheumatoid arthritis (Singh 2012). Opinion is divided on the safety and effectiveness of early initiation of aggressive treatments, especially in community settings and in developing countries with their paucity of rheumatologists, and given the variable course of rheumatoid arthritis (Epstein 2003;Chopra 2011).These interventions have been recommended based on evaluation of their efficacy and safety. Low‐dose oral corticosteroids have been shown to be effective when used in combination with DMARD therapy for the short‐term relief of signs and symptoms, and to minimize radiological damage in the medium to long term (Gøtzsche 2005;Kirwan 2007). There is also limited evidence to indicate that moderate‐term prednisone treatment of rheumatoid arthritis is superior to placebo and similar to aspirin or chloroquine in improving several common rheumatoid arthritis disease activity measures (Criswell 1998).Methotrexate is substantially more beneficial than placebo in the short‐term treatment of people with rheumatoid arthritis, although its use is associated with a high withdrawal rate due to adverse events (Lopez‐Olivo 2014). Trials in DMARD‐naive patients and in those with inadequate response to methotrexate or other DMARDs showed no significant advantage for methotrexate given in combination with non‐biological DMARDs versus methotrexate monotherapy; withdrawals for lack of efficacy or toxicity were similar in both groups (Katchamart 2010). Significant reductions in pain and improvement in physical function (measured by the Health Assessment Questionnaire or HAQ) were found with the combination in a Cochrane review in those who had responded inadequately to methotrexate (Katchamart 2010). However, the balance of efficacy and toxicity from the moderate level of evidence in the systematic review showed no statistically significant advantage for the methotrexate combination over methotrexate monotherapy, prompting the authors of the Cochrane review to call for trials comparing currently used methotrexate doses and combination therapies (Katchamart 2010).An overview of Cochrane reviews of biologicals provided indirect evidence to show that anakinra was less efficacious than etanercept and adalimumab, and that etanercept caused fewer withdrawals due to adverse events than adalimumab, anakinra, and inﬂiximab (Singh 2009). Another overview of Cochrane reviews found that in the short term, biologicals were associated with statistically significantly higher rates of serious infections (opportunistic infections as well as bacterial infections), tuberculosis (TB) reactivation, total number of adverse events and withdrawals due to adverse events (Singh 2011). However, the balance of efficacy and toxicity from the moderate level of evidence in the systematic review showed no statistically significant advantage for the methotrexate combination over methotrexate monotherapy, prompting the authors of the Cochrane review to call for trials comparing currently used methotrexate doses and combination therapies (Katchamart 2010).An overview of Cochrane reviews of biologicals provided indirect evidence to show that anakinra was less efficacious than etanercept and adalimumab, and that etanercept caused fewer withdrawals due to adverse events than adalimumab, anakinra, and inﬂiximab (Singh 2009). Another overview of Cochrane reviews found that in the short term, biologicals were associated with statistically significantly higher rates of serious infections (opportunistic infections as well as bacterial infections), tuberculosis (TB) reactivation, total number of adverse events and withdrawals due to adverse events (Singh 2011). Ayurvedic interventions for people with rheumatoid arthritis are based on the individual's disease status and attempt to restore the imbalance of the threedoshas, and thereby attempt to reduce symptoms, arrest disease progression, and improve functioning and quality of life. Ayurvedic formulations invariably target the gut, joints, and immune system. Their preparation is governed by well‐described pharmacological principles of compatibility and administration. The various formulations prescribed in combination in Ayurveda practice forAmavataare detailed inAppendix 2, and forVataraktainAppendix 3.Ricinus communis(Erand/castor oil) and Guggul extracts (Commiphora mukul,Boswellia serrata) are examples of potent anti‐arthritic medicinal plants listed in Ayurvedic texts (Sharma 1994). Ayurveda therapeutics emphasize enemas of medicated oils and decoctions for rheumatic diseases, often administered alternatively for several days. Specific enemas are indicated to eliminate gut toxins, strengthen joints, and to relieve pain and inflammation. Personalized nutrition plans aim to alleviate symptoms, improve digestion, and facilitate recovery. An extensive list of dietary recipes, including several medicinal herbs, to be used in specific disease subtypes, are described in Ayurveda texts. The principles of Ayurvedic management ofAmavataare briefly described inAppendix 5, and ofVataraktainAppendix 6. Although classic texts contain descriptions of classic formulations, Ayurvedic practitioners often modify them to suit the individual constitution (prakriti) that confers genetic predisposition toward disease, and also determines the response to therapy. The results of trials to date in rheumatoid arthritis and in osteoarthritis suggest that while data for efficacy may, at best, be modest, data for safety in the context of the trials seem more impressive, raising the possibility of integrating Ayurvedic interventions with standard treatment with DMARDs (Chopra 2010). Data on the comparative effects of 'whole systems' Ayurvedic treatments are also currently lacking. An up‐to‐date systematic review using Cochrane methods would be timely and would provide evidence to inform health decisions nationally, regionally, and globally, for this difficult to treat chronic condition.. The muscle wall of the womb (uterus) is called the myometrium and is predominantly made up of smooth muscle. Cancers that arise from smooth muscle are called leiomyosarcomas (LMSs). LMSs are the most common uterine sarcomas. Compared to other types of uterine cancer, LMS is an aggressive tumour associated with a high risk of recurrence and death, regardless of stage at presentation (D'Angelo 2010).LMSs are rare and the overall incidence is around 9 cases per million. Incidence increases rapidly from the age of 35 years and reaches a plateau in those aged 50 years and above (Dennis 2012). Risk factors include nulliparity, increasing age, obesity and history of pelvic radiation.Symptoms of LMS are similar to the symptoms of benign uterine leiomyomata (fibroids). These common symptoms include abnormal vaginal bleeding, a palpable pelvic mass and pelvic pain. Fibroids and leiomyosarcoma often co‐exist which can make diagnosis difficult. LMSs may grow rapidly, leading to tumour rupture and bleeding into the abdominal cavity. Locally advanced disease may cause symptoms due to growth into, or pressure on, other pelvic organs, such as bleeding into the bladder or blockage of the tubes draining the kidneys into the bladder (ureters). LMS can spread (metastasise) early, via the bloodstream, to distant sites and up to 33% of people with newly diagnosed uterine LMS present with distant metastatic disease (stage IVB). However, as microscopic metastatic disease may be present at diagnosis, adjuvant treatment is often recommended following surgery. This may be adjuvant radiotherapy (RT), chemotherapy or a combination of the two (Hensley 2009;Hensley 2013). Chemotherapy agents used include doxorubicin, docetaxel and gemcitabine. Hormonal therapies have also been tried, as these have fewer side effects than chemotherapy (George 2014;Thanopoulou 2014;Sanfilippo 2011). Several case series have supported the role of primary surgery (Dinh 2004;Nassar 2010;Park 2008). In women with extra‐uterine disease at presentation, the role of surgery is controversial and has the potential to cause harm without benefit to survival.For women with disease confined to the pelvis (stage II) or the abdomen (stage III), TAH and BSO with surgical cytoreduction of intra‐abdominal and retroperitoneal disease is often performed. Therefore pelvic lymphadenectomy (removal of lymph glands in the pelvis) may not be necessary. [Exercise therapy following surgical rotator cuff repair] [Description of the condition]Shoulder pain is a common problem; approximately 4.5 million patients in the United States seek medical treatment for their shoulder pain annually (Mather 2013). Rotator cuff pathology is one of the most common shoulder conditions for which patients seek medical treatment (Barr 2004;Tytherleigh‐Strong 2001). Rotator cuff muscles function as dynamic stabilizers of the shoulder joint by keeping the humeral head reduced against the glenoid. They also assist with rotation and various shoulder movements such as reaching one's arm behind the back or overhead to grab an object. As people are likely to use their shoulder joint on a daily basis, over time the rotator cuff muscle tendon unit can experience wear and tear. This wear and tear of the rotator cuff muscle tendon unit can result in no symptoms, or it can lead to pain, weakness, and decreased range of motion in the shoulder.Rotator cuff pathology includes a wide spectrum, from inflammation of the tendon, called 'tendonosis,' to rupture of the tendon, called a 'tear.' Individuals with rotator cuff disease including tendinopathy and tears can be treated with nonoperative or surgical treatment (Coghlan 2008). Based on cadaver studies, it is estimated that more than 30% of adults will acquire a rotator cuff tendon tear over their lifetime (Reily 2006).Rotator cuff muscles consist of the supraspinatus, the infraspinatus, the subscapularis, and the teres minor. The most commonly injured is the supraspinatus; this injury occurs in nearly all rotator cuff tear variants (Jerosch 1991). The supraspinatus is by far the most common of the rotator cuff muscles to be torn and subsequently surgically repaired; however, this review will evaluate all rotator cuff muscles if sufficient randomized controlled trials are available. The different types of tears include partial thickness and full thickness (Tashjian 2012). Partial‐thickness tears are described on the basis of shape and percentage torn. Full‐thickness tears are classified into different sizes. Some partial‐thickness and some small full‐thickness tears of the rotator cuff may heal spontaneously, but the natural history of rotator cuff injury is that it will enlarge over time if not surgically repaired (Jarrett 2011;van der Meijden 2012). Healing of ruptured rotator cuff tendons occurs only when the tendon is surgically repaired back to its bony insertion on the greater or lesser tuberosity of the proximal humerus (van der Meijden 2012). The method of surgical repair—ranging from arthroscopic to mini‐open—has not been found to make a significant difference in functional outcomes or complications (Morse 2008). Following a surgical rotator cuff repair, a period of three to four weeks is required for the remodeling phase and scar tissue organization to take place. This remodeling repair between the tendon and bone interface will not reach maximal tensile strength for three to four months (Carpenter 1998). Our review will focus on studies that compare different exercise therapy protocols that help restore function to the shoulder while healing of the rotator cuff after surgical repair takes place.Although exercise protocols following rotator cuff surgery may have similar goals of improving function and reducing pain, the initiation, timing, and progression of exercises vary widely. For example, one program may prescribe immobilization of the shoulder for six weeks following surgery before passive range of motion is begun, and another program may prescribe passive range of motion immediately; also the timing of progression from passive to active exercise may vary. Traditional slow exercise protocols that begin with shoulder immobilization are designed to protect the surgical repair of the torn rotator cuff muscle while allowing maximum healing of the tendon. Accelerated exercise protocols with immediate passive range of motion exercises aim to prevent stiffness, muscle atrophy, and scar tissue formation that can lead to loss of function and pain (van der Meijden 2012).Rotator cuff surgery rehabilitation programs are often based on both surgeon preference and pathology found at the time of surgery. The surgeon's interpretation of how small or large the rotator cuff tear is, the health of the tissue being repaired, and the strength of the repair influences the postoperative rehabilitation plan.Generally, exercise therapies after rotator cuff surgery emphasize improving range of motion of the glenohumeral joint while maintaining elbow, wrist, and hand range of motion. These goals are accomplished through both passive and active exercises, and timing and progression are highly variable. Additional activities include joint mobilization of both the glenohumeral and scapulothoracic joint and strengthening exercises for the rotator cuff and other supporting muscles.Exercise therapy after rotator cuff surgery is typically performed in three stages, according to the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) (AAOS 2011). The first stage consists of immobilization of the shoulder, so that the repaired tendon can heal. Usually patients are put in a shoulder sling to avoid excessive movement and/or reinjury. The second stage includes passive exercise of the shoulder when the surgeon decides that it is safe for the patient to passively move his/her shoulder. In most cases, this begins within four to six weeks after surgery. The physical therapist helps patients with passive movement of the shoulder to improve range of motion in the operated shoulder. The third and final stage comprises active exercise of the operated shoulder, typically starting eight to 12 weeks post surgery and continuing for up to six months, with the objectives of improving range of motion, strengthening shoulder muscles, and improving control of the arm (AAOS 2011).Although the AAOS includes strengthening as part of the third and final active exercise stage, other sources such as theInternational Journal of Sports Physical Therapy (IJSPT)describe a four‐phase postsurgical rehabilitation protocol. Phase I involves protecting repaired tissue by restricting active movement. Phase II begins when the patient is cleared for active assisted range of motion. Phase III is characterized by initial rotator cuff strengthening. Phase IV begins when the remodeling phase of the repair is close to complete and advanced strengthening exercises can take place (van der Meijden 2012).Immobilization following rotator cuff repair is designed to protect the surgically repaired tendon‐bone interface while healing takes place. Passive range of motion exercises following surgery are used to prevent postoperative scar adhesions and resultant joint stiffness.Huberty 2009reported that the incidence of shoulder joint stiffness after surgical rotator cuff repair followed by six weeks of immobilization and no overhead stretches was 4% (21/500 participants). Active exercises are performed to strengthen the joint overall and to restore full joint function.Currently, expert opinion and clinical experience along with moderate scientific data on tendon histologic healing are used to guide postoperative rotator cuff rehabilitation (van der Meijden 2012). The most commonly injured is the supraspinatus; this injury occurs in nearly all rotator cuff tear variants (Jerosch 1991). The supraspinatus is by far the most common of the rotator cuff muscles to be torn and subsequently surgically repaired; however, this review will evaluate all rotator cuff muscles if sufficient randomized controlled trials are available. The different types of tears include partial thickness and full thickness (Tashjian 2012). Partial‐thickness tears are described on the basis of shape and percentage torn. Full‐thickness tears are classified into different sizes. Some partial‐thickness and some small full‐thickness tears of the rotator cuff may heal spontaneously, but the natural history of rotator cuff injury is that it will enlarge over time if not surgically repaired (Jarrett 2011;van der Meijden 2012). Healing of ruptured rotator cuff tendons occurs only when the tendon is surgically repaired back to its bony insertion on the greater or lesser tuberosity of the proximal humerus (van der Meijden 2012). The method of surgical repair—ranging from arthroscopic to mini‐open—has not been found to make a significant difference in functional outcomes or complications (Morse 2008). Following a surgical rotator cuff repair, a period of three to four weeks is required for the remodeling phase and scar tissue organization to take place. This remodeling repair between the tendon and bone interface will not reach maximal tensile strength for three to four months (Carpenter 1998). Our review will focus on studies that compare different exercise therapy protocols that help restore function to the shoulder while healing of the rotator cuff after surgical repair takes place.[Description of the intervention]Although exercise protocols following rotator cuff surgery may have similar goals of improving function and reducing pain, the initiation, timing, and progression of exercises vary widely. For example, one program may prescribe immobilization of the shoulder for six weeks following surgery before passive range of motion is begun, and another program may prescribe passive range of motion immediately; also the timing of progression from passive to active exercise may vary. Traditional slow exercise protocols that begin with shoulder immobilization are designed to protect the surgical repair of the torn rotator cuff muscle while allowing maximum healing of the tendon. Accelerated exercise protocols with immediate passive range of motion exercises aim to prevent stiffness, muscle atrophy, and scar tissue formation that can lead to loss of function and pain (van der Meijden 2012).Rotator cuff surgery rehabilitation programs are often based on both surgeon preference and pathology found at the time of surgery. The surgeon's interpretation of how small or large the rotator cuff tear is, the health of the tissue being repaired, and the strength of the repair influences the postoperative rehabilitation plan.Generally, exercise therapies after rotator cuff surgery emphasize improving range of motion of the glenohumeral joint while maintaining elbow, wrist, and hand range of motion. These goals are accomplished through both passive and active exercises, and timing and progression are highly variable. Additional activities include joint mobilization of both the glenohumeral and scapulothoracic joint and strengthening exercises for the rotator cuff and other supporting muscles.Exercise therapy after rotator cuff surgery is typically performed in three stages, according to the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) (AAOS 2011). The first stage consists of immobilization of the shoulder, so that the repaired tendon can heal. Usually patients are put in a shoulder sling to avoid excessive movement and/or reinjury. The second stage includes passive exercise of the shoulder when the surgeon decides that it is safe for the patient to passively move his/her shoulder. In most cases, this begins within four to six weeks after surgery. The physical therapist helps patients with passive movement of the shoulder to improve range of motion in the operated shoulder. The third and final stage comprises active exercise of the operated shoulder, typically starting eight to 12 weeks post surgery and continuing for up to six months, with the objectives of improving range of motion, strengthening shoulder muscles, and improving control of the arm (AAOS 2011).Although the AAOS includes strengthening as part of the third and final active exercise stage, other sources such as theInternational Journal of Sports Physical Therapy (IJSPT)describe a four‐phase postsurgical rehabilitation protocol. Phase I involves protecting repaired tissue by restricting active movement. Phase II begins when the patient is cleared for active assisted range of motion. Phase III is characterized by initial rotator cuff strengthening. Phase IV begins when the remodeling phase of the repair is close to complete and advanced strengthening exercises can take place (van der Meijden 2012).[How the intervention might work]Immobilization following rotator cuff repair is designed to protect the surgically repaired tendon‐bone interface while healing takes place. Passive range of motion exercises following surgery are used to prevent postoperative scar adhesions and resultant joint stiffness.Huberty 2009reported that the incidence of shoulder joint stiffness after surgical rotator cuff repair followed by six weeks of immobilization and no overhead stretches was 4% (21/500 participants). Active exercises are performed to strengthen the joint overall and to restore full joint function.[Why it is important to do this review]Currently, expert opinion and clinical experience along with moderate scientific data on tendon histologic healing are used to guide postoperative rotator cuff rehabilitation (van der Meijden 2012). However, recently published randomized controlled trials of rehabilitation following rotator cuff repair (Cuff 2012;Duzgun 2011;Keener 2014;Klintberg 2009;Lee 2012) indicate that an up‐to‐date and rigorous systematic review would be useful for determining the effectiveness of such interventions.. [Non‐drug conservative treatments for acute urinary retention after surgery in adults] [Description of the condition]Acute urinary retention (AUR) is defined as the sudden inability to pass urine spontaneously despite a distended bladder (Armitage 2011;Fitzpatrick 2006). Postoperative urinary retention (POUR) is a type of AUR, but there is no consistent definition for this condition. Some researchers defined POUR as occurring in people who are unable to void after an operation despite a sufficient fluid intake, full bladder and the absence of organic obstruction (Baldini 2009;Buckley 2010;Mohammadi‐Fallah 2012). Other researchers use the post‐void volume of fluid in the bladder to identify POUR (Hansen 2011;Sarasin 2006).Owing to the variety of definitions, a wide range of incidence rates have been reported ranging from 5.7% to 69% (Feliciano 2008;Hansen 2011;Sarasin 2006;Shadle 2009). POUR occurs more frequently after genitourinary, anorectal and orthopaedic (knee or hip) surgery (Lamonerie 2004;Wu 2012). The risk factors for urinary retention also include: older age (over 50 years old), male, extensive infusion of intravenous fluid (greater than 750 mL), longer duration of operation (greater than 120 minutes), anticholinergic medication use, and types of anaesthesia (Baldini 2009;Lamonerie 2004). In addition to the physical factors, some psychological problems can predispose to urinary retention (Treiger 1950).Moreover, POUR may result in several complications such as urinary tract infection, bladder overdistention, bladder dysfunction or even hydronephrosis and kidney damage (Buckley 2010). Studies also indicated that AUR had a measurable impact on people's health‐related quality of life (Donovan 1997;Thomas 2005). Furthermore, people with POUR may have longer hospital stays (Wu 2012;Zaheer 1998), a higher rate of re‐admission to the emergency department (Thomas 2005), and may require more post‐hospitalisation care (Wu 2012).Non‐drug conservative therapies can be grouped into two broad categories.The routine methods to induce spontaneous urination such as making the sound of running water, warm water sitz bath, warm compression and pressing down over the bladder with hands (Fernandes 2007). However, this method is traumatic, can cause urethral injury (Parikh 1992), and has a number of complications (Blacklock 1986;Phipps 2006). [Group B streptococcus immunisation during pregnancy for improving outcomes] [Description of the condition]Group B streptococcus (GBS) is one of the major causes of serious neonatal infection (NCIRD 2010). GBS is a type of bacteria that is part of the normal flora in the gastrointestinal tract and vagina, and is found in 10% to 30% of pregnant women (NCIRD 2010). As most pregnant women do not have sufficient antibody levels to protect against GBS, the bacteria can be transmitted to a neonate before or during childbirth, which is the most common route of transmission to neonates (NCIRD 2010). GBS is classified into nine types of capsular polysaccharides (CPS), which are important to the virulence of the infection (Cieslewicz 2005); however, almost all invasive GBS infections are caused by CPS types Ia, Ib, II, III and V.GBS infection in adults is considered to be less invasive, but recent studies have shown that GBS can cause bacteraemia and cellulitis in non‐pregnant adults (Crum‐Cianflone 2014). In pregnant women, GBS can cause miscarriage, urinary tract infection and chorioamnionitis (Chen 2013), and the condition may lead to neonatal death due to severe neonatal infection including sepsis, pneumonia and meningitis (Baker 1973;NCIRD 2010). A study in the United States (US) (Phares 2008) observed that 95% of infants diagnosed with early‐onset GBS infection, which occurs within the first week after birth, showed positive sterile‐site culture results within 48 hours, most of which were from blood (96%) or cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) (4%) (N = 1232); the mortality rate was 6.8%. Another US study (Jordan 2008) observed that infants diagnosed with late‐onset GBS infection, which occurs at seven to 89 days of life, showed positive sterile‐site culture results, most of which were from blood (67%) or CSF (26%) (N = 1726); the mortality rate was 4.3%. A high bacterial inoculum at the time of birth is associated with early‐onset disease, whereas low concentration of the serum antibody to the colonising strain of GBS is correlated with both early and late onset invasive disease.Strategies to reduce bacterial burden using intrapartum antibiotics have been effective in decreasing early‐onset GBS (Burns 2013). In 1996, consensus guidelines were released by The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) with the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists and the American Academy of Pediatrics to prevent early‐onset GBS infections through administration of chemoprophylactic antibiotics (to prevent infection) to the mother during childbirth (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention 1996). The guidelines recommended a culture‐based strategy which tests for vaginal and rectal GBS colonisation in all pregnant women in the third trimester, followed by the administration of intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis at the time of labour to culture‐positive women (NCIRD 2010). Since publication of these guidelines, the incidence of early‐onset GBS infection has been decreasing, but the incidence of late‐onset GBS infection is still high (Burns 2013). However, this strategy can also cause adverse effects such as allergy and bacterial resistance (Wojcieszek 2014), and is less cost‐effective compared to immunisation strategies if a vaccine coverage rate of 80% and a protection rate of 80% of cases among infants born at or after 34 weeks of gestation can be achieved (Mohle‐Boetani 1993). Immunisation during pregnancy may offer protection against both early‐onset and late‐onset disease.Several types of GBS vaccines have been developed and are currently undergoing clinical trials, including polysaccharide and polysaccharide‐protein conjugate vaccines. The first reported GBS vaccine to be used in a clinical trial was developed as a polysaccharide vaccine (Baker 1978). Polysaccharide‐protein conjugate vaccines have been developed to improve immunogenicity or immune responses. Potential vaccine candidates include not only CPS, but also other GBS surface proteins; however, other surface protein vaccines have not yet been evaluated in clinical trials. Vaccines that have been evaluated specifically target CPS types Ia, Ib, II, III and V as antigens, which induce immune responses and increase the recipient's specific immunoglobulin (IgG) or antibodies that control infection (Baker 2004). Phase 1 and early phase 2 trials for certain polysaccharide GBS vaccines have been completed in healthy non‐pregnant women (Baker 1978;Baker 2003a), and a few trials have also been performed in pregnant women (Baker 1988;Baker 2003b). However, at the current time there are no commercially available GBS vaccines.Neonates of mothers with GBS are at increased risk of serious neonatal infections (Baker 1973). GBS immunisation during pregnancy activates the maternal immune system, and some studies have shown that the mother's specific IgG level increases within four weeks after vaccination (Baker 2004;Baker 2007). Type‐specific capsular polysaccharide antibodies have been shown to promote opsonisation (in which antibodies bind to bacteria), and phagocytosis (in which phagocytic cells ingest bacteria) of GBS, and provide protection in animal models. However, it is still unclear whether immunisation prevents GBS infections in neonates.There is a need to evaluate the available literature on the efficacy and safety of GBS immunisation during pregnancy in order to determine whether the current culture‐based strategy should be changed.[Description of the condition]Group B streptococcus (GBS) is one of the major causes of serious neonatal infection (NCIRD 2010).
