[Built environment interventions for increasing physical activity in adults and children] [Description of the condition]A rising level of physical inactivity has become recognised as one of the major threats to public health, and it is estimated that in 2008 physical inactivity caused 9% of premature mortality and 5.3 million deaths worldwide (Lee 2012). This estimate included between 6% and 10% of all deaths from major non‐communicable diseases globally and their burden continues to increase rapidly in low‐ and middle‐income countries (WHO 2010a). There has been significant research into the determinants of physical activity (PA), which include demographic, biological, behavioural, psychological, socio‐cultural and environmental factors (Trost 2002).Since Sallis, Bauman and Pratt published their landmark paper in 1998 highlighting the need for more research on the links between the built environment and PA (Sallis 1998a), there has been a rapid accumulation of evidence relating features of environments that support or act as a barrier to PA. Concurrently there has been a growth in the recognition of the need for action to improve health‐enhancing built environments. In 2006, the World Health Organization (WHO) issued guidance to governments outlining their role in creating environments that promote opportunities for PA (WHO 2006). This has since been adopted within a range of government strategies around the world. For example, the UK Foresight report on obesity (DoH 2007) emphasised the role of the built environment in addressing physical inactivity and obesity, but highlighted that the longer‐term effectiveness of activity interventions depends on combining appropriate environmental change with strategies that help to sustain new behaviours. Subsequently the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) in the USA (CDC 2011) and WHO highlighted that built environment interventions should be given the highest priority by public health agencies and policy makers, due to their potential for greatest reach, effectiveness and sustainability.There have been large government commissioned reviews of approaches for promoting and creating environments that encourage and support PA in the USA (Transportation Research Board 2005) and the UK (National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence,NICE 2008). These reviews recognised that past policy and practice has prioritised sedentary modes of transport, albeit not intentionally. Based on systematic reviews of policy, transport, urban planning and architecture, NICE (NICE 2008) identified a number of recommendations for practice, including changes to planning, transport and design, in order to improve the accessibility to opportunities in incorporate PA into activities of daily living. NICE also recommended that research councils and funders should prioritise funding for the evaluation of effectiveness of environmental interventions on PA, which has led to an upsurge of research activity in the area. Therefore, an update of the evidence is required.The aim of this review is to assess the effectiveness of interventions at increasing PA levels, through increased use of the built environment, in adults and children. PA is defined as 'any bodily movement produced by skeletal muscles that requires energy expenditure' (Caspersen 1985), which includes activity for work, recreation, travel and domestic duties.Regular PA has proven benefits to cancer, cardiorespiratory, metabolic, musculoskeletal and functional health (WHO 2010b). To avail of these benefits, it is widely recommended that adults (aged ≥ 18 years) accumulate at least 150 minutes of moderate‐intensity aerobic PA throughout the week (WHO 2010b;DoH 2011;Garber 2011). It is also recommended that children aged five to 17 years accumulate at least 60 minutes of moderate‐ to vigorous‐intensity PA daily.However, despite the proven benefits and major initiatives to promote active lifestyles, approximately one‐third of adults globally do not meet the recommended levels of PA (Hallal 2012). In high‐income countries such as the USA (CDC 2012) and the UK (DoH 2011), more than half of adults report not meeting the recommended level of PA, which is estimated to cost the National Health Service (NHS) across the UK over GBP1 billion per year (Allender 2007). Though PA levels in low‐ and middle‐income countries are usually higher, there is some evidence suggesting these levels are decreasing due to reductions in occupational and transport‐related PA (Hallal 2012).This review will assess the short‐ and longer‐term effectiveness of interventions to promote increased use of the built environment in increasing overall PA levels in adults and children.For the purposes of this review, Foster and Hillsdon's definition of the environment has been adapted (Foster 2004). Built environments that influence PA are defined as any aspect of the constructed environment, including modification of natural environments, which subconsciously or consciously relates to an individual and their PA behaviour.Therefore interventions will be included that target changes in PA by (1) encouraging increased use of existing outdoor facilities or activities (e.g. green prescription scheme of informational approaches such as mass media, leaflets or posters) or (2) the introduction of new environmental facilities including improvements of existing facilities (e.g. replacement of playgrounds in a park), improved access to facilities (e.g. improved opening hours, creation of new bridges), creation of new facilities (e.g. introduction of bicycle lanes or walking paths) or wider public transport initiatives (e.g. cycle hire schemes). Informational approaches to encourage individuals to engage in PA have been reviewed previously (Kahn 2002) and these will only be included in this review if they are used within an intervention to encourage the use of existing outdoor facilities or activities. Interventions involving the introduction of new facilities may or may not be accompanied by these informational activities.These interventions would be set in the context of either a specific location (e.g. park) or a type of facility (e.g. cycle lane, walkway) and interventions that target a general encouragement of outdoor activities such as walking or cycling, not set in a specific environmental context, will be excluded. In addition, interventions that seek to promote indoor PA facilities, such as gyms or leisure centres will not be included. Interventions that target the encouragement of PA through behavioural approaches (counselling, etc.) will only be included if they also include the use of specific environmental facilities as a major aspect of the design.The target population of interventions will be described according to the socio‐ecological framework (Sallis 1998b). Interventions targeting broad geographical areas, such as across a city or region, will be defined as community interventions. Those targeting whole organisations, such as workplaces or schools, will be defined as organisational and those targeting specific types of individuals, such as patient groups, will be defined as individual. If sufficient data are available, the relative effectiveness of each of these approaches will be assessed.Many previous interventions to promote PA have targeted individual level behaviour change, resulting in only modest effect (Eakin 2000). A limitation of the individual level approaches is that they often do not consider the role of factors that are outside the control of the individual, such as the built environment (Sallis 2012). This may limit the opportunity for change in the individual.The difficulty in defining an appropriate theory that explains the mechanism of how the environment influences PA has been recognised (Ogilvie 2011). Ecological models are most commonly used to describe the interaction of an individual with their social and physical environment (Pikora 2003;Saelens 2003;Sallis 2006). These models propose, in addition to a direct effect of the environment on PA, that the relationship may also be mediated by factors such as individual demographics (age, gender, income, car ownership) and psychosocial factors (outcome expectancy, social norms). This has been confirmed in a limited number of studies that have assessed the indirect effects of environmental factors on PA, and found they exert influence via psychological and social variables such as self‐efficacy, motivation and social support (McNeill 2006;Ishii 2010).A socio‐ecological logic model is proposed (Figure 1) for how interventions may be delivered and outcomes they would address. Environmental interventions may originate from changes in government strategies or direct investment towards either community development or health improvement initiatives. The resultant interventions may be targeted at relevant transport or recreation policies, specific organisations (schools or workplaces), whole communities, or individuals (with or without an existing medical condition). In accordance with the model proposed by Sallis et al (Sallis 2012), interventions are classified as to the domain of PA that they target (recreational, transport or occupational/school PA), and further classified within these domains according to whether they target engagement of children or adults. Although short‐term outcomes would relate specifically to the domain of PA targeted, this review will primarily focus on the net benefit to overall PA. This would therefore account for possible compensatory behaviour, whereby individuals increase their activity in one domain and subsequently reduce it in another.Logic model. PA: physical activity.Much of the evidence collected to date has been from cross‐sectional studies, demonstrating inconsistent associations between features of the built environment, such as proximity of urban green space (Humpel 2002) or walkability of neighbourhoods (Van Dyck 2010) and PA. However, it is not clear if this is a causal relationship. There are possible confounding factors, such as residential preference (active people choosing to live in supportive neighbourhoods) (Van Dyck 2011), that often are not controlled for in these types of studies. Therefore, there is a need to summarise data from controlled trials, to gain an insight into the direction of effect.One previous systematic review of interventions to increase PA (Kahn 2002) found the creation or enhancement of places for PA combined with informational outreach led to a net percentage increase in PA of 48% (median value), though they were not able to disaggregate the relative effectiveness of each. As part of their review, they also summarised the evidence for the effectiveness of 'informational' approaches such as mass media of pamphlets. Though these included campaigns to raise awareness of opportunities for PA, including environmental prompts, they did not limit their review to interventions to environmental opportunities (e.g. they also included mass media campaigns to alter social norms). The Kahn review (Kahn 2002) was not analysed using a meta‐analytic approach, results were not compared to a control group, the timescales for follow‐up were not reported and the interventions included are now more than 10 years old and therefore there is a need to update the review. One Cochrane review by Baker et al (Baker 2011) sought to evaluate the effects of community‐wide interventions, in combination with multiple strategies to promote PA, on population levels of PA. Among a range of intervention approaches, they included interventions where environmental change strategies were one of at least three different components of a multi‐component intervention. Baker et al (Baker 2011) concluded that the evidence to support the effectiveness of these types of interventions to increase PA levels was inconsistent.Though Baker et al (Baker 2011) discussed interventions that included environmental approaches, the design of their review did not allow them to disentangle the range of multiple strategies used by interventions to make any specific conclusions about the effects of their environmental component. Therefore, the proposed review builds on their work by including a wider set of interventions, including interventions where an environmental strategy was the only component, for exampleSinclair 2007. In addition, we will focus on interventions that have involved an environmental‐based approach and discuss their effects, which were not separately discussed in the review of community interventions on PA (Baker 2011), to help guide the planning of future public health action in this area.A study of English adults has identified that communities who are exposed to green environments also have the lowest levels of health inequality related to income (Mitchell 2008). Therefore built environments that support active lifestyles may also be important in reducing health inequalities and promoting health. There is still a need to review the wider short‐ and longer‐term health benefits from PA in the built environment.Finally, systematic reviews (Yang 2010;Fraser 2011) have provided evidence that environmental interventions (both informational and structural) can lead to change in a specific behaviour (cycling). [Progabide add‐on for refractory epilepsy] [Description of the condition]Epilepsy is a chronic disease suffered by millions of people and associated with significant morbidity and mortality. It is estimated that around fifty million people suffer from epilepsy worldwide. Its incidence is estimated at between 16 and 51 cases of new‐onset epilepsy per 100,000 people every year (Banerjee 2009). Although the majority of people with epilepsy are adequately controlled, up to 30% continue to develop refractory epilepsy, despite adequate doses of antiepileptic drugs (AEDs) (Cockerell 1995). Although various AEDs are available for treatment of refractory epilepsy, it remains a big challenge to find new anti‐epilepsy drugs which are both effective and safe.Progabide, named for 4‐[[(4‐chlorophenyl)(5‐fluoro‐2‐hydroxyphenyl)‐methylene]amino]butanamide, is a γ‐aminobutyric acid (GABA) receptor agonist to which a benzylidine nucleus is added. The benzylidene moiety core facilitates transport across the intestine and blood‐brain barrier. In the brain it is metabolised into GABA, gabamide, and SL‐75102. Extensive preclinical studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of PGB and SL‐75102 against seizures induced by maximal electroshock, pentylenetetrazol, bicuculline, and picrotoxin in mice and other animal models of epilepsy (Bartholini 1984;Cepeda 1982;Lloyd 1982;Loscher 1982;Loscher 1983;Worms 1982).The antiepileptic mechanism of progabide is to stimulate the GABAA receptor complex directly, and increase permeability of the chloride ion of the neuron cell membrane, and generate inhibitory postsynaptic potential (Inhibitory postsynaptic potential, IPSP) to inhibit epilepsy.Progabide has been tested in several animal models of epilepsy. It has been shown to be effective in inhibiting seizures induced both chemically by bicuculline, strychnine, picrotoxin, pentylenetetrazol, penicillin and electrically by electroshock treatment (Lloyd 1981;Lloyd 1982).The role of progabide as an antiepileptic agent in humans is controversial. In one study (Martinez 1984), its broad‐spectrum antiepileptic efficacy seemed to be confirmed as there was a decrease of both generalised and partial seizure rates when progabide was used. Another double‐blind, placebo‐controlled trial (Loiseau 1983) also showed progabide to be effective in partial seizures. However, another trial suggested that there was no difference between progabide and placebo (Dam 1983). In one study (De Pasquet 1991), 59 patients were included, eight patients did not complete the study, four of whom developed adverse drug reactions (elevation of liver transaminases, two; gastritis, one; and acute psychosis, one). Progabide was soon taken off the market because the small study byDam 1983showed no difference compared with placebo soon after it was introduced into the market and hepatoxicity became a serious concern. [Loxapine inhaler for psychosis‐induced aggression or agitation] [Description of the condition]Agitation is described as excessive motor activity associated with a feeling of inner tension (NICE 2011). It is also defined as inappropriate verbal, vocal or motor activity not judged to be directly related to apparent needs (Cohen‐Mansfield 1986). Its hallmark features are motor restlessness and heightened response to stimuli (Lindenmayer 2000). Severe agitation can also manifest as aggression (Citrome 2004) or explicit violent behaviour (Kopecky 1998). Aggression is more consistent with verbal abuse, verbal and physical threats, and threats of violence (Ness 2000).Agitated or violent behaviour constitutes roughly 10% of all emergency psychiatric treatment (Tardiff 1982). Psychotic symptoms such as delusions or hallucinations are significantly and strongly associated with aggressive and violent behavior (Swanson 1990) and people with schizophrenia are particularly likely to present with a high incidence of agitation. Over a lifetime, about 1% of the population will develop schizophrenia (Jablensky 1992) and more than 90% of people with schizophrenia will experience agitation in their lifetime, experiencing an average of 11‐12 episodes of acute agitation each year (NICE 2011). Psychotic agitation is clinically important because of the distress experienced by patients and the risks their behaviours may pose to themselves and others (Brown 2011), particularly to staff and other service users when in emergency departments or in‐patient psychiatric settings (NICE 2005).The many guidelines that describe the management of people with psychosis‐induced agitation and violence recommend both non‐pharmacological and pharmacological interventions (APA 2004;CPA 2005;NICE 2005). In the UK, rapid tranquillisation is described as 'the use of psychotropic medication to control agitated, threatening or destructive psychotic behavior' (Periera 2005).The National Institute of Clinical Excellence (NICE) recommends that rapid tranquillisation should be used in situations requiring the rapid control of agitation, aggression or excitement, when other less coercive techniques of calming such as verbal de‐escalation, and other strategies have failed to calm the service user (NICE 2005).Pharmacological management of acute agitation has been typically limited to four classes of medication: barbiturates, benzodiazepines and antipsychotics (first‐ and second‐generation) (Bellnier 2002;Currier 2006). Loxapine is a first‐generation antipsychotic. Traditionally loxapine is given orally or intramuscularly. A recent Cochrane systematic review analysed the effectiveness of loxapine in schizophrenia (Chakrabarti 2007). One of the conclusions from this systematic review is that loxapine is a viable option for rapid tranquillisation in acute psychosis (Chakrabarti 2007). Other studies have also found that loxapine is effective in the initial management of hostile and aggressive people with schizophrenia (Dubin 1986;Tuason 1986). More recently, loxapine inhalation has been tested for the acute treatment of agitation in schizophrenia. Loxapine is delivered by Staccato inhaler system via a hand‐held, single‐dose inhaler (Lesem 2011). With the inhalation, a chemical reaction occurs to rapidly heat pure loxapine, thereby creating an additive‐free aerosol with particles in the 1–3 μm range. The main neurotransmitter involved is dopamine (Howes 2009). Antipsychotics are thought to produce anti‐agitation effects by inhibition of dopaminergic transmission, along with histamine and noradrenaline blockade, although the blockade mechanism has been less clearly established (Leonard 1992;Altamura 2003). [Perineal dilators for facilitating the second stage of labour] [Description of the condition]During the second stage of labour, considerable stretching of the vaginal and perineal tissues takes place over a relatively short period of time. The stretching is brought about by pressure from the baby's presenting part (usually the head). The distension of the levator hiatus during childbirth in white women has been estimated as a mean increase of 107% (range 25% to 245%) above the dimensions at maximal Valsalva (Svabic 2009). Rapid stretching may result in damage to pelvic tissues, including perineal tears and clinical or occult damage to perineal floor structures, including the anal sphincter. Failure of stretching, for example, due to high tissue resistance (particularly in nulliparous women), insufficient maternal effort or inadequate uterine contractions may result in prolonged second stage of labour. This may be managed by oxytocin augmentation (Goodfellow 1979;Goodfellow 1983), episiotomy, assisted vaginal birth (vacuum or forceps), caesarean section, or waiting for descent of the presenting part before encouraging bearing down (Maresh 1983). In particular, women with epidural analgesia may have prolonged second stage due to reduced urge to bear down due to lack of perineal sensation (Bates 1985a), and blunting of the normal second stage oxytocin surge (Goodfellow 1983) with reduced uterine activity (Bates 1985b), resulting in increased use of forceps or vacuum birth (Bates 1985a;Goodfellow 1983;Hoult 1977). Antenatal education may improve women's ability to push effectively in the second stage of labour, although this could not be demonstrated in a randomised trial (Phipps 2009). In the past, episiotomy has been recommended as a routine method of overcoming perineal resistance, but current evidence supports a restrictive episiotomy policy (Carroli 2009). A retrospective study found ultrasound evidence of levator ani muscle avulsion to be associated with prolonged second stage of labour greater than 110 minutes (Valsky 2009).There is little consensus on what should be regarded as prolonged second stage of labour. In one study, the median duration of second stage of labour for nulliparous and multiparous women was 92 and 20 minutes respectively for the general population, and 54 and 10 minutes for adolescents (Hui 2010). The National Institute of Clinical Excellence (NICE) guidelines regard more than one hour, active second stage for multiparous, and more than two hours for nulliparous women, as prolonged (NICE 2007).Pre‐emptive stretching of the birth canal might 1) reduce the duration of the second stage, or 2) reduce the pressure on the baby's head during the second stage, or 3) reduce damage to the mother's pelvic structures, or all three.Other strategies aiming to improve labour progress and outcomes in the second stage are considered in separate Cochrane reviews. These include: antenatal perineal massage for reducing perineal trauma (Beckmann 2006), position during the second stage of labour (Gupta 2012), and perineal techniques during the second stage of labour for reducing perineal trauma (Aasheim 2011). As these factors may influence the outcomes of interest in this review, we will seek information from the trial reports included in the review regarding these variations in care, and whether their use was balanced between the two groups. A systematic review found that use of the Valsalva manoeuvre, compared with spontaneous bearing down, was associated with a shorter second stage of labour, but had a negative effect on urodynamic factors on follow‐up. A supportive environment and help with relaxation may also facilitate the second stage of labour. A Cochrane review of labour support found reduced overall duration of labour (Hodnett 2011), and one trial found reduction in both first and second stages of labour (Kashanian 2010).Various inflatable or mechanical instruments have been designed with a view to pre‐emptive stretching of the perineum during pregnancy or during labour.The Epi‐No childbirth and pelvic floor trainer is an inflatable, silicone balloon, roughly the shape of a butternut. The larger end is inserted into the vagina with the smaller end protruding and the balloon is pumped up by the woman with a hand pump with pressure gauge similar to that used for a sphygmomanometer. It is used for 10 to 20 minutes, once or twice daily, from 37 weeks' gestation, and the size to which it is inflated is gradually increased according to the comfort level of the woman (up to 32 cm circumference). A non‐randomised, matched pairs study (n = 50 pairs) found a large reduction in: episiotomy (49% versus 82%), duration of second stage of labour (29 versus 54 minutes), and use of analgesia; and improved one minute Apgar scores (Hillebrenner 2001). A subsequent non‐randomised comparison found a large reduction in perineal trauma, but no difference in instrumental birth nor Apgar scores (Kovacs 2004). Another non‐randomised comparison found a large reduction in episiotomy (50% versus 93%), but not overall perineal trauma (Kok 2004). A recent randomised trial has shown non‐significant reduction in pelvic floor muscle injury (Shek 2011) in contrast to another Australian randomised trial, which has shown significant increase in likelihood of intact perineum with the use of Epi‐No and a tendency to lower episiotomy rates (Ruckhäberle 2009). A case of possible venous air embolism following use of a birth trainer during pregnancy at home has been reported (Nicoll 2008).An inflatable birth canal dilator designed for gradual, pre‐emptive dilation of the birth canal during the first stage of labour, was developed in 1986 (Hofmeyr 1991). It was cylindrical in shape with two chambers. The leading end was a disk‐shaped chamber which was introduced into the vagina above the level of the perineum and inflated with saline to prevent the dilator from slipping out of the vagina. The larger cylindrical chamber, which was partially inside the vagina and partially outside, was gradually inflated to stretch the vaginal and perineal tissues until it reached its full capacity (10 cm in diameter) and was removed.Materna Medical (Juravic 2012), has developed a mechanical device to reduce tissue damage from rapid stretching in the second stage of labour, by slowly stretching the tissues of the pelvic floor during the first stage of labour, when the cervix is gradually dilating. [Hypnosis for preventing preterm labour] [Description of the condition]Preterm labour is a major challenge in perinatal medicine. Preterm labour is defined as the presence of contractions of sufficient strength and frequency to effect progressive effacement and dilatation of the cervix prior to the 37thweek of pregnancy (ACOG 2003;Green 2005). Although significant improvements in maternal fetal medicine and neonatology have been achieved, preterm birth remains the leading cause of neonatal morbidity and mortality in many countries all over the world (Goldenberg 2008;Saigal 2008), and every pregnant woman needs to know about preterm labour, why it occurs and what she can do to help prevent it. Preterm labour occurs in about 12% of all pregnancies (Green 2005), with preterm birth as its most significant consequence. In the United Kingdom, infant mortality among preterm births was 42/1000 live births in 2005, compared with 5/1000 live births overall (Moser 2007). In the United States, approximately 467,000 live births occur annually (11.5% of all live births) before term, and preterm births are responsible for three‐quarters of neonatal mortality (ACOG 2003).All preterm babies are at significant risk of health problems. The earlier the birth, the greater the risk. Compared to infants born at term, preterm babies have a higher incidence of hypoglycaemia (low blood sugar), respiratory distress syndrome, hypothermia (low core body temperatures), apnoea (brief moments of cessation of breathing), transient tachypnoea of the newborn (rapid respiratory rate), hyperbilirubinaemia (high levels of bilirubin), and feeding difficulties when compared with infants born at term (Tomashek 2007). Preterm labour is also one of the leading causes of long‐term morbidity, including seizure disorders, cerebral palsy (non progressive brain damage following childbirth), deafness, mental retardation (lower levels of intelligence), blindness, developmental delay, and non‐neurologic disorders such as chronic pulmonary disease, and retinopathy of prematurity (Hole 2001). Respiratory distress syndrome is the most common serious complication of prematurity and is associated with immediate and long‐term mortality and morbidity. Also, the risk of neurosensory disability and death increases with decreasing gestational age (Saigal 2008). Studies have also shown that healthy late preterm infants compared with healthy term infants face a greater risk for developmental delay and school‐related problems up through the first five years of life (Morse 2009).Preterm birth and its consequences may have enormous emotional and psychological effects on the mother, her family, friends as well as being costly for health services (RCOG 2011). Preterm birth accounts for 35% of all United States healthcare spending for infants and 10% of all such spending for children (ACOG 2003). Interventions to reduce the morbidity and mortality associated with preterm birth include treatment with antenatal corticosteroids, tocolytic agents and antibiotics (Reinhard 2009). There is a considerable amount of evidence on the effectiveness of pharmacologic agents in the prevention of preterm labour. However, even with these agents, the incidence of preterm deliveries have not decreased substantially over the years despite technological advancement in the field of obstetrics and gynaecology. Hence, additional ways of preventing preterm labour are needed.Preterm birth, a consequence of preterm labour, is associated with considerable morbidity and mortality, and efforts have been made to inhibit the process, based on the assumption that the more mature the fetus is at the time of delivery, the better the neonatal outcome will be (Bennett 2008). For each additional day or week added in utero, fetal survival increases considerably.Finnström 1997demonstrated improvements from 8% survival at 23 weeks of gestation to 74% survival at 28 weeks of gestation, equating to an improvement of 3% per day at such gestations. Other studies have shown similar large changes in mortality rates for each additional week of gestation and for each 100 g increase in birthweight at lower gestational ages. However, at higher gestational ages (more than 32 weeks) comparable changes in gestation and birthweight only have a relatively small impact on mortality (Groom 2004;Lemons 2001). However, a reduction in morbidity, particularly associated with respiratory distress syndrome, is noted at higher gestational ages (Groom 2004).Risk factors for preterm birth are numerous. These include previous history of preterm birth (Bhattacharya 2010;Bloom 2001;Esplin 2008), previous history of miscarriages (Shah 2009), intrauterine infection of the fetal membranes (chorioamnionitis) (Klein 2004;Norwitz 1999;Salafia 1991), periodontal disease (gingivitis) (Boggess 2006;Goepfert 2004;López 2002), asymptomatic bacteriuria (Villar 1998), smoking (Kyrklund‐Blomberg 1998;Ney 1990) and substance abuse (Boer 1994;Ney 1990). Others include stress (Lockwood 1999;Petraglia 2001), physical exertion and activity (Luke 1999;Newman 2001).The causes of preterm labour are multifactorial in aetiology. These include allogeneic immune reaction against the developing fetus, reduction of blood flow to the uterus (uterine ischemia), intrauterine infection (chorioamnionitis), cervical and uterine anomalies, uterine overdistension and endocrine disorders. These etiopathogenetic processes cause preterm labour through four pathways. [Ponseti method for idiopathic congenital clubfoot in children] [Description of the condition]Clubfoot, also known as talipes equinovarus (TEV), is a common congenital deformity of the foot that affects 0.64 to 6.8 per 1000 live births, with a male‐to‐female ratio of 2.5:1 (Barker 2003). Therefore, it is one of the most common orthopedic conditions that require immediate and extensive treatment. Clubfoot causes the foot to turn inward and point downward; the exact cause of clubfoot is unknown but both genetic and environmental factors are thought to play a role (Cummings 2002;Roye 2004).After treatment ‐ even with a good result ‐ the child with TEVoften has a shorter and wider foot, with a thinner leg, restricted motion of the foot and ankle, reduced strength in the leg and foot, gait anomalies, abnormal radiographic measures, and possible limb length inequality. It is not possible even after successful treatment, by any known means, to get a 'normal' foot. However, the final goal of treatment is to create a supple, plantigrade, 'shoeable' and painless foot that is fully functional (Wimberly 2005).Surgical procedures used to be the standard treatment of clubfoot. The most common surgical procedure is a soft tissue release of the structures that create the deforming forces in the clubfoot. One of the primary disadvantages of soft tissue release in the young clubfoot patient is a high complication rate, which is difficult to treat. The most common complications are recurrence of the deformity, with an average rate of 25% (13% to 50% range). In addition, complications also include, infection, neurovascular injury, loss of limb and overcorrection (Lehman 2003).Another means of treatment is the non‐surgical method, using serial casting and manipulation techniques. The Kite method was commonly used until it was replaced by the Ponseti method, which is the most common method used globally (Herzenberg 2001;Lehman 2003;Ponseti 1963).The time period for the Ponseti method is about two to four years. It starts with brief manipulation of the foot and then casting in maximum correction. The casts are changed each week for a total of five casts, where the adductus and varus (forefoot) is twisted inwards relative to the heel and corrected. A percutaneous heel cord tenotomy (which is a release‐clipping of the Achilles tendon under local anesthesia), is performed in nearly all cases to complete the correction of the foot, and the foot is then placed in the cast for three weeks. This correction is then maintained by night splinting using a foot abduction brace, which is worn until the child is approximately 2 to 4 years of age (Ponseti 2005).The goal of treatment is to correct all components of the deformity so that the patient has a pain‐free, plantigrade foot with good mobility, without calluses, and without the need to wear special or modified shoes.The Ponseti method used for the correction of clubfoot could reduce the need for extensive corrective surgery. With special training, it could be used by different healthcare professionals, especially in areas with a shortage of surgeons (Morcuende 2004). The Uganda Sustainable Clubfoot Care Project (USCCP) aims to build the Ugandan healthcare system's capacity to treat children with the Ponseti method. USCCP has trained 798 healthcare professionals to identify and treat foot deformities at birth. Ponseti Clubfoot Care is now available in 21 hospitals (Pirani 2009).The Ponseti method of cast treatment of idiopathic clubfoot was as effective when it was directed by a physiotherapist as it was when it was directed by a surgeon (Faulks 2005;Janicki 2009).It is important to treat clubfoot in children because if left untreated, the foot remains twisted inwards and becomes painful. [Non‐pharmacological and non‐surgical interventions for managing retained placenta] [Description of the condition]The third stage of labour begins with the birth of the baby and ends with the complete expulsion of the placenta and membranes. While this is normally the shortest stage of labour, it is potentially the most dangerous for the mother. The complete or partial failure of placental separation and expulsion is a significant contributor to maternal morbidity and mortality (Weeks 2008). This is primarily attributable to the risk of postpartum haemorrhage (PPH) associated with a placenta, be it completely adherent, partially, or wholly separated from the uterine wall, remaining in‐situ following birth.Following vaginal birth, there are three main types of retained placenta: placental entrapment (a detached placenta trapped behind a closed cervix), placenta adherens (adherent to the uterine wall but easily separated) and those placentae that are morbidly adherent (a pathological penetration of the placental villi into the myometrium, sometimes beyond, preventing detachment) (Weeks 2008). Occasionally, snapping of the umbilical cord will cause a placenta to be retained.Regardless of type, following vaginal birth, once a diagnosis of retained placenta has been made, the oldest and most conventional treatment is its manual removal under anaesthesia. Manual removal of placenta (MROP) is a surgical procedure that can only safely take place in healthcare facilities with medical and anaesthetic support, since the procedure is not without risk of complications (e.g. uterine inversion, PPH, infection, genital tract trauma, hysterectomy).The desire to minimize the risks associated with MROP and the need for anaesthesia, have led clinicians over the past two decades to study the administration of different pharmacological agents, including those administered by the umbilical vein for the treatment of placental retention with varying degrees of success reported (Abdel‐Aleem 2011;Bennett 2009;Lim 2010;Nardin 2011;O'Brien 1996;Pinho 2008;Visalyaputra 2010;Weeks 2010). While some of the proposed pharmacological agents and their delivery methods show promise for the future, at this time further research is still warranted.The non‐pharmacological and non‐surgical interventions either in use, or proposed for use, for the management of retained placenta, are breastfeeding, acupuncture and other complementary therapies, as well as external manipulation of the uterus and placenta. It is common in clinical practice for midwives to encourage the new mother to initiate breastfeeding at the time of birth to support the ‘normal’ physiological processes of placental separation and expulsion which occur during the third stage of labour. Specifically, breastfeeding is frequently commenced when the placenta has failed to deliver as expected. Acupuncture is a technique of initiating, controlling or accelerating physiological functions in the body (Tiran 2004). This is achieved by penetrating the skin with fine needles in order to stimulate acupoints which correspond to specific organs. Other complementary therapies such as aromatherapy and reflexology may also be considered. Further, historically and culturally many methods of expediting the expulsion of the retained placenta by external manipulation of the uterus, umbilical cord traction and maternal effort have been practised (Beck 1937;Brandt 1933;Lefeber 1998;Spencer 1962). Anecdotally, these methods continue to be used in current clinical practice for this purpose.Nipple stimulation (breastfeeding) as a means of ‘expelling’ a placenta has a sound theoretical basis since it results in the release of endogenous oxytocin thereby stimulating uterine activity (Irons 1994;Johnson 2007).The use of acupuncture for retained placenta involves the stimulation of those acupoints believed to be related to the uterus in order to induce uterine activity. A single retrospective non‐randomised study undertaken byChauhan 1998, compared conventional MROP to acupuncture and revealed that 83% of those receiving acupuncture delivered their placenta within 20 minutes of this treatment commencing. This compared favourably with MROP, where all mothers had a third stage duration in excess of 60 minutes. Furthermore, 57.8% of the MROP mothers experienced complications compared to just 20% of the acupuncture group, mostly attributable to PPH.A contemporary survey undertaken byMårtensson 2011of 45 maternity units in Sweden, revealed that 37 units (82.2%) used acupuncture for the treatment of retained placenta. This made it one of the most common indications for acupuncture use in pregnancy, birth and the postpartum period, exceeded only by its use for relaxation (97.8%) and pain relief in labour (97.8%).The Credé manoeuvre, first advocated in 1861, necessitated exerting manual pressure on the uterine fundus through the abdominal wall as a means of artificially separating and expressing the placenta (Beck 1937;Kimbell 1958). Subsequently methods whereby the umbilical cord is gently and steadily pulled in a downward direction, were also introduced as a means of dealing with a placenta that was retained (Brandt 1933;Kimbell 1958). Contemporary management of the third stage routinely utilises an adaptation of this method, known as controlled cord traction (CCT), incorporating a simultaneous counter‐pressure upwards on the lower segment of the uterus, using a hand placed on the lower abdomen (Spencer 1962), The now familiar CCT technique can also be witnessed as a means of managing retained placenta. However, any intervention that involves traction of the umbilical cord, risks not only the cord 'snapping off' completely but also failure to deliver a placenta that remains adherent or entrapped, leaving placental tissue in‐situ. Moreover, manipulation of the uterus and placenta by the accoucheur in these ways has the potential to increase maternal pain and blood loss as well as risking acute uterine inversion.Efforts to increase maternal intra‐abdominal pressure in order to expel a placenta that has been retained include: inducing sneezing (Beck 1937;Lefeber 1998) and vomiting (Lefeber 1998), blowing into a receptacle and anecdotally, the Valsalva manoeuvre (forcibly bearing down while prohibiting exhalation).A key textbook for many midwives, also promotes the use of complementary therapies such as: aromatherapy and stimulation of pressure points for managing retained placentae (Tiran 2004). However, the author provides little scientific evidence to support the safety and effectiveness of these therapies for this use.Across the world, the rate of retained placenta is increasing (Cheung 2011). However, the incidence and impact of retained placenta following vaginal birth is subject to marked geographical variation. In resource‐poor nations, it affects approximately 0.1% of vaginal births but is associated with a 10% maternal mortality rate (Weeks 2008). In developed countries, the occurrence of retained placenta is more common, about 3% of vaginal deliveries, yet it is rarely associated with mortality (Weeks 2008). [Cranberries for treating asymptomatic bacteriuria during pregnancy] [Description of the condition]Asymptomatic bacteriuria is defined as the presence of greater than or equal to 105colony forming units of bacteria per millilitre (mL) of urine on aseptically collected mid‐stream urine specimens in the absence of symptoms of urinary tract infection (Merritt 1958;Norden 1968). Many studies have shown that the overall prevalence of asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy varies between 2% to 10%, depending on the patient's socioeconomic status (Greco 1997). The women at highest risk for asymptomatic bacteriuria include pregnant women, women with anatomic and functional problems of the urinary tract, women of low socioeconomic status, anaemic women, women with sickle cell trait (Magnus 1999;Wierenga 2001), diabetes mellitus (Hooton 2000) and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection (Alowude 2010).In pregnant women, the urinary tract has a number of mechanisms to prevent the development and proliferation of urinary tract infection. These include the downward flow of urine from the bladder through the urethra; the normal vaginal flora that inhibits the growth of uropathogenic bacteria in the periurethral area and the glycosaminoglycan containing mucin layer of the bladder mucosa which acts as a barrier against urinary tract infection. Urine also contains many antibacterial factors such as urea, organic acids and salts. The presence of Tamm Horsfall protein, a uromucoid shed by renal tubular cells, which traps bacteria and makes it easy to eliminate (Geerlings 1997) and also to protect against urinary tract infections. Free oligosaccharide (short carbohydrate chain) residues in urine also function in a similar manner by binding to adhesins on bacteria. The presence of secretory IgG, IgA and the complement system also help fight urinary tract infections (Stein 1999). When these barriers are breached, bacteria can proliferate in the urinary tract.Proliferation of bacteria in the urinary tract during pregnancy usually results from changes in the anatomy of the urinary tract and an increase in the level of maternal progesterone levels. The mechanical obstruction caused by the enlarging pregnant uterus and the smooth muscle relaxation properties of progesterone cause dilatation of the renal calices, pelvises and ureters, leading to urinary stasis, which predisposes to urinary tract infection. Dilatation of the calyces and ureters are commonly seen on the right side, compared to the left (15 mm versus 5 mm). This dilatation begins by about 10 weeks of gestation and continues throughout pregnancy. Increased excretion of glucose from the urine (glycosuria) and an increase in levels of urinary amino acids during pregnancy are additional factors that predispose to urinary tract infections in pregnancy. Glucose excretion increases in pregnancy by 100‐fold in pregnant women over non‐pregnant women due to an increase in the glomerular filtration rate in pregnancy.The vast majority of urinary tract infections are caused by bacteria and many of these bacteria are bowel commensals. Bowel commensals in the perineum colonise the vagina and lower urethra before causing a urinary tract infection. Sexual intercourse and catheterisation can also facilitate this route of infection. Another unlikely route is the hematogenous route which can be important in immune compromised or septicaemic women. In the majority of the studies on asymptomatic bacteriuria,Escherichia coli (E.Coli)is the most common organism associated with bacteriuria, representing at least 80% of isolates, with other gram‐negative rods and certain gram‐positive organisms includingStaphylococcus saprophyticusandenterococcioccasionally being isolated (Smaill 2007). The diagnosis of asymptomatic bacteriuria is based on isolation of micro‐organisms with a colony count of greater than or equal to105organisms per mL of urine in a clean‐catch specimen (Ojoo 1996). The women are normally instructed to clean the vulva area from front to back to avoid contamination of the urine sample prior to collection of the urine for analysis.Asymptomatic bacteriuria is important because pregnant women are at an increased risk of urinary tract infections, pyelonephritis (infection of the kidneys) and renal impairment (Harding 2002;Nicolle 2000). Pregnancy is characterised by anatomic changes in the kidneys, ureters and bladder due to obstruction of the ureters by the developing uterus. The presence of increased levels of progesterone, a hormone of pregnancy with relaxation effects on smooth muscles, also leads to relaxation of the smooth muscle of the ureters and the bladder. Also, increased excretion of glucose from the urine (glycosuria) of pregnancy provide an excellent medium for bacterial proliferation (Sobel 1984;Stamey 1973).If asymptomatic bacteriuria is not treated in pregnancy, up to 40% of the women will develop urinary tract infection, and approximately, 25% to 30% of women will develop acute pyelonephritis (Stein 1999). However, it has also been shown that treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria would lead to approximately a 75% reduction in the incidence of pyelonephritis (Andrews 1990). Asymptomatic bacteriuria has been associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes such as preterm delivery, miscarriages and pregnancy‐induced hypertension (Romero 1989).Treatment of asymptomatic urinary tract infections may reduce the risk of pyelonephritis based on existing knowledge that untreated asymptomatic bacteriuria in the pregnant population is associated with at least a 30% risk of future development of pyelonephritis (Kass 1960). There is growing evidence of the potential role of cranberry products in treating asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy (Cowan 2011;Ferrara 2009). However, there is limited evidence whether cranberries reduce adverse pregnancy outcomes in these women. Cranberries contain tannins called proanthocyanidins which are stable phenol compounds exhibiting potent in vitro anti‐adhesion activity against both antibiotic sensitive and resistant strains ofEscherichia coli(Cowan 2011;Howell 1998). However, it is not clear how long cranberries need to be taken in pregnancy to be effective in treating asymptomatic bacteriuria and preventing any associated adverse pregnancy outcomes, or what the required intake in pregnancy should be. Also, there are no recommendations on the optimal dose of cranberries, amount per day, concentration of cranberry juice, and the management form (juice, capsules or tablets) in which it should be prescribed.Cranberries are made up of about 80% water and 10% carbohydrates (Pérez‐López 2009). Cranberries also contain a large amount of organic acids, including ascorbic acid, malic acid, salicylic acid, oxalic acid, benzoic acid and citric acid, and these make up the remaining 10% (Neto 2007). Due to the presence of these acids, cranberries taste very sour. Therefore, moderate quantities of sugar are often added to cranberry juice to improve its taste (Pérez‐López 2009). Cranberries also contain a host of other substances such as catechins, fructose and flavonoids (Pérez‐López 2009).Cranberries contain three different flavonoids (flavones, anthocyanins and proanthocyanidins), catechins, hydroxycinnamic acid, other phenolic acids and triterpenoids. Among the flavonoids, proanthocyanidins (PAC) is considered the most active (Pérez‐López 2009). Vaccinium fruits are among the most abundant food sources of proanthocyanidins (Wang 2001). It has been estimated that the therapeutic dose of cranberry juice is at least 300 mL daily (Avorn 1994;Howell 1998). A study by Lavender suggests that one glass of cranberry juice in the morning and evening might be therapeutic (Lavender 2000). Due to problems that exist with standardising the therapeutic dosage of cranberry, it has been difficult to compare various dosage regimens (Guay 2009).There have been few reports on the adverse effects of cranberries. However, they prevent bacterial adherence to uroepithelial cells, thus reducing the development of urinary tract infections in women with asymptomatic bacteriuria (De Martino 2006). The most vulnerable bacteria to the anti‐adhesion effects of cranberries areE.coli.UropathogenicE.colicarry chromosomal gene clusters that encode adhesins and other virulence factors (Pérez‐López 2009). The most important of these are probably the adhesins that aid bacteria in the uroepithelial adherence process (Pérez‐López 2009). This anti‐adhesion effects of P‐fimbriated uropathogenicE coli.to uroepithelial cells are related with A‐linked proanthocyanidins (Cowan 2011;Howell 1998;Howell 2005). The A‐type linkage in cranberry proanthocyanidins enhances urinary bacterial anti‐adhesion activities. This proanthocyanidins fraction then binds to the most potent lipopolysaccharide, a major component of the outer membrane of Gram‐negative bacteria (Howell 2005). The most potent lipopolysaccharide‐binding activity of cranberries is contained within a proanthocyanidin fraction composed of polymers with an average degree of polymerisation (Delehanty 2007;Siciliano 1996).Results from two independent double‐blind, randomised, placebo‐controlled trials have shown the ability of cranberries to inhibitE. coli'sability to adhere to uroepithelial cells (De Martino 2006;Lavigne 2008). Vaginal fluid significantly alters the adherence of type one piliatedE. colito epithelial cells (Gaffney 1995).Another potential mechanism of action against uropathogenicE. coliis the non‐enzymatic generation of nitric oxide (NO) by dismutation of nitrite to NO and nitrogen dioxide (NO2) under mildly acidic conditions (MacMicking 1997). Nitric oxide possesses potent antimicrobial activities that are both time‐ and concentration‐dependent. In urinary tract infections, acidified nitrite may be a physiologically relevant source of NO produced by bacterial nitrate reductase activity or the local induction of inflammation‐driven NO synthase activity (Rhee 2004). The consumption of cranberries may also prevent the adhesion of antibiotic‐resistant P‐fimbriated uropathogenicE. colito the uroepithelium (Pérez‐López 2009).In recent years, as problems with antibiotic resistance have increased, there has been a renewed interest in the use of cranberries for the treatment of urinary tract infections in women with asymptomatic bacteriuria (Pérez‐López 2009). It has been shown that asymptomatic bacteriuria is associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes such as pyelonephritis, preterm labor, prematurity, low birthweight, maternal anaemia and hypertension in pregnancy. Treating asymptomatic bacteriuria reduces the risk of these adverse pregnancy outcomes. Recent literature has shown that cranberries can be effective in the treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria (Jepson 2008). However, whether this evidence applies to pregnant women is still unknown. A randomised clinical trial by Wing DA et al (Wing 2008) showed that the frequency of pyelonephritis in the group of pregnant women taking cranberries was higher than the frequency in women who did not take cranberries (2.4% versus 1.4%) (Wing 2008). This finding among pregnant women may be due to the effects of the hormones of pregnancy. There are several other factors such as urinary stasis and the presence of vesicoureteral reflux that predispose pregnant women to urinary tract infections, acute pyelonephritis and other adverse pregnancy outcomes. In the Cochrane review byJepson 2008, which examined the use of cranberries for treating urinary tract infections, the review focused on urinary tract infections and outcomes in non pregnant women ‐ no outcomes related to pregnancy were examined. [Selenium supplementation during pregnancy for improving maternal and newborn outcomes] [Description of the condition]Because of the impact of maternal nutrition on pregnancy outcomes, there is a great interest in the study of the role of micronutrients during gestation. It is very likely that maternal micronutrient status influences maternal and newborn outcomes, although the only current recommendation for this period relates to iron and folic acid use (Allen 2005;Black 2001;Christian 2000;Glenville 2006;Hong 2007).A micronutrient which can be important in this period is selenium, a mineral known especially because of its antioxidant activity (Pappas 2008). It is essential for the synthesis and function of several selenoenzymes such as glutathione peroxidases, selenoprotein P and thioredoxin reductase, which play important roles in antioxidant defences and thus help reduce oxidative damage (Lei 2007;Navarro‐Alarcon 2008;Pappas 2008;Ravn‐Haren 2008;Tapiero 2003). Because the literature has reported that oxidative stress might be increased during pregnancy and that exacerbated oxidative stress in this period could be associated with the occurrence of diseases and adverse outcomes such as miscarriages, pre‐eclampsia, gestational diabetes, premature rupture of membranes and intrauterine growth restriction, selenium could be an important micronutrient in the gestational period (Biri 2006;Chamy 2006;Chen 2008;Dobrzynski 1998;Grissa 2007;Holmes 2005;Longini 2007;Mehendale 2008;Janiaux 2006;Surapaneni 2007;Tastekin 2005).In spite of being widely distributed in animal and plant foods such as meat, seafood, grains, dairy products, fruits, and vegetables, selenium content in food depends on its bioavailability in the soil. Thus, there can be a great variation in selenium intake across different populations. Its deficiency is rare, and is usually reported only in areas where soil is poor in the mineral. Literature points out that its deficiency rarely leads to Kashin‐Beck and Keshan disease. Kashin‐Beck disease (KBD) is a chronic, endemic osteochondropathy (a disease involving both bone and cartilage) which can result in growth retardation and secondary osteoarthrosis (Yao 2011). Keshan disease is a dilated cardiomyopathy (Lei 2011); both diseases are especially prevalent in some areas in China. Insufficient selenium intake might reduce glutathione peroxidase, needed to make selenium available for synthesizing selenoproteins, causing a reduction in oxidative defence (Institute of Medicine 2000).During pregnancy, dietary intake should provide enough selenium for the maternal metabolism and allow enough selenium to be transferred to the fetus so that its selenoproteins become saturated and its antioxidant defences improved. In this period, the selenium recommended dietary allowances are 60 µmg (0.76 µmol) selenium/day (Institute of Medicine 2000).Regarding selenium status assessment, selenium plasma and serum levels are the most frequently used biomarkers, and concentrations above 0.8 to 1.1 µmol/L (7 to 9 µmg/dL) indicate plasma selenoprotein maximization. Erythrocyte (red blood cell) selenium concentration reflects a longer term selenium status. Hair and nail selenium concentrations reflect selenium intake in the previous six to 12 months. Although some studies assess these biomarkers, the latter might not be good indicators of mineral status, since they depend on factors such as the form in which selenium is ingested, the amount of methionine in the diet, hair colouring, smoking habit and the presence of the mineral in beauty products. As for selenium urinary excretion, it is affected by short‐term changes in ingestion, being only useful for assessing intake adequacy, and not nutritional status. It is highly associated with plasma selenium and dietary selenium intake in populations with low selenium status. When assessing selenoprotein activity, plasma glutathione peroxidase activity is believed to be a better indicator than erythrocyte enzyme activity. However, these biomarkers are useful for the assessment of low selenium status, because the maximum activity of this enzyme can be reached with blood levels above 1.27 µmol/L (100 µg/L), as mentioned above. Platelet glutathione peroxidase activity has been suggested to be the most sensible indicator of selenium intake since it is increased after one to two weeks from the start of supplementation (Holben 1999;Institute of Medicine 2000;Thomson 2004).In a systematic review,Ashton 2009assessed the usefulness of biomarkers of selenium status in healthy people, based on changes in the mineral status promoted by selenium supplementation in its organic form. They suggested that plasma, erythrocyte and blood selenium concentrations, plasma selenoprotein P concentration, plasma, blood and platelet glutathione peroxidase activity are possibly useful markers. Nonetheless, there is a great heterogeneity among studies with respect to the physiological response to supplementation for all biomarkers assessed, and further studies with higher methodological quality are still needed in order to establish which are the best biomarkers.In addition, the great variability of serum and plasma selenium concentrations among populations makes it difficult to establish universally‐accepted levels for nutrient status adequacy and the assessment of selenium status during pregnancy is not frequently carried out in clinical practice, especially in areas where selenium deficiency is not common.Many studies assessing selenium status during pregnancy have shown a progressive reduction in selenium concentrations during this period, regardless of the presence or not of gestational complications (Desai 2006;Gromadzinska 1998;McLachlan 2004;Perona 1979;Pinheiro 2005;Reyes 2000;Tan 2001;Wasowicz 2003). There are at least three possible explanations for such reduction. Firstly, it could be a consequence of haemodilution caused by maternal plasma expansion (Ferrer 1999;Kantola 2004). Secondly, it could reflect the transport of selenium to the fetus (Kantola 2004). Finally, it is hypothesized that in this period, a higher amount of selenium is used for producing antioxidant compounds such as glutathione peroxidase and selenoprotein P, which in turn can explain the reduction in the antioxidant defence system frequently observed during gestation (Mihailovic 2000;Mukherjee 1998).Oxidative stress is characterized by the modification of pro‐oxidant‐antioxidant balance leading to lipid peroxidation, protein oxidation and damage to DNA bases. The role of selenium during pregnancy, especially in relation to the occurrence of oxidative‐stress‐related adverse outcomes, has been investigated. Spontaneous abortion, miscarriages and premature births have already been reported in the presence of lower selenium status (Al‐Kunani 2001;Barrington 1996;Dobrzynski 1998). Reduced maternal serum selenium concentrations may be related to the occurrence of neural tube defects (Cengiz 2004), and low selenium dietary intake could be associated with the occurrence of congenital diaphragmatic hernia (Yang 2008). The literature has described that selenium concentrations of preterm and term newborns can be related to the selenium status of their mothers (Dobrzynski 1998;Micetic‐Turk 2000) and also that preterm infants born to healthy mothers have lower serum selenium concentrations than full‐term infants (Al‐Saleh 1998). Preterm infants can also have reduced erythrocyte glutathione peroxidase activity, a selenium‐dependent enzyme, which in turn can be associated with a higher incidence of oxygen dependence at 28 days of life (Mentro 2005). Hence, this reduction in antioxidant activity could be lined to lower selenium status. There still seems to be a great deal of controversy about the relationship between the selenium status of newborns and their birthweight (Bogden 2006;Kantola 2004;Makhoul 2004;Odland 1999;Perona 1979). Given the transient increase in oxidative stress observed during pregnancy (Holmes 2005), selenium status might have an important role on maternal antioxidant status due to the antioxidant functions of the mineral. Thus, it is possible that selenium supplementation, regardless of maternal nutrient status or selenium intake, could improve maternal antioxidant status and also bring benefits to the fetus, because maternal oxidative stress can be related to that of the child (Koklu 2007). In addition, although free radical production occurs continuously in every cell as part of their normal metabolism, when both endogenous and exogenous free radicals are excessive, they can play an important role in many diseases (Holmes 2005;Orhan 2003). Some pregnancy complications already reported to be associated with increased oxidative stress include pre‐eclampsia, gestational diabetes, nausea and vomiting, as well as intrauterine growth restriction (Biri 2006;Chamy 2006;Dennery 2007;Grissa 2007;Holmes 2005;Koklu 2007;Mehendale 2008;Verit 2007). Increased oxidative stress could also be related to premature rupture of membranes, causing preterm birth (Dobrzynski 1998;Longini 2007). It is important to point out that the role of selenium in the aetiology of diseases is not well established given that low levels of the mineral could be an underlying factor, or a consequence of, the disease itself (Navarro‐Alarcon 2008). Hypothetically, in both cases, correcting selenium status could contribute for both maternal and child health.Selenomethionine is the best supplemental form of selenium for several reasons. First of all, this selenium compound is the one most frequently found in food products, especially staple foods. It is also very well absorbed (more than 90%) and can be directly metabolized into body proteins. Selenium inorganic forms (selenite and selenate) are widely used for fortifying foods and as supplements as well. Selenate absorption is very efficient, while only 50% of the selenite consumed is absorbed (Institute of Medicine 2000;Schrauzer 2001).Most frequently, interventions include daily doses of tablets or capsules containing up to 200 mmg of selenium in its elemental form (selenomethionine). The supplementation period can vary, and the intervention can be carried out from antenatal period to postpartum (Kupka 2008;Kupka 2009;Moore 2000;Negro 2007). Supplemental doses up to 200 µmg of the mineral (four‐fold the recommended daily average for pregnant women) should not cause adverse effects, even if temporarily exceeded, since the selenium upper tolerable intake (UL) for this group is established as 400 µmg (5.1 µmol) selenium/day. Given the high UL and the regulation of body homeostasis through urinary excretion, selenium supplementation can be regarded as a safe intervention. Adverse effects include hair and nail loss and weakness, gastrointestinal disturbances, skin rash, garlic breadth odour, fatigue, irritability, and central nervous system abnormalities, and are not likely to occur. Clinical signs of selenosis have been reported at intake levels between 1200 and 5000 µg Se/day and biochemical alterations (increased prothrombin time and reduced glutathione blood levels) at intakes ranging from 700 to 850 µg Se/day (Institute of Medicine 2000;Schrauzer 2001;Sandstrom 1998).Although selenium deficiency is rare and only observed in areas where soil is selenium deficient, it is possible that selenium supplementation might reduce oxidative stress and thus improve maternal and newborn oxidative stress‐related newborn outcomes.Selenium exerts its metabolic role when participating in selenoprotein synthesis and function after incorporated into selenocystein. Selenoproteins that have been reported to have antioxidant functions include glutathione peroxidases, selenoprotein P and thioredoxin reductase. An increase in their expression can lead to reduced oxidative damage to DNA, lipids and proteins because these selenoenzymes protect cell components such as membranes, enzymes, proteins and DNA against oxidative damage and inhibit pro‐inflammatory cell metabolism (Lei 2007;Navarro‐Alarcon 2008;Ravn‐Haren 2008;Tapiero 2003).Selenium acts as a co‐factor of glutathione peroxidase enzymes. Seleno‐dependent glutathione peroxidases reduce peroxides, including hydrogen and lipid peroxides (Lei 2007;Navarro‐Alarcon 2008). Glutathione peroxidase keeps intracellular peroxide levels low and thus reduces damage to membrane and other cell structures caused by free radicals (Tapiero 2003). Its physiological role on the protection against oxidative stress caused by reactive oxygen species depends on both selenium nutritional status and the severity of the stress (Lei 2007). Selenoprotein P is an extracellular antioxidant that reduces nitrogen reactive species in the vascular endothelium. Both selenoprotein P and glutathione peroxidase are involved in inflammatory response regulation (Navarro‐Alarcon 2008). Selenium also participates in thioredoxin reductase production, which reduces intracellular substrates, regulates other antioxidant enzymes, modulates transcription factors, regulates apoptosis (cell death) and modulates protein phosphorylation (Navarro‐Alarcon 2008;Pappas 2008).Iodothyronine reductase, another enzyme which has selenium in its composition, participates in thyroid metabolism converting thyroxin to triiodothyronine (Pappas 2008). Since thyroid hormones are essential for fetal brain development, it has been suggested that maternal hypothyroidism could have effects on the cognitive development of the child (Gyamfi 2009). Thus, selenium supplementation in this period could help improving fetal brain development and consequently the child’s cognitive function in the future.High prevalences of selenium deficiency have been reported in areas where the soil is deficient in the mineral. Althouh, there are not worldwide estimates of such prevalences, studies assessing selenium status during pregnancy have found dietary intake levels below recommendations (Derbyshire 2009;Mathews 1998;McLachlan 2004;Micetic‐Turk 2000;Nichols 2008), particularly in populations living in areas where soil is deficient in this micronutrient. In countries such as Switzerland, for instance, although soil is selenium deficient, adequate selenium status is achieved due to the consumption of American wheat, which is rich in selenium due to its availability in the soil, while in Finland fertilizers have been enriched with selenium since 1984 (Eichholzer 2003;Kantola 2004).Despite using nutritional supplements, many pregnant women still might not achieve their recommendations, especially because many supplements do not contain selenium (Mathews 1998). Even though healthy women who plan pregnancy can have higher selenium intakes compared to women who do not plan gestation, their selenium intake can be frequently below recommendations (De Weerd 2003).Some of the positive effects of selenium supplementation already reported in the literature include increased plasma selenium levels and increased breast milk glutathione peroxidase activity and selenium content, which can be maintained up to 12 weeks postpartum (Moore 2000); lower frequency of pre‐eclampsia, reduction in maternal systolic and diastolic blood pressures, lower incidences of abortion and preterm delivery (Rumiris 2006); reduction in thyroid inflammatory activity and incidence of hypothyroidism (Negro 2007); reduced risk of maternal acute and watery diarrhoea and occurrence of maternal diarrhoea‐related morbidity (Kupka 2009); as well as lower risk of infant death after six weeks (Kupka 2008).
