[Chinese medicinal herbs for vaginal bleeding of medical abortion] There are about 150 thousand cases of induced abortion every day, or 53 million each year (WHO 1997). First trimester abortion can be performed by either using medical or surgical methods. Some studies have reported that 64% to 90% of women prefer medical abortion (Hill 1990; Tang 1991; Sun 1995). Approximately 670,000 women undergo abortions annually in the US early enough in pregnancy to be candidates for medical methods (Kahn 2000). Over 15 million medical abortions have been conducted in China in the past decade alone (Zhou 2002). Women reported that 'avoiding surgery', 'having a more natural experience ', 'being easier', 'more private', and 'can be done earlier in pregnancy' as reasons to opt for medical termination (Creinin 1996). In addition, other features such as 'less invasiveness', 'simplicity' and 'self‐administration' can be the reasons for choosing medical abortion (Rosen 1979; Bachelot 1992; Sun 1995).Compared to surgical abortion, medical abortion takes longer time and is associated with more blood loss, (Chan 1993; Henshaw 1994; Winikoff 1996). The duration of bleeding has been reported to range from 10 to 15 days with medical methods (Peyron 1993; Spitz 1998). Bleeding was significant enough to necessitate vacuum aspiration or a dilatation and curettage (D&C) in 0.8% of the cases. A blood transfusion was necessary in 0.1% of the women (Ulmann 1992). Excessive bleeding has been a major concern for women undergoing medical abortion and has not been solved till now.Some causes for heavy bleedingThe mechanism of Chinese medicinal herbs for reducing bleeding. [Loop diuretics during blood transfusion for anemia in preterm infants] Etiology of anemia of prematurityThe physiological drop in hemoglobin (Hb) after birth is due to expanding blood volume, shortened red blood cell survival and blunted erythropoietin (EPO) response. In premature infants, the Hb falls earlier and to a lower level than term babies, due to blood loss and depressed bone marrow activity. EPO production shifts from the liver to the kidney shortly after birth in the term infant, and the EPO produced primarily in the fetal liver is much less responsive to hypoxia than that produced in the kidney (Yu 1994). A 1000 g baby has a blood volume of 80 ml and despite micro‐testing assays, a significant amount of blood is lost by phlebotomy within a short period during intensive care.The physiology and evaluation of anemiaTissue oxygenation is influenced by cardiopulmonary function and a variety of factors that affect the hemoglobin‐oxygen dissociation curve (concentration and type of hemoglobin, concentration of 2,3‐diphosphoglycerate within red blood cells) (Murray 2004). The hemoglobin or hematocrit often correlate poorly with clinical signs of anemia and response to red cell transfusion. Red cell volume (RCV) may be a better guide regarding the need for transfusion since it takes into account circulating blood volume [Hct = RCV/(RCV + Plasma volume)] (Wardrop 1991;Yu 1994). Peripheral fractional oxygen extraction, monitored non‐invasively, correlates with variables that determine oxygen availability to the tissues, namely RCV and HbF, and is higher in babies with symptomatic anemia and decreased after transfusion (Wardle 1998). Tachycardia, tachypnoea, apnea, feeding difficulties, and poor weight gain are frequently attributed to anemia, but studies to support this association are conflicting (Cohen 1998).Transfusion practiceBlood transfusions are given to improve tissue oxygenation. In clinical practice, the sicker the baby and the greater the oxygen requirement, the higher the hemoglobin ought to be maintained to help improve recovery. Suggested transfusion thresholds vary with the clinical condition. Proposed thresholds include a Hb of 12 g/dl for neonates receiving intensive care, 11 g/dl for infants with chronic oxygen dependency, 7 g/dl for infants with late anemia, and transfusion once 10% blood volume has been removed (Gibson 2004). Most blood transfusions are 10 ‐ 20 ml/kg of blood (Gibson 2004). In a study using atrial natriuretic peptide as a marker of fluid status, a slow blood transfusion of less than 10 ml/kg did not cause volume expansion. There is wide variation in transfusion practices between neonatal units and countries (Ringer 1998;Engelfriet 2001;Murray 2004;Levy 1993). More restrictive transfusion practices did not lead to adverse outcome.Rationale for using loop diureticsDevelopment of patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), respiratory distress syndrome, necrotizing enterocolitis, chronic lung disease and intraventricular hemorrhage have been associated with increased fluid intake (Goldberg 1980;Bell 1980;Betremieux 1997;Van Marter 1990;Bell 1998). A study of 10 preterm infants showed a deterioration in lung function associated with a 10 ml/kg blood transfusion (Sasidharan 1990). Furosemide is often administered with blood transfusions in preterm infants to prevent potential problems related to volume expansion. A study that assessed changes in pulmonary function and ventilator settings with a single dose of intravenous or nebulised furosemide demonstrated no changes in oxygen requirement, ventilator pressure or ventilator rate (Prabhu 1997). Diuretics have commonly been used as treatment for chronic lung disease, but most studies failed to evaluate important clinical outcomes (Brion 2002).Side effects of loop diureticsThe side effects of loop diuretics include hypovolaemia, hyponatraemia, hypokalaemia, hypochloraemia, metabolic alkalosis and hyperuricaemia (Green 1987). In addition, there is an increased incidence of PDA related to increased production of prostaglandin E2 (Green 1981) ototoxicity, particularly if administered with aminoglycosides (Brummett 1980), and hypercalciuria leading to hypocalcaemia, calcium oxalate or calcium phosphate stones and nephrocalcinosis (calcium deposition within medullary pyramids of renal parenchyma) (Ezzedeen 1988).. [Interventions for preventing pre‐eclampsia and its consequences: generic protocol] [Generic protocol]This is a generic protocol for the development and maintenance of reviews evaluating interventions for prevention of pre‐eclampsia. The protocol outlines a common methodology for selection and assessment of studies. It was developed in consultation with existing review authors, who are listed under 'Contributions of reviewers'. We hope that the use of this protocol will provide a systematic and comprehensive approach to the topic and increase consistency across these reviews, making them easier to read and to use. If any review deviates substantially from this protocol, the reasons will be stated.Unlike other protocols inThe Cochrane Library, this generic protocol will not become a full review, but will remain permanently as a protocol. Reviews developed or updated using this protocol will be available separately inThe Cochrane Library.Hypertension (high blood pressure) is common during pregnancy. Around 10% of women will have their blood pressure recorded as above normal at some point before delivery. Pre‐eclampsia (toxaemia) is defined as hypertension accompanied by proteinuria (protein in the urine) (NHBPEP 2000). It usually occurs during the second half of pregnancy and complicates 2% to 8% of pregnancies (WHO 1988). For women who have hypertension alone, pregnancy outcome is similar to that for women with normal blood pressure. Outcome deteriorates once proteinuria develops. Women with mild pre‐eclampsia generally have no symptoms. Women with severe pre‐eclampsia, or very high blood pressure may feel unwell with symptoms such as headache, upper abdominal pain or visual disturbances. Pre‐eclampsia can lead to problems in the liver, kidneys, brain, and to abnormalities of the clotting system. Rare but serious complications include eclampsia (seizures in a woman with pre‐eclampsia), stroke, HELLP syndrome (haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelets) and disseminated intravascular coagulation. These complications are associated with an increased risk of maternal death (DH 2001). The placenta is also involved in pre‐eclampsia, and so risks for the baby are increased. The most common problems are those related to poor growth and premature birth.Although the outcome following pre‐eclampsia or eclampsia is good for most women, these conditions remain major causes of maternal mortality. Over half a million women die each year from pregnancy related causes, and 99% of these deaths occur in the developing world (WHO 2000). An estimated 10% to 15% of maternal deaths in developing countries are associated with pre‐eclampsia or eclampsia (Duley 1992), as are 13% to 15% of the direct obstetric deaths in the UK (DH 2001) and USA (ACOG 1996). Perinatal mortality is also increased following pre‐eclampsia (Ananth 1995;DH 2001).There is less information about morbidity for either mother or baby, but it is likely that this too is high. For example, pre‐eclampsia accounts for an estimated one fifth of antenatal admissions (Rosenberg 1990) and two thirds of referrals to day care assessment units (Anthony 1992) in the UK, and a quarter of obstetric admissions to intensive care units in France (Bouvier‐Colle 1996). For many women, developing pre‐eclampsia can be a difficult and unexpected experience, especially if they become ill, give birth too early (Engelhard 2002), or iftheir baby dies. Psychological morbidity following a difficult pregnancy or labour, or perinatal death is well documented (Clement 1998), although there are few data specific to pre‐eclampsia. There is also growing evidence that women who have had gestational hypertension or pre‐eclampsia may be at increased risk later in life of hypertension, stroke, and ischaemic heart disease (Hannaford 1997;Wilson 2003). For the babies, pre‐eclampsia is an antecedent for up to 12% of those born small for gestational age (Kramer 2000) and 19% of those born preterm (Hewitt 1988). Such babies are at an increased risk of developmental delay and chronic ill health in childhood.Pre‐eclampsia is part of a spectrum of conditions known as the hypertensive disorders of pregnancy. These disorders have a continuum with normal pregnancy. During normal pregnancy there is enormous maternal physiological adaptation to accommodate the growing fetus and placenta. For example, cardiac output increases by about 40% in the first trimester. In contrast, blood pressure remains relatively unchanged in the first trimester, falling by about 5 to 10 mmHg in the second trimester, and rising back to pre‐pregnancy levels by term. Cardiac output is influenced by peripheral resistance and blood pressure. As normal pregnancy is associated with increased cardiac output and normal or slightly lowered blood pressure, peripheral resistance falls (de Swiet 2002). Changes in kidney function also occur in normal pregnancy, with increased protein excretion especially in the third trimester. In pregnancy, up to 300 mg protein in 24 hours urine is accepted as normal.Classification and definitions of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy have, in the past, been controversial. More recently, there has been a shift towards agreeing standard definitions, and ensuring they are relevant for clinical practice (Brown 2001). What follows is based on current consensus.Hypertension in pregnancy is usually defined as systolic blood pressure of at least 140 mm Hg and/or diastolic blood pressure of at least 90 mmHg. Any rise in blood pressure should be confirmed by a second measurement, ideally at least four hours later. Blood pressure should be measured with an auscultatory device, as oscillometric techniques systematically under record during pregnancy (Quinn 1994). The debate over which auscultatory sound to use for assessment of diastolic blood pressure, muffling (Korotkoff phase IV) or disappearance (Korotkoff phase V), has been resolved, and Korotkoff V is now recommended as more reliable (Brown 2001;Rubin 1996).The suggestion that a change in blood pressure is more important than any absolute level (Redman 1988) is no longer included due to lack of evidence that it is related to outcome (Brown 2000;Brown 2001;NHBPEP 2000).Proteinuria during pregnancy is defined as 300 mg protein, or more, in 24 hours. In a single midstream urine sample, this usually correlates with 30 mg/dL, 1+ or more on a dipstick, or a spot urine protein/creatinine ratio of at least 30 mg/mmol (Brown 2000;Brown 2001).Four main categories are now widely agreed.This is hypertension detected for the first time during the second half of pregnancy (after 20 weeks gestation) in the absence of proteinuria. It resolves within three months of birth.Pre‐eclampsia is defined as hypertension and proteinuria detected for the first time in the second half of pregnancy (after 20 weeks gestation). Eclampsia is the occurrence of seizures in a woman with pre‐eclampsia.There is no widely accepted definition of severe pre‐eclampsia. Nevertheless, the following are generally regarded as features of severe disease: severe hypertension (blood pressure at least 160 mmHg systolic, or 110 mmHg diastolic), severe proteinuria (usually at least 3 g (range 2 g to 5 g) protein in 24 hours, or 3+ on dipstick), reduced urinary volume (less than 400 ml to 500 ml in 24 hours), neurological disturbances such as headache, visual disturbances, and exaggerated tendon reflexes, upper abdominal pain, pulmonary oedema (fluid in the lungs), impaired liver function tests, high serum creatinine, low platelets, intrauterine growth restriction or reduced liquor volume (ACOG 1996;Brown 2000;Brown 2001).This is hypertension known to be present before pregnancy, or detected before 20 weeks gestation. It is essential hypertension if no underlying cause is found, and secondary hypertension if there is an underlying cause such as renal, cardiac, or endocrine disease. Chronic hypertension may present for the first time as gestational hypertension. Hence, gestational hypertension that does not resolve after birth should be reclassified as chronic hypertension.Women with chronic hypertension may develop pre‐eclampsia. This is diagnosed where there is new onset of proteinuria, or sudden worsening of either hypertension or proteinuria, or development of other signs and symptoms of pre‐eclampsia after 20 weeks gestation.Despite a growing understanding of the pathophysiology of pre‐eclampsia, the underlying cause of the syndrome remains unclear. Factors that appear to have a role include the placenta, maternal immune response, genetic predisposition, maternal vascular disease, and diet. Whether an individual woman will develop this syndrome probably depends on which of these factors she has, and how they interact.The placenta plays a key role in pre‐eclampsia. Pre‐eclampsia occurs only in the presence of a placenta, and its resolution begins with the removal of the placenta at delivery. Pre‐eclampsia can occur when there is no fetus, as in a molar pregnancy (Scott 1958), and when the pregnancy is not in the uterus, as in an abdominal pregnancy (Piering 1993). Abnormal implantation of the placenta (Khong 1986) and excessive placental tissue are both factors in the underlying pathology of pre‐eclampsia.Normal pregnancy requires adaptation of the maternal immune response, so that the fetus, who also carries the father's genes, is not rejected as foreign tissue. It has been suggested that for some women pre‐eclampsia may occur because this adaptation is inadequate, for example in a first pregnancy with a new partner (Roberts 1998). In subsequent pregnancies with the same partner the immune tolerance is more complete, and the risk of pre‐eclampsia is therefore lower. Even a first trimester miscarriage or termination provides some protection (Dekker 1998;Strickland 1986).Pre‐eclampsia tends to run in families, suggesting that genetic predisposition is a factor. The risk is higher for sisters and daughters of women who had eclampsia and pre‐eclampsia (Adams 1961;Chesley 1968). A number of genes are currently under evaluation for possible links with pre‐eclampsia (Pridjian 2002).Medical conditions associated with vascular (blood vessel) disease also increase the risk of a woman developing pre‐eclampsia. For example, the risk is doubled with diabetes (Garner 1990), and one fifth of women with chronic hypertension develop pre‐eclampsia (Rey 1994). In addition, thrombophilia is associated with severe early onset pre‐eclampsia (Dekker 1995). This is a group of conditions with a tendency for thrombosis, or blood clotting. They include disorders such as protein S deficiency, activated protein C resistance, Factor V Leiden mutation and autoimmune diseases such as antiphospholipid syndrome and systemic lupus erythematosus. A raised blood level of homocysteine, a metabolite of the amino acid methionine, has also been linked to pre‐eclampsia (Powers 1998).Certain nutritional factors have been linked to the risk of pre‐eclampsia. For example, Mayan Indians in Guatemala, who traditionally soak their corn in lime before cooking, have a high calcium intake and a low incidence of pre‐eclampsia and eclampsia. This led to the hypothesis that an increase in calcium intake during pregnancy might reduce the risk of pre‐eclampsia among women with low calcium intake. Similarly, pre‐eclampsia is relatively infrequent in Greenland Inuits who eat a lot of oily fish (Dyerberg 1985), suggesting consumption of fish oil might prevent pre‐eclampsia. Other nutritional factors that have been suggested to have a role in preventing pre‐eclampsia include magnesium, zinc, selenium, antioxidants such as vitamins C and E, folic acid, garlic, and rhubarb.Pre‐eclampsia is thought to occur as a result of inadequate blood supply to the placenta. In normal pregnancy, as the placenta implants in the uterus, important changes take place in the uterine blood vessels to ensure that the growing placenta and fetus have adequate blood supply from the mother. During implantation, the placental cells invade blood vessels in the uterus known as spiral arterioles, replace their endothelial lining and remodel them into large diameter vessels with more capacity to handle blood flow to the placenta (Brosens 1972). In pre‐eclampsia, these vascular adaptations may be patchy or fail to extend into the deeper layers of the uterus (Khong 1986), resulting in small diameter, high resistance blood vessels that are unable to meet the increasing demand for blood supply to the placenta. Alternatively, placentation may be normal but there may be a relative reduction in placental blood flow, where the normal uterine blood supply becomes inadequate because the placenta is large, for example in a multiple pregnancy. Implantation and vascular changes are complete by 20 to 22 weeks gestation. So, although pre‐eclampsia is usually diagnosed in the second half of pregnancy, the antecedents are present much earlier.Current thinking is that inadequate blood supply to the placenta leads to the release of unknown factors or materials into the maternal circulation which activate or injure the endothelial cells, resulting in endothelial dysfunction (abnormal functioning of cells lining blood vessels) (Roberts 2002). Several pathways for this link between reduced perfusion of the placenta and endothelial dysfunction have been proposed. One hypothesis is that reduced placental perfusion may give rise to oxidative stress. In an environment where oxidants exceed neutralizing antioxidant (Hubel 1997), excessive formation of free radicals leads to lipid peroxidation and cell membrane damage (Hubel 1997). Alternatively, lack of oxygen in the placenta may trigger the release of small proteins, known as cytokines, that start an inflammatory response in the endothelium (Conrad 1997). Another proposed mediator for the endothelial cell injury is micro fragments of placental tissue. These are transferred into the maternal circulation in increased amounts in women with pre‐eclampsia (Knight 1998), and have been shown to alter endothelial function in laboratory studies (Cockell 1997).Endothelial dysfunction results in a series of changes including reduced production of vasodilators and anticoagulants (such as prostacyclin and nitric oxide), increased production of vasoconstrictors and platelet aggregators (such as thromboxane A2 and endothelin), increased responsiveness of endothelium to the vasopressor Angiotensin II, and an elevation in the proteins of the coagulation cascade (such as von Willebrand factor). These changes result in widespread vasoconstriction and activation of platelets and the coagulation system. Injured endothelial cells allow leakage of fluid out of the blood vessels and into surrounding tissues, causing oedema and a reduction in the circulating blood volume. There is then inadequate blood flow to many of the woman's organs, especially the kidneys, liver, and brain. It is the vasoconstriction, micro clots, and reduced circulating blood volume that result in the clinical manifestations of pre‐eclampsia.Reduced perfusion of the placenta is not sufficient to explain pre‐eclampsia. The abnormal implantation needs to interact with maternal constitutional factors (genetic, environmental and behavioural) to produce the syndrome of pre‐eclampsia. The contributions of reduced perfusion and maternal factors may be balanced differently in different pregnancies. For example, profoundly reduced perfusion could lead to pre‐eclampsia in women with minimal predisposing risk, while for others the maternal constitution might present such a high risk that even minimal reduction of placental perfusion would be sufficient to result in pre‐eclampsia.Screening for women at risk of pre‐eclampsia is an important part of antenatal care. Once women are identified as high risk, they can be targeted for more intensive antenatal surveillance and prophylactic interventions. Most current strategies for risk assessment are based on the obstetric and medical history, and clinical examination. However, there is surprisingly little reliable evidence on the actual risk associated with individual factors, and how they might interact. Systematic reviews of strategies for predicting pre‐eclampsia are under way (Gupta 2004). When available, results from these reviews will be incorporated into this protocol.Risk factors with a particularly high association with pre‐eclampsia (more than one in 10 risk) include maternal diabetes (Caritis 1998;Conde‐Agudelo 2000;Ness 1999), chronic hypertension (Caritis 1998;Conde‐Agudelo 2000;Rey 1994), and renal disease (Cunningham 1990). Thrombophilia and autoimmune disease have a strong association with severe early onset pre‐eclampsia (Dekker 1995). Obstetric factors associated with high risk are multiple pregnancy (Conde‐Agudelo 2000;Long 1987), history of pre‐eclampsia in a previous pregnancy especially if severe or early onset (Caritis 1998;Hnat 2002;Sibai 1991) and a current hydropic (Scott 1958) or molar pregnancy (Taylor 1988). Other factors linked with pre‐eclampsia, but associated with a somewhat lower risk include first pregnancies (Brown 2000;Conde‐Agudelo 2000;Taylor 1988), age less than 20 or more than 35 years (Conde‐Agudelo 2000;Ness 1999), a family history of pre‐eclampsia (Adams 1961;Chesley 1968), and obesity (Baeten 2001;Conde‐Agudelo 2000;Sebire 2001).Routine screening for pre‐eclampsia is based on measurement of blood pressure and urinalysis for proteinuria. Overall, 15% to 25% of women with gestational hypertension progress to pre‐eclampsia (Saudan 1988). Although various physiologic and biochemical screening tests have also been developed (Friedman 1999), so far none have proved to be of good predictive value and few are used in clinical practice. Doppler ultrasound of the uterine arteries is a non‐invasive imaging test to assess blood flow to the placenta, and at present holds more promise (Papegeorghiou 2004).Primary prevention is preventing the onset of a disease, for example prevention of any signs or symptoms of pre‐eclampsia. Secondary prevention is the reversing, stopping or slowing down of its progress, for example prevention of proteinuria in a woman with gestational hypertension. Tertiary prevention is the prevention of complications in established disease, for example, prevention of eclampsia in a woman with pre‐eclampsia. This protocol covers primary and secondary prevention. Tertiary prevention is dealt with in other Cochrane reviews such as those on anticonvulsants for pre‐eclampsia (Duley 2003c), and eclampsia (Duley 2000;Duley 2003b;Duley 2003d), plasma volume expansion (Duley 1999b), corticosteroids for HELLP syndrome (Matchaba 2002), timing of delivery for severe pre‐eclampsia (Churchill 2002), and alternative antihypertensive agents for very high blood pressure (Duley 2002).As the cause of pre‐eclampsia is not completely understood, and screening tests remain unreliable, it is difficult to develop rational strategies for prevention of pre‐eclampsia. Current strategies for prevention focus on antenatal surveillance, modification of lifestyle, nutritional supplementation, and pharmacological therapy.Antenatal care is a complex package of interventions. The components may vary, dependent on factors such as country, setting, and the characteristics of the individual woman.Evaluation of antenatal care for women at risk of pre‐eclampsia should include an evaluation of individual components, such as how to measure blood pressure or proteinuria. It should also include comparisons of packages with different settings, providers of care, and frequency of visits.Certain lifestyle choices have been suggested to influence risk of hypertension, such as whether to exercise, how much to rest in bed, and whether to modify salt content in the diet. As these would normally be matters of personal preference, it is important that any recommendation that women modify their life style should be based on adequate evidence.Various hypotheses have been proposed to link pre‐eclampsia with specific dietary deficiencies, either before or during pregnancy. For example, calcium (Atallah 2002) and fish oil supplementation were suggested based on observations of an association between dietary intake and the incidence of pre‐eclampsia in various communities. Zinc (Mahomed 1997a) and magnesium supplements (Makrides 2001b) were suggested to optimise normal physiological function during pregnancy. Antioxidants such as vitamin C and E, selenium and garlic have been suggested to counteract oxidative stress. Folic acid may correct raised blood levels of homocysteine.A wide range of drugs have been advocated for primary and secondary prevention of pre‐eclampsia. For example, diuretics were popular when oedema was considered to be an important symptom of pre‐eclampsia. Antiplatelet agents were suggested based on the hypothesis that they would increase production of the vasodilator prostacyclin, and reduce the vasoconstrictor thromboxane, hence reducing the risk of pre‐eclampsia (Duley 2003a). Anticoagulants have also been suggested for women at particularly high risk, such as those with thrombophilia (Walker 2003). Antihypertensive drugs are widely used for women with gestational or chronic hypertension in the hope that early control of blood pressure may prevent progression to pre‐eclampsia (Abalos 2001). Recently, there has been interest in nitric oxide, a vasodilator and inhibitor of platelet aggregation. Alternative therapies such as Chinese herbal medicine have also been used for pre‐eclampsia.A number of reviews and protocols evaluating interventions for prevention of pre‐eclampsia are already available onThe Cochrane Library. Some of these reviews have prevention of pre‐eclampsia and its complications as their main focus. We refer to these as 'core reviews'. For other reviews, the aim is to assess the impact of a specific intervention on a range of outcomes, one of which is pre‐eclampsia. We refer to these as 'non‐core reviews'. This generic protocol will serve as a template for core reviews for prevention of pre‐eclampsia, either in the development of new reviews or in the updating of existing reviews. Reviews developed or updated using this protocol will be available separately inThe Cochrane Library.[Introduction]Hypertension (high blood pressure) is common during pregnancy. Around 10% of women will have their blood pressure recorded as above normal at some point before delivery. Pre‐eclampsia (toxaemia) is defined as hypertension accompanied by proteinuria (protein in the urine) (NHBPEP 2000). It usually occurs during the second half of pregnancy and complicates 2% to 8% of pregnancies (WHO 1988). For women who have hypertension alone, pregnancy outcome is similar to that for women with normal blood pressure. Outcome deteriorates once proteinuria develops. Women with mild pre‐eclampsia generally have no symptoms. Women with severe pre‐eclampsia, or very high blood pressure may feel unwell with symptoms such as headache, upper abdominal pain or visual disturbances. Pre‐eclampsia can lead to problems in the liver, kidneys, brain, and to abnormalities of the clotting system. Rare but serious complications include eclampsia (seizures in a woman with pre‐eclampsia), stroke, HELLP syndrome (haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelets) and disseminated intravascular coagulation. These complications are associated with an increased risk of maternal death (DH 2001). The placenta is also involved in pre‐eclampsia, and so risks for the baby are increased. The most common problems are those related to poor growth and premature birth.Although the outcome following pre‐eclampsia or eclampsia is good for most women, these conditions remain major causes of maternal mortality. Over half a million women die each year from pregnancy related causes, and 99% of these deaths occur in the developing world (WHO 2000). An estimated 10% to 15% of maternal deaths in developing countries are associated with pre‐eclampsia or eclampsia (Duley 1992), as are 13% to 15% of the direct obstetric deaths in the UK (DH 2001) and USA (ACOG 1996). Perinatal mortality is also increased following pre‐eclampsia (Ananth 1995;DH 2001).There is less information about morbidity for either mother or baby, but it is likely that this too is high. For example, pre‐eclampsia accounts for an estimated one fifth of antenatal admissions (Rosenberg 1990) and two thirds of referrals to day care assessment units (Anthony 1992) in the UK, and a quarter of obstetric admissions to intensive care units in France (Bouvier‐Colle 1996). For many women, developing pre‐eclampsia can be a difficult and unexpected experience, especially if they become ill, give birth too early (Engelhard 2002), or iftheir baby dies. Psychological morbidity following a difficult pregnancy or labour, or perinatal death is well documented (Clement 1998), although there are few data specific to pre‐eclampsia. There is also growing evidence that women who have had gestational hypertension or pre‐eclampsia may be at increased risk later in life of hypertension, stroke, and ischaemic heart disease (Hannaford 1997;Wilson 2003). For the babies, pre‐eclampsia is an antecedent for up to 12% of those born small for gestational age (Kramer 2000) and 19% of those born preterm (Hewitt 1988). Such babies are at an increased risk of developmental delay and chronic ill health in childhood.[Definitions and classification]Pre‐eclampsia is part of a spectrum of conditions known as the hypertensive disorders of pregnancy. These disorders have a continuum with normal pregnancy. During normal pregnancy there is enormous maternal physiological adaptation to accommodate the growing fetus and placenta. For example, cardiac output increases by about 40% in the first trimester. In contrast, blood pressure remains relatively unchanged in the first trimester, falling by about 5 to 10 mmHg in the second trimester, and rising back to pre‐pregnancy levels by term. Cardiac output is influenced by peripheral resistance and blood pressure. As normal pregnancy is associated with increased cardiac output and normal or slightly lowered blood pressure, peripheral resistance falls (de Swiet 2002). Changes in kidney function also occur in normal pregnancy, with increased protein excretion especially in the third trimester. In pregnancy, up to 300 mg protein in 24 hours urine is accepted as normal.Classification and definitions of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy have, in the past, been controversial. More recently, there has been a shift towards agreeing standard definitions, and ensuring they are relevant for clinical practice (Brown 2001). What follows is based on current consensus.Hypertension in pregnancy is usually defined as systolic blood pressure of at least 140 mm Hg and/or diastolic blood pressure of at least 90 mmHg. Any rise in blood pressure should be confirmed by a second measurement, ideally at least four hours later. Blood pressure should be measured with an auscultatory device, as oscillometric techniques systematically under record during pregnancy (Quinn 1994). The debate over which auscultatory sound to use for assessment of diastolic blood pressure, muffling (Korotkoff phase IV) or disappearance (Korotkoff phase V), has been resolved, and Korotkoff V is now recommended as more reliable (Brown 2001;Rubin 1996).The suggestion that a change in blood pressure is more important than any absolute level (Redman 1988) is no longer included due to lack of evidence that it is related to outcome (Brown 2000;Brown 2001;NHBPEP 2000).Proteinuria during pregnancy is defined as 300 mg protein, or more, in 24 hours. In a single midstream urine sample, this usually correlates with 30 mg/dL, 1+ or more on a dipstick, or a spot urine protein/creatinine ratio of at least 30 mg/mmol (Brown 2000;Brown 2001).Four main categories are now widely agreed.This is hypertension detected for the first time during the second half of pregnancy (after 20 weeks gestation) in the absence of proteinuria. It resolves within three months of birth.Pre‐eclampsia is defined as hypertension and proteinuria detected for the first time in the second half of pregnancy (after 20 weeks gestation). Eclampsia is the occurrence of seizures in a woman with pre‐eclampsia.There is no widely accepted definition of severe pre‐eclampsia. Nevertheless, the following are generally regarded as features of severe disease: severe hypertension (blood pressure at least 160 mmHg systolic, or 110 mmHg diastolic), severe proteinuria (usually at least 3 g (range 2 g to 5 g) protein in 24 hours, or 3+ on dipstick), reduced urinary volume (less than 400 ml to 500 ml in 24 hours), neurological disturbances such as headache, visual disturbances, and exaggerated tendon reflexes, upper abdominal pain, pulmonary oedema (fluid in the lungs), impaired liver function tests, high serum creatinine, low platelets, intrauterine growth restriction or reduced liquor volume (ACOG 1996;Brown 2000;Brown 2001).This is hypertension known to be present before pregnancy, or detected before 20 weeks gestation. It is essential hypertension if no underlying cause is found, and secondary hypertension if there is an underlying cause such as renal, cardiac, or endocrine disease. Chronic hypertension may present for the first time as gestational hypertension. Hence, gestational hypertension that does not resolve after birth should be reclassified as chronic hypertension.Women with chronic hypertension may develop pre‐eclampsia. This is diagnosed where there is new onset of proteinuria, or sudden worsening of either hypertension or proteinuria, or development of other signs and symptoms of pre‐eclampsia after 20 weeks gestation.Despite a growing understanding of the pathophysiology of pre‐eclampsia, the underlying cause of the syndrome remains unclear. Factors that appear to have a role include the placenta, maternal immune response, genetic predisposition, maternal vascular disease, and diet. Whether an individual woman will develop this syndrome probably depends on which of these factors she has, and how they interact.The placenta plays a key role in pre‐eclampsia. Pre‐eclampsia occurs only in the presence of a placenta, and its resolution begins with the removal of the placenta at delivery. Pre‐eclampsia can occur when there is no fetus, as in a molar pregnancy (Scott 1958), and when the pregnancy is not in the uterus, as in an abdominal pregnancy (Piering 1993). Abnormal implantation of the placenta (Khong 1986) and excessive placental tissue are both factors in the underlying pathology of pre‐eclampsia.Normal pregnancy requires adaptation of the maternal immune response, so that the fetus, who also carries the father's genes, is not rejected as foreign tissue. It has been suggested that for some women pre‐eclampsia may occur because this adaptation is inadequate, for example in a first pregnancy with a new partner (Roberts 1998). In subsequent pregnancies with the same partner the immune tolerance is more complete, and the risk of pre‐eclampsia is therefore lower. Even a first trimester miscarriage or termination provides some protection (Dekker 1998;Strickland 1986).Pre‐eclampsia tends to run in families, suggesting that genetic predisposition is a factor. The risk is higher for sisters and daughters of women who had eclampsia and pre‐eclampsia (Adams 1961;Chesley 1968). A number of genes are currently under evaluation for possible links with pre‐eclampsia (Pridjian 2002).Medical conditions associated with vascular (blood vessel) disease also increase the risk of a woman developing pre‐eclampsia. For example, the risk is doubled with diabetes (Garner 1990), and one fifth of women with chronic hypertension develop pre‐eclampsia (Rey 1994). In addition, thrombophilia is associated with severe early onset pre‐eclampsia (Dekker 1995). This is a group of conditions with a tendency for thrombosis, or blood clotting. They include disorders such as protein S deficiency, activated protein C resistance, Factor V Leiden mutation and autoimmune diseases such as antiphospholipid syndrome and systemic lupus erythematosus. A raised blood level of homocysteine, a metabolite of the amino acid methionine, has also been linked to pre‐eclampsia (Powers 1998).Certain nutritional factors have been linked to the risk of pre‐eclampsia. For example, Mayan Indians in Guatemala, who traditionally soak their corn in lime before cooking, have a high calcium intake and a low incidence of pre‐eclampsia and eclampsia. This led to the hypothesis that an increase in calcium intake during pregnancy might reduce the risk of pre‐eclampsia among women with low calcium intake. Similarly, pre‐eclampsia is relatively infrequent in Greenland Inuits who eat a lot of oily fish (Dyerberg 1985), suggesting consumption of fish oil might prevent pre‐eclampsia. Other nutritional factors that have been suggested to have a role in preventing pre‐eclampsia include magnesium, zinc, selenium, antioxidants such as vitamins C and E, folic acid, garlic, and rhubarb.[Mode of development of pre‐eclampsia]Pre‐eclampsia is thought to occur as a result of inadequate blood supply to the placenta. In normal pregnancy, as the placenta implants in the uterus, important changes take place in the uterine blood vessels to ensure that the growing placenta and fetus have adequate blood supply from the mother. During implantation, the placental cells invade blood vessels in the uterus known as spiral arterioles, replace their endothelial lining and remodel them into large diameter vessels with more capacity to handle blood flow to the placenta (Brosens 1972). In pre‐eclampsia, these vascular adaptations may be patchy or fail to extend into the deeper layers of the uterus (Khong 1986), resulting in small diameter, high resistance blood vessels that are unable to meet the increasing demand for blood supply to the placenta. Alternatively, placentation may be normal but there may be a relative reduction in placental blood flow, where the normal uterine blood supply becomes inadequate because the placenta is large, for example in a multiple pregnancy. Implantation and vascular changes are complete by 20 to 22 weeks gestation. So, although pre‐eclampsia is usually diagnosed in the second half of pregnancy, the antecedents are present much earlier.Current thinking is that inadequate blood supply to the placenta leads to the release of unknown factors or materials into the maternal circulation which activate or injure the endothelial cells, resulting in endothelial dysfunction (abnormal functioning of cells lining blood vessels) (Roberts 2002). Several pathways for this link between reduced perfusion of the placenta and endothelial dysfunction have been proposed. One hypothesis is that reduced placental perfusion may give rise to oxidative stress. In an environment where oxidants exceed neutralizing antioxidant (Hubel 1997), excessive formation of free radicals leads to lipid peroxidation and cell membrane damage (Hubel 1997). Alternatively, lack of oxygen in the placenta may trigger the release of small proteins, known as cytokines, that start an inflammatory response in the endothelium (Conrad 1997). Another proposed mediator for the endothelial cell injury is micro fragments of placental tissue. These are transferred into the maternal circulation in increased amounts in women with pre‐eclampsia (Knight 1998), and have been shown to alter endothelial function in laboratory studies (Cockell 1997).Endothelial dysfunction results in a series of changes including reduced production of vasodilators and anticoagulants (such as prostacyclin and nitric oxide), increased production of vasoconstrictors and platelet aggregators (such as thromboxane A2 and endothelin), increased responsiveness of endothelium to the vasopressor Angiotensin II, and an elevation in the proteins of the coagulation cascade (such as von Willebrand factor). These changes result in widespread vasoconstriction and activation of platelets and the coagulation system. Injured endothelial cells allow leakage of fluid out of the blood vessels and into surrounding tissues, causing oedema and a reduction in the circulating blood volume. There is then inadequate blood flow to many of the woman's organs, especially the kidneys, liver, and brain. It is the vasoconstriction, micro clots, and reduced circulating blood volume that result in the clinical manifestations of pre‐eclampsia.Reduced perfusion of the placenta is not sufficient to explain pre‐eclampsia. The abnormal implantation needs to interact with maternal constitutional factors (genetic, environmental and behavioural) to produce the syndrome of pre‐eclampsia. The contributions of reduced perfusion and maternal factors may be balanced differently in different pregnancies. For example, profoundly reduced perfusion could lead to pre‐eclampsia in women with minimal predisposing risk, while for others the maternal constitution might present such a high risk that even minimal reduction of placental perfusion would be sufficient to result in pre‐eclampsia.[Identifying women at risk of pre‐eclampsia]Screening for women at risk of pre‐eclampsia is an important part of antenatal care. Once women are identified as high risk, they can be targeted for more intensive antenatal surveillance and prophylactic interventions. Most current strategies for risk assessment are based on the obstetric and medical history, and clinical examination. However, there is surprisingly little reliable evidence on the actual risk associated with individual factors, and how they might interact. Systematic reviews of strategies for predicting pre‐eclampsia are under way (Gupta 2004). When available, results from these reviews will be incorporated into this protocol.Risk factors with a particularly high association with pre‐eclampsia (more than one in 10 risk) include maternal diabetes (Caritis 1998;Conde‐Agudelo 2000;Ness 1999), chronic hypertension (Caritis 1998;Conde‐Agudelo 2000;Rey 1994), and renal disease (Cunningham 1990). Thrombophilia and autoimmune disease have a strong association with severe early onset pre‐eclampsia (Dekker 1995). Obstetric factors associated with high risk are multiple pregnancy (Conde‐Agudelo 2000;Long 1987), history of pre‐eclampsia in a previous pregnancy especially if severe or early onset (Caritis 1998;Hnat 2002;Sibai 1991) and a current hydropic (Scott 1958) or molar pregnancy (Taylor 1988). Other factors linked with pre‐eclampsia, but associated with a somewhat lower risk include first pregnancies (Brown 2000;Conde‐Agudelo 2000;Taylor 1988), age less than 20 or more than 35 years (Conde‐Agudelo 2000;Ness 1999), a family history of pre‐eclampsia (Adams 1961;Chesley 1968), and obesity (Baeten 2001;Conde‐Agudelo 2000;Sebire 2001).Routine screening for pre‐eclampsia is based on measurement of blood pressure and urinalysis for proteinuria. Overall, 15% to 25% of women with gestational hypertension progress to pre‐eclampsia (Saudan 1988). Although various physiologic and biochemical screening tests have also been developed (Friedman 1999), so far none have proved to be of good predictive value and few are used in clinical practice. Doppler ultrasound of the uterine arteries is a non‐invasive imaging test to assess blood flow to the placenta, and at present holds more promise (Papegeorghiou 2004).[Strategies for prevention]Primary prevention is preventing the onset of a disease, for example prevention of any signs or symptoms of pre‐eclampsia. Secondary prevention is the reversing, stopping or slowing down of its progress, for example prevention of proteinuria in a woman with gestational hypertension. Tertiary prevention is the prevention of complications in established disease, for example, prevention of eclampsia in a woman with pre‐eclampsia. This protocol covers primary and secondary prevention. Tertiary prevention is dealt with in other Cochrane reviews such as those on anticonvulsants for pre‐eclampsia (Duley 2003c), and eclampsia (Duley 2000;Duley 2003b;Duley 2003d), plasma volume expansion (Duley 1999b), corticosteroids for HELLP syndrome (Matchaba 2002), timing of delivery for severe pre‐eclampsia (Churchill 2002), and alternative antihypertensive agents for very high blood pressure (Duley 2002).As the cause of pre‐eclampsia is not completely understood, and screening tests remain unreliable, it is difficult to develop rational strategies for prevention of pre‐eclampsia. Current strategies for prevention focus on antenatal surveillance, modification of lifestyle, nutritional supplementation, and pharmacological therapy.Antenatal care is a complex package of interventions. The components may vary, dependent on factors such as country, setting, and the characteristics of the individual woman.Evaluation of antenatal care for women at risk of pre‐eclampsia should include an evaluation of individual components, such as how to measure blood pressure or proteinuria. It should also include comparisons of packages with different settings, providers of care, and frequency of visits.Certain lifestyle choices have been suggested to influence risk of hypertension, such as whether to exercise, how much to rest in bed, and whether to modify salt content in the diet. As these would normally be matters of personal preference, it is important that any recommendation that women modify their life style should be based on adequate evidence.Various hypotheses have been proposed to link pre‐eclampsia with specific dietary deficiencies, either before or during pregnancy. For example, calcium (Atallah 2002) and fish oil supplementation were suggested based on observations of an association between dietary intake and the incidence of pre‐eclampsia in various communities. Zinc (Mahomed 1997a) and magnesium supplements (Makrides 2001b) were suggested to optimise normal physiological function during pregnancy. Antioxidants such as vitamin C and E, selenium and garlic have been suggested to counteract oxidative stress. Folic acid may correct raised blood levels of homocysteine.A wide range of drugs have been advocated for primary and secondary prevention of pre‐eclampsia. For example, diuretics were popular when oedema was considered to be an important symptom of pre‐eclampsia. Antiplatelet agents were suggested based on the hypothesis that they would increase production of the vasodilator prostacyclin, and reduce the vasoconstrictor thromboxane, hence reducing the risk of pre‐eclampsia (Duley 2003a). Anticoagulants have also been suggested for women at particularly high risk, such as those with thrombophilia (Walker 2003). Antihypertensive drugs are widely used for women with gestational or chronic hypertension in the hope that early control of blood pressure may prevent progression to pre‐eclampsia (Abalos 2001). Recently, there has been interest in nitric oxide, a vasodilator and inhibitor of platelet aggregation. [Interventions for psychosis in adolescents] The term 'Adolescent schizophrenia' represents a sub‐group of individuals with schizophrenia with an onset over the age of 12 and up to and including those aged 17 (Werry 1992;Hollis 2000a). The upper age cut‐off is based largely on the age interface between child and adolescent mental health services (CAMHS) and General Adult services, which can vary according to local policy. Onset below the age of 13 is extremely rare and is often referred to as 'childhood‐onset' (APA 1994) or 'very early onset' schizophrenia. This group, the subject of a review in progress (Kennedy 2003), will not be considered directly here.Adolescent schizophrenia is currently diagnosed using the same criteria as those used for adult onset schizophrenia (ICD‐10 (WHO 1992), DSM‐IV (APA 1994)). It does, in general, have a more severe and unremitting course along with a poorer outcome than is true for schizophrenia as a whole (Hollis 2000b). There is an understandable reticence among clinicians to progress to a formal diagnosis in many cases, despite the reduced likelihood of a full or prolonged remission following a first episode of psychosis (Hollis 2000b). Additional factors may also conspire to confuse or delay a diagnosis (and potentially the implementation of an appropriate treatment plan). These factors include a greater prominence of negative symptoms, a more insidious onset and poorer pre‐morbid functioning.The treatment of schizophrenia or other psychotic disorders in adolescents is largely reliant on evidence from studies on adults. Antipsychotic drugs are of prime importance, and widespread confidence in these products may encourage the generalisation of adult‐based evidence to the younger age group. However, important differences between adolescents and adults with psychosis (e.g. the prominence of negative symptoms and the increased frequency of extra pyramidal adverse effects) suggest that response rates, tolerability and other outcome measures might differ significantly. Specific trials relating to adolescents are lacking and are needed to clarify whether or not there is an evidence‐based rationale for treating adolescents in the same way as adults.Non‐pharmacological interventions are widely used to compliment pharmacological approaches and differ more overtly from their counterparts within adult services. The fact that the two services are often discrete in parts of the world and that the service provision may be structured differently is another key concern when looking to generalise evidence. Family and individual therapy, as well as assessment of social and educational needs, are all provided in line with best practice guidelines (Clark 1998). Early intervention programmes are targeted specifically at first‐episode psychosis and are very relevant to adolescent‐onset cases. Their effectiveness has yet to be adequately demonstrated, however, and this has been subject to a recent Cochrane review (Marshall 2004). The adolescent years incorporate the most crucial period of schooling for most individuals and educational attainment has prognostic implications for everyone, let alone those with an illness that impacts directly on cognitive and social development. Interventions within educational settings may also, therefore, form an important part of the treatment plan.. [Non‐hormonal therapy for hot flushes in postmenopausal women] The hot flush (or flash) is the most common feature of the menopause (climacteric). The climacteric can be defined as the physiological and pathological events that directly follow the onset of reduced ovarian function, both before and after the last menstrual period (MacLennan 2001). According to the World Health Organization, hot flushes are defined as the sudden feeling of heat in the face, neck and chest (WHO 1996). Hot flushes can occur with differing severity and at different frequency during the day or night (Porter 1996;Freedman 1995). At night, these changes may be recognized and referred to as night sweats. Together, hot flushes and night sweats have been described as the most common characteristic of the vasomotor menopausal symptoms (WHO 1996).The aetiology of the hot flush is complex and uncertain, but it is probably caused by instability of the thermoregulatory centre of the hypothalamus, induced by the withdrawal of oestrogen and progesterone (Freedman 2001). In these circumstances, the occurrence of hot flushes can be influenced by external factors including tension or nervousness, which may affect neuroendocrine pathways culminating in increased hypothalamic norepinephrine and serotonin release (Shanafelt 2002;Stearns 2002). This instability of the thermoregulatory centre leads to sudden, transient, and erratic peripheral vasodilatation in the skin blood vessels, with a concomitant sensation of flushing and a measurable increase in core body temperature (Freedman 1999). There are differences in the prevalence of hot flushes associated with the menopause in different cultures, with the lowest prevalence reported in Maya Indians who do not report any menopausal symptoms at all (Martin 1993). Other prevalences reported are 10 to 22% in Hong Kong women, around 17% in Japanese women, 23% in Thai women, 45% in North American women and up to 80% in Dutch women. Although some studies have inconsistencies in the reported prevalence, hot flushes and night sweats are more commonly reported in Western countries than in other populations (WHO 1996).For those women who do have them, the prevalence of hot flushes reaches its peak between the early perimenopausal and late perimenopausal period, the latter defined as symptomatic woman with 3 to 11 months of no menstrual periods. Hot flushes are most prevalent during the first two years after the menopause and then usually lessen with increasing years, but may persist for longer (Stearns 2002;Dennerstein 2000). There is agreement from both cross‐sectional and longitudinal studies that 10% to 20% of women still have climacteric complains even 15 years after the menopause (Berg 1988;Rodstrom 2002). In women seeking assistance for menopausal symptoms, hot flushes are the most frequent physical complaint, occurring in approximately 80% of these women (Anderson 1987;Guthrie 2003). A longitudinal study in Sweden describes the prevalence and treatment for hot flushes over 25 years. In the late 1960s a large number of women who received treatment for hot flushes were treated with non‐hormonal forms of medical treatment, including antidepressants, sedatives, and anticholinergic drugs. Few women at this time received hormonal replacement treatment (HRT) and less than 50% of all treated women considered their treatment to be effective. The number of woman receiving HRT increased markedly in 1980s and up to 87% considered HRT to be effective treatment for their hot flushes (Rodstrom 2002).The North American Menopause Society (NAMS) recently published a position statement for the treatment of menopause vasomotor‐related symptoms, proposed a classification for treatment options and described the quality of evidence that support their use (NAMS 2004).Lifestyle modifications that potentially could be beneficial for mild hot flushes are: maintaining lower core body temperature, losing excess weight and stopping smoking, all based on observational studies. No randomised controlled trials have examined the efficacy of such interventions. Relaxation techniques performed when the hot flush begins has shown some efficacy in reducing hot flushes in randomised clinical trials (RCT).Non‐prescription remedies include some with clear hormonal properties such as isoflavones and topical progesterone, others with inconclusive evidence of oestrogenicity (black cohosh, dong quai, ginseng or licorice) and interventions with no hormonal known effect (vitamin E, acupuncture, and magnet therapy). Evidence is generally lacking regarding efficacy and long‐term safety of these remedies. Randomised, controlled clinical trials have shown that, in general, hot flushes are only slightly reduced in women who consume soy‐derived isoflavones or vitamin E when compared with control. For topical progesterone, black cohosh, dong quai, ginseng, chinese herb mixtures, and magnet therapy there are no benefit than placebo in RCTs. There is no clinical data provided by RCTs for acupuncture or licorice in the NAMS position statement.Prescription therapies, hormonal options: a systematic review including 21 RCT enrolling 2,511 women found that oral hormonal replacement therapy (HRT) with oestrogens or oestrogens plus progesterone is highly effective in reducing hot flushes and night sweats with a 77% reduction in frequency (95% CI 58.2 to 87.5) and significant severity reduction (OR 0.13, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.22) compared to placebo (MacLennan 2001). Alone progestins have been shown in several RCT to relieve menopause‐associated hot flushes. Oral contraceptives in selected perimenopausal women have been evaluated in two RCT; only one of them found significant reduction in hot flushes compared to controls. Evidence to support androgen‐estrogen therapy for reduction of hot flushes is lacking.Prescription therapies, non‐hormonal options: certain antidepressants may decrease hot flushes in women based on possible effect in central serotonin or norepinephrine concentrations. The NAMS describes evidence based on RCTs for venlafaxine, paroxetine and fluoxetine. Gabapentin, an anticonvulsant, has been studied for treating hot flushes in one RCT, the mechanism of action on hot flushes is not known. Antihypertensives have been studied as hot flush treatment in two RCTs for clonidine and two RCTs for methyldopa with more side effects for clonidine than placebo and modest reduction of hot flushes for methyldopa. Tibolone (a synthetic form of HRT with oestrogenic, progestagenic, and androgenic effect) have been included in the hormonal options with one RCT who shows that it was as effective as oestrogen‐progesterone combination for relieving hot flushes and other menopausal symptoms (Hammar 1998). On the other hand, data from Women Health Initiative (WHI) and the Heart and Estrogen/progestin Replacement Study (HERS) links HRT with increased risk for breast cancer, cardiovascular risk, thromboembolism, stroke, and dementia (Grady 2000;Rossouw 2002;Hulley 2002;Shumaker 2003;Wassertheil‐S 2003). Breast cancer risk is increased with oestrogen and, in a greater magnitude, with oestrogen plus progesterone use beyond five years (Chlebowski 2003;Beral 2003) Direct extrapolation of the data from WHI and HERS to perimenopausal women is not possible because the greater mean age of women involved in both studies and the inclusion of only women with coronary disease in HERS; however many women may prefer not to use or continue with HRT in the light of this evidence (Bestul 2004;Haas 2004). Therapies purported to reduce such symptoms need to be assessed in blinded trials against a placebo or standard therapy, as placebo effect is very high. [Surgical management of Perthes disease] Perthes disease is defined as an 'osteochondrosis that affects the capital epiphysis of the femoral head' (Herring 1996). The condition has been recognised since 1910 when it was independently described by Legg in Boston (Legg 1910), Calve in France (Calve 1910) and Perthes in Germany (Perthes 1910). The disease remains elusive in that while a great deal of literature has been written on the topic over the years, the field of research is complicated by the wide diversity of clinical course, treatment, and subsequent outcome. Disagreement persists amongst authors and the medical community regarding aetiology, classification and prognosis increasing the difficulty of ascertaining the true nature of the disease.Perthes disease occurs predominantly in boys (ratio 4‐5:1) aged between 4‐8 years, although it can occur anytime between 2‐12 years (Roy 1999). Bilateral involvement occurs in approximately 15% of cases and is usually asymmetric (Hubbard 1995). There have been occasional reports of recurrent disease (Stevens 2001).Incidence varies from area to area.Hall 1983reported the highest incidence at 15.6 per 100 000 in Liverpool between 1976‐81. Sweden has a reported incidence of 8.5 per 100 000 (Moberg 1992) whereas the incidence among the black population in the eastern cape region of South Africa has been cited as 0.5 per 100 000 (Purry 1982). The incidence in Northern Ireland has recently been cited at 11.6 per 100 000 (Kealey 2000).The management of Perthes disease is not straightforward. The choice of technique and its effectiveness remains controversial, and consequently there is wide variation in current clinical practice, treatment often being directed by individual orthopaedic surgeon opinion (Gigante 2002). The main principles of treatment are load relief and containment (maximally encasing the femoral head within the acetabulum), which can be achieved using various methods. Age at onset of symptoms is a key prognostic factor in the disease process with those children younger than 7‐8 years at onset generally having a favourable natural history (Ismail 1998), although this is not always the case. These children are normally treated by conservative measures such as bed rest, traction, plaster casts placing the hips in abduction, and splinting.Those who develop the condition after 7‐8 years of age tend to have a less satisfactory result (Yasuda 1996), and may require more active intervention. Reasons for the older child having a gloomier prognosis include, less remaining time for growth and remodeling at the hip joint (Mazda 1999), decreased elasticity of the acetabulum (Bellyei 1988), an increased likelihood of femoral head collapse in the larger and consequently heavier child, and the probability that a larger head may take longer to revascularize.Over time many attempts to surgically treat Perthes disease have been made however the effectiveness of many of these procedures remains questionable. Many studies have used a mixed selection of Perthes disease patients with varying ages at onset of disease, and with varying levels of disease severity. Often outcomes following different treatments to small numbers of patients are analysed, without any control groups for comparison.The three techniques that are predominantly used to surgically manage this condition are femoral osteotomy, pelvic osteotomy and lateral shelf augmentation procedure.Femoral and pelvic osteotomies have been used extensively in Perthes disease since the 1960's to improve containment by redirecting either the femoral head or the acetabulum. Lateral shelf arthroplasty is often used as a salvage operation for Perthes disease increasing the capacity of the acetabulum after the outcome of the hip joint is known, although it can also be used as a primary containment treatment.Undoubtedly, the ideal primary research for this purpose would consist of large, fully blinded randomised controlled trials (RCT) incorporating appropriate subgroup analysis (McKee 1999). It would not be feasible however to conduct a blinded trial of surgery as it would be unethical to submit children to a sham procedure which would have all the risks associated with surgery yet with no discernable benefits to the child. Consequently the majority of studies in this area are historically controlled trials, conservatively controlled trials or uncontrolled observational studies. Non randomised studies can lead to bias with the actual treatment effect of intervention being thought to be larger than in studies using random allocation (Chalmers 1977,Kunz 1995,Egger 2000). Recently several trials have been published that find no significant over‐estimation in treatment effect in well designed observational studies as compared to RCT's (Benson 2000,Concato 2000), although this view would be held very much in the minority. Deeks and colleagues (Deeks 2000), after studying the biases associated with non randomised controlled designs, predicted that 'studies included in systematic reviews of non‐randomised evaluations of healthcare interventions would often be conflicting, and that in many situations the overall results of these reviews may be misleading'. This acknowledged, in an area where there are few if any randomised‐controlled studies, the reviewer must consider whatever study designs are available (CRD report No4), and through stringent quality assessment, glean what, if any supporting evidence for intervention exists. The fact that there are some areas of healthcare in which there are few randomised controlled trials has been recognised by the Cochrane Collaboration who have established a Non‐Randomised Studies Methods Group (NRSMG) who are currently developing guidelines for systematic reviews falling into this category (Clarke 2001).As there are no existing systematic reviews on the surgical management of Perthes disease, and due to the wide variation in current clinical practice, it was felt that a systematic appraisal of the available evidence was warranted.
